The Golden Temple of Dambulla is the largest and best-preserved cave-temple complex in Sri Lanka, comprising five sanctuaries with numerous statues, murals, and paintings. Visitors should dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered), remove their shoes, and be respectful of the sacred site by not posing disrespectfully with a Buddha statue. No flash photography permitted inside. There were shaming photos posted of foreigners posing inappropriately inside the cave.

There are few facilities in the world that have been operating continuously for two millennia.  These are usually buildings that have been rebuilt many times, where the only constant is just the location. Dambulla is a rare example of a continuously functioning Buddhist temple. From the third century BC to the present day! Of course, even here, most of the artifacts do not have the back of the 22nd century. Frescoes, for example, from the 17th century. However, we know for sure that Buddhists came here, it was into these caves and looked at these walls. It all started at the end of the 2nd century BC.  When King Valagambahu fled here from Anuradhapura, he lived in this cave for 14 years while gathering an army to regain his throne. The first painting of the walls and vaults is the king's gratitude for the help. Over the following centuries, Sinhalese kings came here and continued to make gifts and decorate the cave temple. Eventually, there was so much gold in the temple that it was named Ranagiri, from Sinhalese "Golden Rock". To get to the Cave Temple, it is necessary to repeat the path of the pilgrims and climb the stone steps, starting from the giant 30-meter statue of the seated Buddha. This Buddha is a new model, don't waste your time on him. An important point is that tickets are sold at the bottom, but they are checked only at the top, so you can go up without tickets and have to go down again, because tickets are not sold at the top of the caves! The temple consists of 5 caves, each of which is unique in its own way. In total, there are about 150 Buddha statues inside. The first cave is called Devaraja lena (lena means "cave" in Sinhalese) or "Cave of the Divine King". This is the oldest cave, and the Buddha statues found in it date back to the 4th century AD. It houses a well-preserved 14-meter reclining Buddha statue, made in the tradition of Anuradhapura sculpture. The Buddha's face is expressionless, he is entering nirvana. Despite the abundance of Buddhas, the cave is dedicated to Vishnu, whose statue is located in the depths of the cave. This statue has a whole story. Having been stolen from the temple by the Portuguese, she sailed to Trincomalee after a shipwreck in the Indian Ocean and was solemnly placed in the temple as a miracle of return. The second and largest cave is called Maharaja Lena ("Cave of the Great Kings"). The cave is named after two kings, whose statues are located in the caves of Valagamba and Nishankamala. One third of all the Buddhas of Dambulla are here: 16 of them are sitting, 40 are standing. There are 150 Buddha images in the cave, along with frescoes. The main image of the Buddha is located under the arch (Makara Torana) and was previously decorated with gold plates, some of which have been preserved in some places. As in the previous cave, you can see the god Vishnu and, in addition, the god Saman. The water dripping from the ceiling is considered sacred and it is collected in a special vessel. In the third, Maha Alut Viharaya, there was a warehouse before the XVIII century, which was converted into a temple by order of Prince Rajasinghe II, whose statue commemorates this. There are also a huge number of Buddhas in this cave: in addition to the 9-meter reclining Buddha, 14 more Buddhas are sitting in the lotus position, and 42 are standing. The number of Buddhas on the frescoes is incalculable - under a thousand.  The other two caves are less interesting. In the fourth cave, the frescoes were executed later in the 19th century, and in the fifth, the symbiosis of the Buddha with a collection of Hindu gods.

The theme of cave temples for me is a godless terra incognita. And if I understand at least a little about above-ground religious buildings, then underground and other cave buildings are just a complete novice. Preparing for a trip to Sri Lanka and monitoring the information about the local must-sees, I simply could not pass by such an interesting place as the Dambulla cave temple. It is for this reason that it was immediately included in my travel itinerary. As for Dambulla itself: it is a relatively small city in Central province of Sri Lanka in the north of Matale district. From the capital - Colombo - only about one and a half hundred miles. Before starting to get acquainted with the temple, let’s immediately “agree on the shore”: the Dambulla cave Temple and the Dambulla Golden Temple are two different objects, although they are located side by side. I believe that by mistake or simple ignorance, these two attractions are often called one object. But it should be remembered that the Golden Temple is a remake, created in 2000. But the Cave Temple, which is the object of my humble post, is the thousand-year past of Ceylon, its sacred history... Both temples are located on a cliff overlooking the surrounding plains. What's funny is that the English-speaking Wikipedia says that the temple complex consists of several caves located at an altitude of 350 meters, while the Russian-speaking “partner” claims that the cave temple complex rises 160 meters above the surrounding plains. Without knowing the theme of cave temples, it will be quite difficult to perceive the Dambulla cave Temple as a religious building: there is no narthex, naos, transept, apse, side naves and chapels familiar to Catholics, as well as for Orthodox Christians - a porch, narthex, side chapels, altar, pulpit , mountainous place, salt, choir... Just CAVES... In reality - a cavity of natural origin, located in the upper part of the earth's crust, connected to the surface by one or more entrance holes. True, in Dambulla there is not just one cave, but as many as FIVE (these are the so-called main ones) plus, as they say, another two and a half dozen rock cells. Buddhist monks have been meditating in these very cells since time immemorial. And in these very caves there are Buddhas... Tens, hundreds of Buddhas!!! Lying, sitting, standing... It is in Dambulla, if you have enough patience, that you can see 153 statues of Buddha, 3 statues of the kings of Sri Lanka, 4 statues of gods and goddesses (which you can read in more detail in many guidebooks). For me, it just went off scale. And if the first, fifth, tenth Buddha is perceived with reverent awe, then after the second ten - just like another cult figure frozen in stone. But everything I saw was unusual, original, creative. And although the emotions from what I saw, alas, did not exceed what was expected, I still did not regret for a second that I had come to Dambulla. At least once in your life, you definitely need to see this. I recommend!!!

(How many times does this need to be said?)  And yes, there is a monk who offers to tie a white cotton thread around your right wrist and pray over it to bring you good life.  It is up to you to decide if you want this.   If you do, it is customary to leave a small donation.

One of few things to see in Dimbulla. The place is a temple with a small yard in front of it. As with just looking at the temple form the yard, the place is free of entrance. You will probably take a picture of the temple, and that's it. There is a lot of monkeys all around the place, and quite aggressive ones. Combined with a lot of food stands that you find on your way to the place down from the hill with Cave Temple, holding a paper corn with mango is a hazard. Either eat your food quickly, or don't buy it at all.

One of few things that can be seen in Dimbulla. The place is unique and I think it's worth of visiting. The tickets are bought at the ticket office under the hill. The place is totally not suitable for wheelchairs or people with any joint problems, as you need to walk a lot of stairs. It was raining at the time when I was visiting the place. This itself is not a problem, it was not even cold, but count with the fact, that you will be walking through water puddles and make your feet especially dirty. I would see it as a part of the experience. What looked like a scam to me was the place where you needed to leave the shoes before entering the place. That place was paid and at the same time, there were signs everywhere that you can't put your shoes e.g. to your backpack. Which I don't see any other reason for than just to get some extra money out of people. The price for keeping your shoes at shoe parking place is not defined and you can give to the guy working there as much as you consider as a reasonable price. I recommend to take some clothes that cover the knees. Otherwise you need to borrow and pay for some scarf to put around your waist to cover the knees.

Located in central Sri Lanka, about 2.5 hours from the port, are the UNESCO Caves of Dambulla.  Access requires walking up about 400 steep steps or use of a flat pathway, removal of shoes since this is an active temple complex and covering of shoulders and knees.  Rental of a leg covering is available for one dollar.  The caves that date back to the first century BC, contain dozens of Buddha statues and wall and ceiling murals.  Near the entrance are many souvenir booths where you can pick up a magnet, local garment or small statue of Buddha.  Definitely worth a visit.  Photography is allowed without restriction.

It's only 364 steps up, but can be an effort if you're like me, and not good with steps. But, oh!! So worth it!! So take your time, and keep going. Our guide gave us history of the place as we went into each cave. The temples are of all different ages, and it was good to get some knowledge about it. If you don't have a guide (though I recommend one) it's still worth it, for the beauty and amazement of what was achieved. *To others- stop whining about having to pay to rent a shoulder/leg cover. Just do your research before you go, or put up with it. Or don't enter.

Beautiful cave temples with many Buddha statues. We originally did have a guide but after the first temple did go back and ask for one as there is so much to learn about the caves and Buddha hand positions.
Must visit Locations and make sure you have sholder covered Tshirt or top and something long below the knee for the bottom. Restpect the cukture and tradistion of this beautiful place,
We were there in August 2022. At that time there were very few foreign tourists so we could visit everything in peace. A magical place worth recommending
Coming down from the cave temple, you will see the biggest Buddha statue from the different angles, very impressive.

What a way to ruin what is quite an impressive temple. First you buy your ticket, walk up some steps, get fleeced by two old ladies for some flowers. Next take your shoes off, fleeced for storing them in 'safe place'. Next need a sarong, fleeced for the hire of it. Next an old man gives some kind of blessing, fleeced for a 'donation'. I gave 100 rupees for his 20 seconds of work, to which he rolled his eyes in disappointment. Next get hounded to buy random souvenirs. All in all you better be extremely hard faced or have lots of surplus money to come here.. what a way to ruin the experience. Not authentic at all, a complete tourist trap. Don't bother.
Large Buddhist temple and surrounding buildings and ground. There are unique Sri Lankan styled architecture and paintings. Make sure when you enter shoulders and knees are covered.

We visited Dambula cave temple in our road trip in Sri Lanka. We both were speechless by the beauty and the uniqueness of the temple. Beautiful Buddha statues that are made out of natural rock, painted in gold and beautiful colors. The caves are covered by beautiful paintings. Our tour guide gave us lots of knowledge about this temple and they truly fascinate us. Worth of visiting. A must of visiting this temple.
Huge, beautiful and unique. You must visit. Very imposing Buddha on the top this statue is really impressive and magnificent.

Very imposing Buddha on top of this temple, shining bright in the sun, you can access the top floor via the steps to the right of the temple, remember to remove you shoes before walking around the top and beware the floor gets blisteringly hot on your feet!!

After a long walk up many steps to the cave temple, there seemed to be a lot of people trying to take your money, shoe stall I understand but a guide (not needed) sarong for hire and lots of other stuff from postcards to carvings. The views from the top are quite impressive

If you're into temples and history, I would recommend checking this place out. Be prepared though, you need to be covered (at least a t-shirt and long skirt/shorts - past the knees). There's also lots of walking up stairs to reach the temple. Once at the top, you need to remove your shoes while walking through the temple grounds , so wear sneakers or have socks prepared. My sister and I luckily both had a cover up on hand and were wearing sneakers. They do sell cover ups, shirts and souvenirs on the way up. Our driver was our tour guide and explained everything. It isn't necessary but it adds to the experience. Oh and beware of the monkeys. Wild monkeys roam about and if you're holding flowers or food in your hand, or even on your backpack, they will try to snatch it from you. Don't forget to look back as you are walking up the stairs to the temple as the views are gorgeous.
Remarkable cave and architecture, however not many signs in how to access the place and only 5 small caves which won’t take you more then 10 minutes to see all of them

The Golden Temple is the oldest and the most well preserved rock temple monastery in Sri Lanka, and has been standing for 22 centuries as of now. Whilst the climb to the rock cave temple would be strenuous be it on the bear rock or with the use of the steps, once you reach the top you would accept it was worth the climb, for someone who appreciates ancient architecture, and for the breath taking view of the surrounding. The temple caves do have many of the traditional Buddha statues, and ancient art that make a person go awe, and the wonder of the water vessel where a drops of water that fill the pot every few seconds placed in one of the caves is a must see. Ideally recommends to climb the rock during the early hours of the morning as this is the best time to climb.

The caves are painted in such a beautiful and detailled way that the rocky ceiling seems to be covered by a silk cloth. The Buddha statues are beautiful too and the visit is worth the not cheap price required for the ticket and the 1,250 steps to the top. Be careful not to get to the entrance on the main road at “Golden Temple”, because the ticket office is on the other side of the moutain, so you will have to go up, get down and go up again.
The rockcaves are stunning. One of the highlights on our trip. Comparable to Ellora and Ajanta. Don't miss them!

An interesting combination of More modern "gold and akward" architecture with late colonial cave facade buildings and more ancient cave architecture. Mix it with a nice walk and great views and you have a nice day in Damnbulla. Recommend to go early or in the evening to skip the heat waves. Do not rush on the grounds, take the time to walk around (altough watch out for the monkeys). Highly recommend to take a walk from the cashier and stop over for the pictures.
Golden temple of Dambulla is world heritage site. This is a Buddhist shrine.The caves of this temple has beautiful drawings & Buddha statues.
We have seen innumerable caves in India. Hence this cannot be in the MUST list unless you haven't been to a Buddhist cave in your life.
It was very quiet considering the times, lovely to have the place to ourselves. I didn't see a lot of information around the place in English, I could be mistaken.

Beautiful and quiet temple. There was a information book in front of temple, he only said “take one” I said “Thank you” he said “250” so i put it back. Paid Rs1500 (Local free)+ shoes counter Rs 20 or 50 forgot(there is a sign that Do not put your shoes in your bag, must keep in the shoes counter+ Donation.
This is a world heritage site declared by UNESCO in 1991. This cave temple was established in the 2nd century BC and developed & renovated by various kings of Sri Lanka.

The authentic cave temple was one of a kind place to visit. The buddha statues surrounded by the rock, the surprising water drop from the top of the rock and the beautiful surrounding was eye catching.

We entered via the Kings Way which is a series of stairs which are not onerous, if you are reasonably fit. Great site to see painted frescos amazingly painted on uneven rock. There were five caves open at the time of our visit and all had something of interest to see. If you are not in a rush then try to make time to visit here.
Peaceful place. On a hill top and quite a large statue of Lord Buddha. There is a cave temple at the top of the hill.

World heritage site in Dambulla city symbolizes the great Buddhist culture in ancient Sri Lanka. This beautiful cave with buddha statues and drawings is a great place to visit. There is a modern temple and a huge statue of lord buddha at the entrance as well.
A historical and cultural site with breathtaking views. Most recommended and easiest climb to the Rock Temple is through the side of the Golden Temple...

Tourist site to see the Rock Caves and access to the Golden Temple. It is  very large site with many steps, so not wheel chair friendly. Leave adequate time to get around. If you decide to walk to the Golden Temple, walk back the way you came otherwise it's a very long walk back via the main road and not very clearly sign posted. The caves are very peaceful and impressive with lots of carvings inside each cave. When we went they were restoring some of the statues so there was some scaffolding in the way. There were lots of monkeys on the walk to the Golden Temple who are very curious and follow you about but very tame. Before entering the rock temple there is a separate locals and foreigners shoe store which you have to pay for and the visitors prices are considerably more. It does get hot & takes time so take plenty of water with you, Worth the visit if you are in or passing Dambulla.

We visited the Dambulla Caves with our driver guide - absolutely recommend a guide to find out all about the area and the different temples here. Just off the main road (you can't miss it!) - quite a few steps to the top but the views are lovely on the way! You will need to take your shoes off to go into the temple area - take socks and the ground can be very hot! No shorts and cover your shoulders as with all temples. Beautiful but very busy - lots of schools trips too! But a wonderful experience - not to be missed.

This is an interesting temple.   Several separate caves with amazing Buddha's and painting.  It was very helpful having our excellent guide Lucky to explain the history around the paintings and the eras that they are from.  That was helpful, otherwise it would be a "very good" rating as we wouldn't have understood what things were.

You'll see this giant Buddha statue from the main road in Dambulla. The building by the road with the giant Buddha on top is mainly a Bhuddism museum, but serves as a good landmark for the start of the steps that will take you up to the cave temple at the top of the hill which is what most people are looking for.

This is a small temple complex at the top of a hill accessed from the main road in  Dambulla town. Easy to find right by the giant Golden Buddha statue. It is a moderately steep climb from the Golden Buddha statue up the steps to the caves, especially in the daytime heat so take your time. You have to leave you shoes at the entrance so take some socks with you as the stone floor in the courtyard can be very hot underfoot. There are five caves which you can enter via a small temple facade which is built into the rock face. The caves contain a lot of Buddha statues, some standing and some giant ones lying down. Something else to note - be sure to take a look at the ornately painted cave ceilings. The monks will occasionally shut the caves for prayer but it's only for about 15 minutes so not a problem. Tip - if you're driving or being driven, try to find the other entrance a little further into town, not by the Golden Buddha as this way in takes you past the ticket office. Otherwise you'll climb all the way up to the entrance from the Golden Buddha, and then have to climb down about 100 steps to buy your ticket, then climb back up again to get back to the entrance.

Best done with a guide to tell you all about the history and explain what you are seeing.  All-in-all very impressive.  Practical notes: it is a long climb up many stone steps to get there, so take plenty of water and wear good shoes.  For the temples, ladies must cover their shoulders and legs, and everyone must take off their shoes - take a pair of socks with you if not already wearing them, as some of the pavings are outdoors and red hot!
Wonderful temple carved high in the rocks.  A succession of rooms, some very grand indeed and retaining the colours and gold making an awesome sight.

we only had a few minutes to see just beyond the golden stupa at the front gate.. We realise just how many stairs it would take to climb to the painted caves.for sure it will take  few minutes to climb to the top. So we didn't get time for this  journey .. Hope I will visit this place in future

There is a beautiful buddha Statue and Buddhist temple in this place.Better for preparing Hot and Sunny weather before visiting. The statue was very big and beautiful. and there is a Museum inside they charging 20 sri lankan rupees for Local travelers and not sure about the price for foreigners. But there is nothing special for watch inside the Museum. Waste of time.

Very beautiful place. There is a beautiful ancient Buddhist temple top of the Mountain. I’ve seen lot of Buddhist statues builded by ancient Sri lankans. there are lot of monkeys around here. Very sunny. Better to take Sun Glass and sun protection cream when traveling.

The temples have an incredible history and are so impressive to see! I have never seen so many Buddhas! And they are all maintained very well! It is impressive to see how much effort was put into this temple and learn about some of the history of buddhism in Sri Lanka.

If u drive from Colombo it take 3 hrs 45 min to reach dambulla town.it s in 5 minutes away from Dambulla city , u hv to come through Colombo Trincomalee road . Best time to visit s early morning. Before 9 am, because these days really hot weather In outside. royal cave temple built in before 1 st Centuries. U hv to climb steps to reach 5 caves. Well maintained foot path & steps. Bring water bottle & cap , sunglasses also..  major attraction s are spread over 5 caves .which contains statues & paintings . There are 153 - gautama buddha statues. 3 statues of Sri Lankan Kings, paintings about the lord buddha & his life. Never be missed to visit dambulla royal cave temple.
Very hot day and some struggled to make it up the steps. Very impressive statues and frescoes worth the climb

It is a bit of a climb up to the cave temple area but this is well worth the effort that is required. The three caves are different as are the many statues that they contain. On the way back down use the larger path and visit the "modern" temple at the foot of the hill.Sorry,  im not sure of the distance to walk back to the start point as we were dropped off there and picked up at the "modern" temple.

It is also known as Golden Temple of Dambulla with impressive collections of Buddha statues and wall paintings since 1st century and the wall was repainted since 18th century in Kandy Kingdom. Entrance fee of LKR1,500 per person and LKR25 for shoe storage. Proper attire is a must and security check before entry to the temple. One of the must visit cultural site in Sri Lanka with great representation of the Cave Temple culture for Buddhism/ Hinduism where is the most well-preserved cave temple in Sri Lanka.

Interesting facts in history on this place. Really unbelievable the work done at the time by hand tools only. Today it would be a problem to get a job such as this done with all modern equipment available. The Huge Buddha figures are really spectacular. Bit of a climb but not really hard. The usual no shoes and covered knees that applies in most of these temples.
I did this the day after I did sigireya fortress, there are 5 caves, the largest ones have the most amazing statues of Buddha. Well worth a visit.

This is also one of the UNESCO World Heritage Site in Sri Lanka within the Cultural Triangle in Sri Lanka - Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa & Kandy (including Sigiriya & Dambulla within the triangle). It is also called the Dambulla Cave Temple. Cave temple was one of the Buddhist culture since Anuradhapura Kingdom in 1st century having to build temple in a cave. This cave temple is the most preserved and well-maintained cave temple in Sri Lanka. Entrance fee of LKR1,500 per person and walk-up staircase less than 30 mins after the ticketing office. The mountain view while climbing the staircase are stunning with many frangipanni trees along the way till reaching the entrance of cave temple. Appropriate attire is required and no shoes  are allowed in the cave temple. There is a shoe storage service charged at LKR25 per pair of shoes. Security check at the main gate prior entry to the temple. The exterior of the cave temple is a pure white facade of temple with a Bodhi tree in front of the temple. Once stepping into the cave temple, it gives an overwhelming effect with the numerous Buddha statues with the wall paintings of the entire cave surface and interior of the temple. There are 5 caves with total more than 150 statues including Buddha figures, Vishnu God & Goddess, Ganesha (Hindu God with elephant head) and a few statues of the Great Kings. The murals/ wall paintings was restored by the Kandy Kingdom in 18th century, which basically are the depiction of Buddha’s life and Buddha images. After the visit, we walked down the staircase connecting to the Golden Temple & Museum. We were practically blown away by the magnificent wall paintings inside the temple and took lots of photos. Must visit for cultural and history buff!!!

Nice temple located on the mountain. If you go there make sure you enter there where you buy the tickets, otherwise you need to go down again. Temple itself is very nice, different rooms with drawings and statues of Buddha

A impressive temple the golden temple very nice to see . We went for a good clim to go up to see the cave temple we really enjoyed she views going up but 1500 r a person is in our eyes to much over priced we have seen  cave temples With no entrance price just go up for the view

Very beautiful Buddha statues of many sizes, colours and shapes, exquisitely painted walls and ceilings, in five caves. Reaching these requires some serious climbing (on decent stairs and with beautiful views). Don't forget to buy the ticket before going up. Compulsory fee for leaving shoes (very small) once at the top. The place itself is beautiful,  and the caves are spectacular. Start at the far end (number five) and then move to the other caves. This way each cave is more beautiful and some are really spectular. This was,  for us, one of the most special places and beautifiul Buddha statues of the country (and we have seen many such places). Recommended!

This is a must for visitors touring Sri Lankan , the are 5 temples all separate and in caves , which once inside are breathtaking with the statues they present, the temple is very reasonable admittance price just be aware there are many steps to walk up to get the the entrance so better visited when cooler in the morning or later in the afternoon
Between Kurunegala and Habarana , u can find this age old , buddhist cave temple with so many  artistic statues of Lord Buddha . Have to climb bit of a distance but worth the effort .

We arrived at prayer time, so had to wait 45 mins before we could enter. But we got our breathe back after the climb up. There are 5 caves with numerous Buddha states in varying sizes and positions. Very moving experience and some amazing engineering to build the temples. Be aware of the monkeys outside, and as ever no shoes for the entirety of the palace and dress respectively (long sleeves and below knees)

After you've been in Sri Lanka a while, you start to wonder why it is that all the interesting places are up steep flights of stairs! This is another place that you have to climb a lot of steps to get to - I forgot to count them, but there are lots - and there's very little shade. So first up - no disabled access. Once you're at the top, you can stop for a rest, while being entertained by some costumed dancers. Interesting, but not what we came for. The caves appear more like little houses, with ornate fronts built on to the openings. Inside, there are lots of statues and pictures of Buddha. I new LOTS - big ones, little ones, lying down, standing up, sitting down - you get the picture. Hundreds of them, all shapes and sizes. Every now and then you get a picture of something else, but generally speaking, it's floor to ceiling Buddha. And on the ceiling as well.  The best one is a huge recumbent Buddha in a cave that must have been carved out around him - he only just fits. Fantastic colours, and all in remarkable condition. Like a lot of things in this country, this place gets busy, so if you want to take clear photos without including lots of tourists, get there early.

A lot of steps some very irregular is height to reach the temple. There are 5 temples cut into the hillside rock and each one has many statues and wonderful roof paintings. Well worth the walk to the top.
We can see different postures of Lord Buddha seating, lying, Sleeping, Dhayan Mudra. Magnificent very old cave with carving and paintings  with natural colours

This place blew my husband away....and that isn't easy to do! 5 amzing caves filled with 'treasures' from enormous recling buddhas, resting buddha and sitting buddhas. Some caves have been beautifully restored, whilst others are as they originally were - a little faded but equally if not more amazing. Surprisingly it was very hot inside the caves, so bear that in mind and bring plenty of water. There are also a great number of steps to climb to get to the caves, so best to do early in the day if possible before it gets too hot! A must see if in the Dambulla area.

The step climb offers some quick and intense exercise before the mind-blowing experience. Even the most seasoned traveler is likely to be wowed here! The 153 Buddhas in the five caves, were built over more than two millennia, from 100 BCE. The statues are as beautiful as they are impressive, the heat is scorching, and there is obviously no a/c. Sweating is part of the experience! The temple is an intensely holy site so be prepared to walk barefooted on some very hot stone tiles. Shoes have to be left behind at the entrance, so drop the idea of showing off your new Gucci sneakers! The hill is crowded with monkeys, so watch out for your belongings, and enjoy the beautiful view from the top!
a fairly steep walk up to these stunning cave temples but worth it, they are stunning, highly recommend

One the world heritage sites in Sri Lanka, the largest and best- preserved cave temple complex with its fife sanctuaries, has been a pilgrimage site for 22 centuries. A world Heritage Centre. There are a total of 153 Buddha statues, three statues of Sri Lankan kings and four statues of gods and goddesses. The later include Vishnu and Ganesha. Prehistoric Sri Lankans would have lived in these cave complexes before the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka as there are burial sites with human skeletons about 2700 years old in this area.

We had to climb up steps to this temple so can take a while, my friend had to keep stopping as she has problems with her lungs so be aware! Take plenty of water for the journey up and admire the views. Once up the top you leave your shoes at the shoe rack for a couple of pence. Inside you will see amazing paintings and more. Worth a visit if you in the vicinity.
It’s worth a visit if your in the area, the views above are lovely so don’t forget your camera and your water

First note that this is a sacred place and so dress accordingly, covering shoulders and knees. This is also a very confusing place to find the entrance to on your own (without a guide). When you approach the area, you are first drawn to the gigantic golden Buddha, temple, and Buddhist museum right on the road. It would appear that you walk up to the Dambulla Cave Temples from there, but you in fact do not. There are officials in uniforms who tell you “get the ticket at the top”, but I’d already heard that this was not the case. So, we asked around and found out that there is a rear entrance and THAT is where the ticket office is. So, you need to drive past the shiny temple and past the Museum of Wall Painting and take your next right and then uphill about .5km. It is on Google Maps as “Dambulla Cave New Car Park” Very confusing, but if you walk up the other way and get to the top without a ticket, then you will have to walk down the back stairs to get the ticket and back up before they’ll let you in! Crazy but true. So, once you find the ticket counter and avoid getting mauled by the very aggressive monkeys there, you will climb a rather large number of stairs. Not impossible, but in the heat it can be sweaty and tiring. Go slowly and drink water. Then, you must give your shoes to the shoe man (25 rupees a pair) and then give your tickets to the ticket takers. There are five caves and they are simply delightful and a beauty to behold. Each one is a little different and I recommend finding some literature to read as you go so you know what you are looking at. There are brochures available at the top for 250 rupees. You can then either walk down the way you came up (the back) or go down the golden temple route (I recommend this). Again, avoid the aggressive monkeys who await unsuspecting people eating snacks on their way down. Many hawkers selling drinks, fruits, and souvenirs. Highly recommend despite the crazy entrance situation and lack of information or signage anywhere.
Soaked in history and art, a place that so much to offer for both art lovers and history buff’s. Like all public places in SriLanka comes with a price for foreigners

The temple itself is a small place, of course the sculptures and paintings are impressive and beautiful. So it might be a short but interesting visit. The rest of the time you can enjoy walking around, there is a great view and many monkeys on the way. Also on the route is the Golden Temple, so it is a 2x1. It is advisable to enter by the opposite entrance to the Golden Temple, since there is the ticket office. Otherwise it is a long way back. Also as always, go early, so it will be quieter and free of crowds.
Another one if many sites worthwhile if you are in the area. We were staying a few km’s away. An interesting site.
Quite a climb up to this place but well worth it. Temples carved out of the rock, very ornately decorated. Visit late afternoon for spectacular views of the sunset.

Nice place to visit. The ticket office is far away from the main road so you should first climb up (or take a tuktuk) via the road because after that you have to walk up the stairs from ticket office to the temple. After the visit in temple go down the other steps to the golden temple near the main road. Lots of cute monkeys outside the temple.

Beautiful frescoes cover the walls of the temple and the statues are impressive as well. As a bonus the views from the entrance are wonderful. Totally worth it. You can walk down the hill on the opposite side to end at the Golden Temple.

there is a bit of a trek to these five temples. Once you reach the top,you keep your shoes at the shoe rack place.they charge 25 LKR per person for one pair of shoe to keep. once you enter the sanctum,it is astonishing. Never i have seen so many statues of Lord Buddha at one place.Also the paintings on the wall and the roof are equally spell binding. the place is well maintained too. it is absolutely bliss ful experience.

Since I’m in Dambulla,so i decide to visit this place since this temple is quite famous.But turns out to be worst decision ever! After i reach the security check in front of the temple,they i ask me to take off my hijab which i would not do it just because i want to visit the temple Plus,entrance fee for 1500 is quite expensive and there is nothing special with this temple.I pay for nothing!

A bit of a climb to reach the caves, but this is by steps with terrace areas so you can rest easily every so often, also a wall you can use as a hand rail or seat should you feel the need. The views of the surrounding area are stunning on the way up and at the top. There are about 5 caves to view, each elaborately decorated with numerous buddhas , statues and paintings
Enjoyed the experience, worth it! Not expensive. 5 temples each very similar. Good piece of history.
We had a tour guide for our holiday, but he arranged a guide on site to give us a more in-depth tour of the Golden Temple. It was a very informative trip and most appreciated.

Be sure to buy a ticket where the steps (250 of them) to the temple begin. Decent toilets by car park. The 2100+ year old temple consists of 5 caves that have been expanded, and include ancient wall and ceiling paintings, as well as many Buddha statues, some of which have been carved out of the living rock. Popular with tourists (gets crowded) this temple is seen as possessing miraculous powers.
Such interesting history! A large range Buddha’s in a number of caves and differing history and time lines.

We visited the place on 31st January 2020. It is required to climb around 15minutes to reach the cave temple from parking area. Ticket price is 1500LKR. On the top view is great with gentle and soothing breeze. Inside the cave there are many resembles of Buddha and also cave paintings of Buddha. It has good historical aapects. But to be honest i have seen many Buddha temples, its unique that its inside the cave but not much different about anything else. U need to remove your shoes before entering and to secure u have to pay 25 LKR. Then u can take different way to get down it will take u to Golden temple which has a big golden buddha statue with a museum not different than other buddha temples. I would recommend it to people visiting dambulla to give a try if u have enough time and for the view upstairs.
Nice upstairs walk to the temple.. on the hill is lot of monkeys. I expect little bit bigger temple few rooms with the same statues... but its interrested.
Honestly I was expecting more A little climb but nothing crazy! Monkeys where the best part It’s pretty amazing in the caves the carvings.

Call me a humbug but I think the Temples are overrated. There is quite a hike up a few hundred steps & the views are spectacular. Once at the top you give over your shoes then walk around 100m to & around the 5 temples on scorching hot stone floors. I don’t regret the climb or the entry cost but for the scenery not the Temples. Watch out for the many monkeys all over the mountain.

World Heritage site. Wonderful Buddhist temples ranging in date from 2100 to 200 years old. Very steep climb to get there, well over 1000 steps and can be very uneven and worn in places. The views from the temple are worth the climb alone. At the top you are required to remove your footwear and cover your shoulders and legs. Sarongs can be hired for this purpose. A guide will cost you 750 Rupees (about £3.50) plus tips. Amazing carvings and decoration and is worth the climb. Take your time on the climb up, it's very warm and very humid. Photography is allowed both inside and outside the Temples. Watch out for the monkeys on the way up and down, if you have any food in your hand, they will try and grab it. Just one note of warning, If you are staying in a hotel on the coast South of Colombo, it takes over 4 hrs to reach the Temple on a private trip (By car) it will take longer in a coach. It doesn't look that far on the map!!!
A really unique set of ancient rock temples, all in still an amazingly good shape. The small climb up there is easy & the reward is huge ! You will be very impressed with these temples !

The Dambulla caves and temples are one of the best things to see in this part of Sri Lanka.  It's a bit of a climb up to get to them (though nothing like Sigiriya Rock), but well worth it.  You will need to cover your legs and shoulders to go in, but you can rent appropriate costume at a modest cost from an establishment near the main entrance.  The caves themselves and the images inside of the Buddha, elephants and many other things are stunning.  I found the whole experience quite moving.  If you can, it's a good idea to arrive early in the morning before the crowds and the heat.

A worthy World Heritage Site, the cave temples have that wow factor after you have made the steep climb. There is a fascinating story of King Vattagamini Abhaya losing his throne in 103 BC, seeking refuge in the area of the caves. Able to secure the crown again fourteen years later, the king constructed temples here in gratification. The caves are rather warm as caves go but worth the effort. Some caves afford better lighting. Secondly, you'll see monkeys that are actually adorable!  I am not a monkey fan, but these were very cute.  They did not bother you at all. Third, leave your shoes and enter the complex.  There are five caves.  We found the second the most spectacular, but they are all adorned with reclining buddhas, interesting statues, and amazing murals on the ceilings.  Really mind-blowing and one of the highlights of our trip to Sri Lanka. Fit the Dambulla Caves into your itinerary and enjoy!

Dambulla is a world heritage site declared by UNESCO in 1991. The rock towers 160 m over the surrounding plains. This complex of caves is one of the most impressive Buddhist temples in the world with it’s great number of Buddha statues and more than 23000 sq. ft. of paintings.The Buddha images and paintings belongs to 17th & 18th centuries but a part of paintings belongs to 5th century which can be seen outside between 3rd & 4th caves. There are 161 Buddha statues within whole temple. The cave is divided into five caves by inserting dividing walls in single overhang. 1. Devaraja Lena -15 meters long painted stone image of reclining Buddha. 2. Maharaja Lena- Most spectacular cave out of five because it has largest number of sculptures. 3. Maha Aluth Vihara 4. Pacchima Vihara- 27 feet high at entrance. 5. Devana Aluth Vihara- 10 meter Buddha. There is no discount for residents of SAARC. Carry enough water, climb slowly, wear full pants or wrap sarong, cover shoulders. Shoes rack guy charges Rs. 25 per pair so carry change.

On your way to Sigiriya, it is worth stopping over at Dambulla to catch a glimpse of these wonderful cave temples, ironwood forest and rose quartz mountain. This temple was built in the 1st century BC, by King Valagamba. Mahawansa (old book) says about invasion of seven Tamils from South India in Vlagamba’s reign, (103 BC). The king was unable to fight against them so he fled. Driven out of Anuradhapura by Tamil and remained in exile for 14 years. He came to Dambulla and took refuge in the cave for 14 years. In the meantime he collected an army and went back to Anuradhapura and regained the throne and his second reign was (89-77BC). After regaining the power the king wanted to show his gratitude to the temple. He converted this cave into an interior carved beautiful Buddhist temple. Before the valagamba’s arrival, this cave was donated to the Buddhist monks as dwelling place by king Saddhatissa (137-119 BC).Under the drip ledge of the main cave there is a Brahmi letter inscription. Many other King added to it later and by the 11th century, the caves had become a major religious place. King Nissankamalla gilded the caves and added about 70 Buddha statues in 1190 AD. During the 18th century, belong to kandyan period. This complex of the cave at Dambilla is one of the most impressive Buddhist temples in the world with its great number of Buddha statues and more than 20,000 feet paintings.Todat Dambulla is a world heritage site declared by UNESCO in 1991.

My wife and myself are currently holidaying in Sri Lanka and this morning we visited the Golden Temple of Dambulla. We arrived at the site at 0900 and our luck was in asit was very quiet so - after paying our SLR1,500 (£7 approx) Entrance Fees at the nearby Ticket Office - we began our ascent up the relatively steep 350+ steps. There were very few other people on the steps but no shortage of dogs and monkeys - fortunately, they left us alone and we arrived at the Temple area in 10-15 minutes. Once there - and as this is a religious site - we left our shoes at the designated site (a SLR25 fee per pair has to be to paid on your return) and donned our sarongs before showing our tickets to gain entry to the site. This is relatively small as there are only 5 caves to see but very impressive nonetheless. All in all, this is an impressive site and well worth visiting but give some thought to when you carry it out as that should make that much more enjoyable! Unlike most others, we decided to start our tour at the last cave and work back towards the entrance. This worked very well as we were able to see the many (well over a hundred) of different Buddha Statues at our leisure. Even so, after collecting our shoes and heading back down the steps with 30 minutes.

I am laughing at other reviews here of people whining about having to climb steps, having to go bare foot. People you are in SRI LANKA, in a scared building, you knew what you signed up for when you booked your holiday and if not, silly you for not doing research. Yes it's a temple , its beautiful, has history, not huge so does not take that long to walk round, and each room is pretty similar in terms of what's inside it. its worth a view, but not worth a full day out, I would tag this onto doing Sigariya rock in the same day.
In my opinion this temple is not very attractive. It is quite modern but it is also very kitsch. Maybe the most interesting thing is the image of Buddha at the top of the roof.
These caves are very beautiful and inside there are a lot of Buddhist statues. But the best things are the frescos in the wall of these caves. Fascinating.
Actually there were nothing inside their temples. You should walk barefoot and it was annoying because the floor was hot.
Ruthless inconsiderate rude staff, including police who were there for safety reasons.

In order to teach the temple you have to climb about 300 steps. The temple is atop a hill and it consists of a few chambers which have been carved off the Rick's in the mountain. It's better to go on a sunny day as you will have to take off your shoes and you will have to walk in areas which are not covered. Inside each chambers, there are numerous Buddhist statues and a number of monks stay there. It's worth a visit

We first arrived by the main road. We had this awesome views on the gold buddha. We the climbed all the stairs, and discovered that the ticket office was on the other side of the temple. Anyway, we payed the 1500Rp fee and went to this huge place. It was actually pretty quiet when we were there, Had the time to look to everything. Lot of little rooms, Looking a bit the same. Still nice to visit. My advice is to go dorectly to the ticket office, climb to the temple, and leave by the other side, to see the Gold buddha (And the museum).

There are five smallish caves A long walk up  and thought that the entrance fee of 15 us dollar was to high I like visiting caves and temples  but was disappointed. The entrance doesn't even get you into the Buddhist museam  at the base of the hill. Add in a few aggressive hasselers  trying to scam money. Disappointed   and a rip off

Bring water - none is sold up at the top! Follow dress code, no bare shoulders or knees and they will not rent you something to cover up so have a sarong with you or you won't get in. Pay to have your shoes watched or they could get stolen. I had on socks as the rocks are really hot in the sun. I went up all the stone steps and there are a lot of them with no railing and it is hot! Go early in morning or just before closing. It only takes an hour or so to go thru the 5 caves. It is amazing cave art with about 150 stunning buddhas and stupas and the mural paintings on the ceilings - wow! A lot of see. This has been a sacred pilgrimage site for 22 centuries and is a World Heritage Site.  It is also called the Rock Temple Complex of Dambulla. I discovered the path leading down so didn't use the steps and came across some tuk tuks to take me down to the car park where my driver was. Might be able to do this also on the way up??? if you have mobility issues. The rock steps going up are a lot of work.
Well worth a visit. I would recommend not in the heat of midday as it can be a bit hot.The toilets are a bit basic.

This Buddhist Temple is in Dambulla, Sri Lanka. It is near to the Dambulla Cave Temple and is a very impressive Buddhist temple and Golden statue. I was also very impressed with the unique line of monk statues leading to the Golden Buddha statue and for those alone the temple is worth a visit. The temple is free.

Situated on the A9 highway, 72 kms from the sacred city of Kandy, the Dambulla golden temple is one of the most important spiritual center for Buddhism in Sri Lanka. The whole place includes the golden temple and the historic cave temple on the massive mountain rock above.It is a world heritage site. It was an ancient monastery still functional and is the largest cave temple in Sri Lanka. After worshipping the golden temple, you have to climb up a steep staircase to get to the cave temple. You can enjoy a breathtaking view of the Dambulla town and green surroundings as well as enjoy a breeze and pure air. There are 5 caves with full of murals and lots of statues of Lord Buddha and some kings of Sri Lanka. No matter you are Buddhist or not, just visit this holy place to enjoy the serene spirituality! There is a traditional food corner operating adjacent to the vehicle parking where you can enjoy some traditional Sri Lankan food and snacks. The Sri Lankan Buddhist television channel Rangiri Dambulla also operates from here. Not to miss if you are in Sri Lanka.

Visited in May over the Vesak day holiday so mostly locals visiting.  We used Simply Ceylon Tours to book our private car and driver which worked so well for visiting the temple.  Inside the cave is incredible!  The murals on the ceilings are impeccably preserved and the statues inside are stunning.  Highly recommend visiting despite the dreaded “tourist price” entrance fee.   Look for wildlife on the way up.  We saw three hornbills in the trees about halfway up.  You do have to take off your shoes once you reach the top, leave them with the guard for a small fee.  I do recommend wearing socks since the ground gets hot. Take plenty of water!
The beauty of the statues and the highly decorated walls and ceilings of the temple made the climb up to the caves worthwhile.

as a tourist destination, dambulla provides excellent experience. unfortunately there is limited facilities for tourists or locals, everything is charged( entrance fees, shoe keeping fees, as well as donations for "shawl" to cover your shoulders if you happened to wear sleeveless( cultural police is everywhere) and exorbitant entrance fee from my wife who is a foreigner( they had the audacity to ask for marriage certificate to waive the fees). if you can tolerate menacing monkeys and faecal smell, its a site worth visiting. but make sure you empty your bladder and take your own water since no public facilities are available even after charging so much to enter.
Bit of a hike up a hill to access the temple, have to take shoes off so suggest you wear socks as the path is stinking hot !  Worth it, statues & rock art is stunning.

The Golden Rock Temple was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Today it consists of five parts, in total there are 150 Buddha statues. The oldest temple dates from the first century BC. It is unique place, because of its location in natural caves and on the hill has an amazing atmosphere. Nice view of the beautiful surroundings Dress appropriately - covered arms and knees. You enter the temples without shoes, so you can take a socks with you because going through heated stones is a real challenge.

The Dambulla Royal Cave Temple is at the top of the hill after a walk up the steep stairs.  While this isn't an overly hard walk, it might be difficult for someone who is out of shape, or frail and elderly.  The view of the valley before entering the gate to the temple area is nice and makes for good photos.  The temple inside the gate is built under a rock overhang and inside there are many Buddhas for viewing.  Wear comfortable shoes and watch for monkeys who will quickly try to steal a snack or drink if not hidden from view.

The Golden Temple is right off the main road in Dambulla and is visible as one drives past.  There is a large golden Buddha statute that appears impressive at first glance, but as we got closer we could see it was beginning to show signs of wear.  Repairs are needed.  There is also a golden Stupa, and vendors selling typical Sri Lankan treats.  If you are going to come here, make the trek up the stairs to the Dambulla Royal Cave Temple.  Watch out for monkeys.

A few steps to climb to get to the caves. Be warned you must have your knees and shoulders covered so take something with you otherwise you have to hire a sarong! Also wear socks as you have to take shoes off and the ground gets very hot! It is worth it though as the cave paintings are amazing and all the buddhas. Well worth a visit.
Climbed some steep steps to reach the caves, had to wait for the 12 noon offerings to be made.  Make sure you have socks on your feet as no footwear allowed.

A visit to the cave temples in Dambulla is a must when visiting the Cultural Triangle. While you will see lots of statues of buddha during your time in Sri Lanka, nothing compares to the cave temples of Dambulla. Accessed via a hill climb, the temples afford great views of the area. There are a series of 5 caves. I would recommend starting at the one furthest from the entrance as this is the smallest and most modern of the caves. This way you save the best for last too. Inside each cave are statues of buddha as well as paintings. Its really atmospheric even when there are others around. The second temple is by far the most impressive and is the largest by far - there must be 30 or 40 statues in there. When we came it was quite busy as a tour group must have just arrived, so we waited a short while and they quickly moved on. A visit here doesn't take too long but its well worth it. Be mindful to cover knees and shoulders when visiting.
very nice place,lots of forigners and locals visit this temple,good location,worth to visit in Dambulla,
well,interesting to climb the rock and see inside the cave and outside the cave,really good place in Dambulla,Srilanka, 1-2 hr is enough to visit the cave,

We found these caves to be really interesting. We didn’t have a guide but you can read a lot about them beforehand. We stayed in the Dambulla area but in hindsight would just stop in at the caves on the way to or from Sigiriya. It is a hot climb and we wore socks to protect our feet as you must remove shoes before entering. I found them to be more interesting than the tooth temple in Kandy. There are a few people trying to sell trinkets after you collect your shoes, and selling water and fruit.

Maybe it’s because we were in many similar places already, but this one did not make too much of the impression on us. Interesting paintings on the walls. Lots of very similar Buddha statues, with few a bit more unique. Massive Buddha of course makes impression. Slightly irritating was need to pay for leaving shoes outside (on top of standard ticket). Absolutely minimal cost, but the concept did not fit us. If you haven’t seen any of such establishments, then it may make much bigger impression on you, so if you’re in the area, probably worth going if time permits.

A unique tourist and cultural site in Sri Lanka. This cave temple is one of the few found in the world were you can experience how the ancient people build shrines inside rock caves. Similar sites can be found in Thailand, Burma, middle east etc....
I visited this place whilst on tour of Sri Lanka. Amazing temple to see. Best to go to this temple in the morning as your will not  be able to enjoin in the afternoon.

This is an ancient complex of caves dating back to the 1st century BC tucked beneath a vast overhanging rock.  The rock towers 160 metres over the surrounding plains and there are 80 known caves in the vicinity. There are five main caves and they contain an astounding 153 statues of Buddha, including an impressive 14 m carved statue.  We actually thought there might have been even more than that - the Buddha’s were absolutely everywhere - paintings, rock carvings, statues - simply everywhere..  The paintings on the roof off each temple were so intrictate, it almost looked like woven fabric was spread over the ceiling above us.  There is evidence from skeletal human remains going back over 2700 years that the Sri Lankans lived in the caves long before the arrival of Buddhism. The Sri Lankans are, in their own way, just as devoted to their respective religions, but they have a far more a la carte approach than the Indians do to say Hinduism.  For instance, the temples at Dambulla are definitely Buddhist, but there are also some alcoves and niches devoted to various Hindu gods.  The odd juxtaposition is due to Buddha being seen as a guiding light in the big picture - however the Hindu gods come in handy for everyday issues - crops failing, ill health etc. The only downside to visiting Dambulla is the 500 odd steps to be climbed in the blazing heat.  Our guide in Sri Lanka has already proved himself to be 100% on the bus and directed our driver to take us to a sneaky side entrance, which cut out some of the steps - so a mere 364 (odd) or around 1 km and a significant climb  Still felt like 500, but we made it and it was certainly worth the visit.  Mind you, because we had to take our shoes off before even reaching the ticket office, we felt like we were firewalking on the phenomenally hot stones to get to the caves. And back again. However, the caves an experience not to be missed

A very famous religiously important landmark in Sri Lanka. The cave temples are located at the top of a rock mountain which involves a climb which is slightly difficult. But once you reach the top, the view is amazing and the paintings inside the ancient Buddhist cave temples are mesmerizing. Totally worth the effort. Highly recommenced for anyone visiting the city of Dambull.

It is also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla. There are more than 80 documented caves in the surrounding area. Major attractions are spread over five caves, which contain statues and paintings. These paintings and statues are related to Gautama Buddha and his life. There are a total of 153 Buddha statues, three statues of Sri Lankan kings and four statues of gods and goddesses.

After viewing a number of Buddhist Temples and sites were surprised by the extent, size and quality of the artifacts at the Cave Temple. The sheer energy and skills of the artisans who built this shrine to Buddha so many years ago i.e. early 300 to 500 ad, is amazing. How did they manage to carve out so many statues, paint those amazing ceilings and preserve them all for all these years. Well worth a walk up the steep steps to view.
Steep stairs. Need to take shoes off and walk fair distance bare feet. So be prepared, or take socks. Was hot and need to take own cover. Some shops on way, good prices

Definitely a must-do. Bring water, there are no services at the top but there are some vendors along the path (don't buy/bring food or the monkey's will stalk you), and bring temple socks as the grounds get too hot to walk barefoot on.  The long walk up the hill in extreme heat and high humidity can be hard work, but well worth the effort to see this centuries-old temple. Inside the cave, five temple rooms, each overflowing with golden statues of Buddha, many carved from the natural rock. Elaborate murals completely cover the ceilings and walls. An amazing site!

Our driver assured us that there weren't too many steps to climb at this temple......but it was roasting hot in the midday sun and we were dripping wet by the time we reached the top.  Early into our trip in Sri Lanka, we stupidly didn't realise we would have to cover our knees as well as our shoulders to go into the temple and even more stupidly didn't think through the fact that we also needed to relinquish our shoes and that stone temple courtyards  are more than hot enough to fry eggs and therefore tender Western feet!  OMG.  I swear my feet would have sizzled if I'd put them in water - thought of pouring my drinking water over them!  We quickly noticed that people with tour groups all had sock on.  Ahhhh. You live and learn, always the hard way!  Is it worth all this?  Yes.  The view is great and the paintings in the many temple rooms are interesting.

Arrived at our hotel and had a nice dinner. Next day we travelled to the Dambulla Cave Temples in the early morning. Mornings are best as the 160 m climb to the caves can get very hot The first site you see is a large unpleasant grinning head. Stairs lead up and through the mouth and into the building where I assume there are restaurants and souvenir shops. Our guide just shook his head and led us to the left and up to the temple site. Your appearance is judged by morality "police" who may insist that women's legs and shoulders be covered or men's shorts must hang below the knee. You are warned beforehand of this scrutiny, but you still  see people continually turned away. Always carry a sarong if in doubt. The cave temples are very popular and rightly so. In total there are 153 Buddha images in the cave complexes, most sitting and some reclining. There are also images of saints, kings, gods and Goddesses. The walls and ceilings are beautifully decorated with geometric murals. We had only 4 hours here, but a longer visit is well worth your time especially if you have a guide who is well versed in the stories and meanings involved.
Worth the visit. Go early in the morning to avoid the heat. You must cover knees and shoulders and this includes the men

We were lucky because our driver dropped us by the golden Buddha then took the car round to the car park by the other entrance, and met us at the top with our tickets. We were prepared with socks against the hot stones, and with shoulders and legs covered. Our driver knew the  times a temple was temporarily closed and gave us good advice on which order to see them in, and we ended up at the most impressive one. We were waiting to get in when it re-opened and so had it almost to ourselves for a few minutes before the crowds poured in. Sometimes there was a bit of a crush to see a particular Buddha, but it wasn't threatening at all, and the whole place is extreme;y impressive

This iconic golden Buddhist temple is located in the town of Dambulla. The temple is on the main road and is heavily policed which prevents tourist buses and similar vehicles from stopping outside for more than a very brief period. To experience the temple you need to ensure women have their shoulders covered and men are wearing pants or shorts that extend below the knees. You also need to remove shoes to walk around bare footed.

A sacred pilgrimage site for 22 centuries, this cave monastery, with its five sanctuaries, is the largest, best-preserved cave-temple complex in Sri Lanka. The Buddhist mural paintings (covering an area of 2,100 m2 ) are of particular importance, as are the 157 statues. An awesome place to visit. Better if you could visit this place in the evening time due to hot sun

This was one of the most impressive of the temple visits and is well worth a visit. We had a guide who knew to get tickets before parking at a nearer point to the caves. This was a shorter walk up quite a few steps. You need to follow a strict dress code of shoulders and legs covered to gain entry and there is quite a long walk around the caves which you must do bare foot. It is possible to borrow a covering garment for a small cost in rupees.
I could not go inside because my dress was not ok but i saw the big gold buddha from out side. It was nice for seeing it but i dont know how is inside of top temple.

When heading up the stairs to the caves the view of Dambulla is breathtaking. You can get a few good pictures up there. Entering the caves there is a since of calmness and tranquility. The caves are filled with many different Buddhas and each having a different meaning..Its was very interesting and informative.

By far, for me, the most impressive of the UNESCO sites in Sri Lanka. Here, you will enjoy the visit of 5 beautiful caves, adorned with marvellous paintings and (about 150) statues of Buddha, some of the country's most important and evocative religious art. USEFUL INFO Entry ticket: 1500 LKR per person (excellent value for money of compared to other sites on the island) Journey time from Sigiriya by tuk tuk: around 35mins PRO TIP Since it is a religious place, please bear in mind that everybody is asked to dress properly (shoulders and knees must be covered, and shoes and hats must be removed too). Because of this latter point, I highly suggest to carry a pair of socks into your bag as sometimes ground can be very warm/hot.
A very very interesting temple with wonderful history. We had a guide who walked with us and explained the different aspects of the temple. We thoroughly enjoyed the experience.

You have to go this place by climbing around 500 steps under the hot sun that is the difficult part but after you arrived you will be surprised by the temple and wonderful Budda  statuses and beautiful religious paintings on the roof of temple. Everything inside is made by nature and handmaded large stone buddas.
the temple is frequented by many locals and tourists alike, it is worth visiting because of the Buddha monument

I really don’t know how they managed to build temples within the caves, the place is fantastic. The climb took about 15-20 minutes and in all fairness wasn’t too bad for the wifey and I. It’s advisable to keep water with you and no carrier bags as there are monkeys around who may try to take it off you. Some of the steps are more steep, so ensure to wear comfortable clothing. At the top you can go into each cave and see the Buddha, the caves are not as big as I anticipated nowhere near like Batu caves down Kuala Lampur. All in all, it shouldn’t take longer than 1.5 hours including both the climbs, but worth the visit.
Very impressed with the beautiful temple and holy atmosphere. Quite crowed for a weekend but very orderly devotees. Golden Temple wasvery well maintained.

Had a really good time wondering around the grounds of the temple. The extremely large golden buddha dominates the whole place and is beautiful. We really like the statues of Buddhist priest all lined up leading to the Golden Buddha!
Following our visit to the Cave Temple which has more historical value, we questioned if this new temple was really necessary?

Impressive caves with over 2000 square metres of painted walls & ceilings where the ancient King once worshipped. Short climb up compared to Sirigiya. A few vendors will pester you to buy trinkets here. .
We stopped here in passing for a photo opportunity at the behest of our guide on a large group tour en route to Sigiriya. It is a big! Impressive golden Buddha and definitely worth a brief visit.

We hired a personal driver to take us to the Dambulla Temple after visiting the Sigiriya and Pidurangala Rocks from Colombo. The Dambulla Temple cost 1500 rupees to enter and when we reached the top of the steps (after passing lots of monkeys!) you could leave your shoes in a shoe storage for 25 rupees. Walking around the Temple was a very worthwhile experience and it didn’t feel to overcrowded so you could enjoy it at your own pace. It is a very interesting temple which has been built into the rock face and has lots of relics within. It’s the best temple that I’ve visited during my time in Sri Lanka and would encourage travellers to visit.

A very nice temple caves to visit. We did Sigiriya from 7 am and was a hard climbing and later around midday we did these temple climbing and was much easier. So you can do both of them in one day but better to do Sigiriya first.
Amazing place to visit..a must to go ...the statues are splendid and we will never think of seeing some of them Please do not forget to put a visit in ur agenda
But has not left a great impression on me.  Very easy walk...and I,m not good with heights...many steps but easy...didn’t impress me like lion  rock

Dambulla is a site worth seeing if you are in Sri Lanka. The entry fee for foreigners was 1500 Rupees (about USD 8). There is a moderate walk up a hill either on stairs or a more gradual slope that provides lovely views of the nearby foothills and plains. The cave rock temple was constructed in a large mass of rock by King Walagambahu in the 1st century BC. There are several different caves with paintings on the walls and ceilings as well as numerous images of Buddha. As it is a temple, legs must be covered for women and men (although this temple was less strict than others like the Temple of the Tooth so I was able to wear a long pair of shorts that barely covered by knees). You also need to leave your shoes outside the temple (there is a stall that will store them for you for a small price). During the midday, the rocks in the direct sun were very hot so be forewarned. In summary, this is a highly impressive set of caves with more than 2,000 year old paintings and statues of Buddha that is well worth a visit.

This is the most recent and tallest Buddha of them all, some people say it looks cheap but who am I to comment on a religious site. I did see that there were large nests o mud wasp’s building their nests on the Buddha. This is a free site and you can also get a good cheap feed from the restaurant there which is run by the monks I believe. It is unique and worth a stop after the caves. There is also a museum on site but I didn’t go.

WOW this would have to be the most original and complete cave temple I have seen. Be warned though go as early as you can go to avoid the crowds and start at the last cave and work your way back to the entrance as this is another way of missing the crowds. For the small entrance fee and shoe security amazing a must see. Please remember this is a sacred temple so shoes must be removed and clothes below the knees and over the shoulders must be worn. Once. You have seen this you can then travel down the hill to the massive 30 meter high golden Buda and Stupa.

The Golden Temple is quite impressive.  It is actually a series of temples that are carved out of the rock.   The first one houses the reclining Buddha as well as seemingly countless smaller Buddhas.  The interior is covered with gold paint, as you might expect.  The walls and ceiling are painted vivid colors that have lasted over the centuries.  That particular temple is very crowded.  The others are larger and also lavishly decorated.  To get to the temple you will have to walk up many steps, possibly several hundred if you start from the very bottom.  There is a way to shortcut some of those steps by walking up ramps.  You might ask someone before you take the hike up.  This is a very unique site and well worth the effort.

The temple stands on an elevated rock and upon entering the site you make the 20 minute climb up steps and steep slopes to reach the site. Beware the monkeys that seem to be everywhere. There are 5 caves to visit' after leaving your footwear at the entrance, each vary in size. Despite the notices not to use flash photography there were plenty of ignorant tourists who chose to ignore this request. The site is a spiritual place for most of Sri Lanka's Buddhists. Good views over the surrounding area and well worth a visit.

Magnificent. From outside it doesn't look any nice but once inside the paintings and sculptures are awesome. It's a long climb to go upto the caves. The steps are not steep but look like they go up forever! Worth the efforts. Photography is allowed inside. Foreigners pay a hefty fee, while SAARC countries fee is affordable and locals go free. Worth the visit.
Was amazed at the paintings in the caves . The stairwell was steep was didn’t take too long. If you go through the golden Buddha that takes longer. Really recommend seeing this great place to visit.

We walked to the temple complex from our hotel (the Sundaras ), we accessed the Golden Budha entrance on the main road, the Golden Budha can be seen from miles away, there were a lot of local pilgrims visiting the temple complex due to it being the last Sunday of the month lots of excited kids which added to the overall experience , we walked to the left of the Golden Budha and climbed a flight of stairs past some stalls selling local treats, then keep left and descend more steps on to the road at the back of the Golden Budha then walk 500 meters down the road to the ticket office, where you can buy your tickets to gain access into the cave temple (note its cash only and you can't buy a ticket at the top). Then climb the stairs at the side the office through a wooded area full of monkeys with fantastic views. when you reach the top you go into the cave temple you must wear modest clothing or you have to hire some to cover up. inside there are 5 caves each with many buddhas and wall murals, each one beautifully atmospheric well worth the climb, there was a small lotus pond in the grounds to sit near and take in the views.Then you can walk down to the Golden Buddha straight ahead, a lovely way to spend couple hours.

As there are over 5,000 reviews of Dambulla Cave Temples I can't possibly advise anything new that hasn't been said. It's a magnificent series of 5 temples and well worth a visit. They contain over 150 Buddhas and date from the first century AD. To reach them there are many steps to climb, but I can assure you the exertion is worth it. Ensure you dress appropriately for entering a religious site. If you can try to secure the services of a local guide, it's well worth it and our guide really enhanced our visit with his excellent knowledge. I'd be very happy to visit the Temples again in future if I ever had the chance, it's a memorable place and very high up on the MUST SEES in Sri Lanka. Enjoy!

Five caves over 2000 years old greet you after a decent one kilometre climb. You need to dress modestly & touring the caves is done in your bare feet. We had a torrential rain shower while we very visiting so we had the experience of walking around in warm puddles. The steps up & down were quite slippy after the rain. We were part of an Exodus group so we had our own guide. Because of the historical importance of the temple & the caves,I think it would be important to get a guide to get the most from your visit. You will see hundreds of Buddha statutes in various poses & great ceiling & wall murals. You will also see lots of monkeys.

We visited when there was a ceremony on and hundreds of pilgrims were visiting with offerings of the most beautiful flowers. We were moved by the ceremony and devotion. Our guide was very knowledgable and understanding the history of the temple added context. A very special place.
When you descend from Cave temples you should pass Golden temple with huge statue of golden Budha. It’s worth seeing, just beware of monkeys.

A unique look into the ingenuity of the people living in this era by turning the caves into a place of worship. Cut into the side of this granite rock the reclining Buddha is truly incredible. I couldn’t find out how long it took them to carve the Buddha so all I could do was look at it in awe. The paintings on the ceilings are repetitive but once again the patience of the artists is incredible. All three caves reflect different attitudes, so draw your own conclusions. Thoroughly enjoyed our visit here A tip....if you want an incredibly cheap and tasty lunch the cafe in the tourists car park is subsidised. The food is amazing and freshly cooked, we had a chicken Dosa each with a large bottle of water. The price 150 rupees or 70p.....!!!!
Serene and beautiful. A wonderfully calm place despite the crowds. Historically very interesting also
Well worth visiting but it is a steep climb and is a very busy place. Make sure you take a bottle of water

There are a lot of steps to climb but the visit to the 5 chambers of this temple are worth it. The display of Buddha’s is incredible as is the painting on the ceiling of the chambers. Truely incredible how this was done and it’s so well preserved over the years.
We could not give any ratings because of my wife who takes hijab. Unfortunately, the temple requires to take off hijab and head covering. My wife chose not to.

Make sure you take the time to stop by if you are around.   Amazing paintings and sculptures. Getting there is quite a climb and if it’s hot.... well you’ll work to get there but is is quite impressive to see.

A long climb up the hill to the rock caves (340 metres) but worth it for the view and the sites. For 2000 years monks have been painting inside the caves and carving statues. The colours are spectacular, it is difficult to understand how they were painted with just canle light.

Bit of a trek up to the complex itself, lots of steps! Remember to cover knees and shoulders and bring socks to protect your feet from the scorching rocks! Lots of history and wonderful sculptures within the caves

Amazing piece of rock and easily accessible. Royal cave temple also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla is a World Heritage Site in Sri Lanka, situated in the central part of the country. This site is situated 148 kilometres east of Colombo and 72 kilometres north of Kandy. Dambulla is the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka. Hint: always need a guide, suitable footwear and clothing for a temple, sunscreen, sunhat, good camera

The climb to the cave is really significant for the unfit and we saw quite a few people at the bottom who I would not recommend to try.  However, for the relatively fit the climb is definitely well worth it.  There were large school parties and to go in any cave with the chatter of kids completely ruined the peace and tranquility needed for a beautiful area such as this.  However, we waited until the cave emptied and were rewarded with a much more pleasant experience.  The first cave with reclining buddha was very cramped and humid so the less people the better.
