Take 25 rupees cash to pay for shoe minding at the top, and wear very old socks (to protect from hot rocks) or bare feet as plant seeds on ground are sticky and will ruin good socks. The caves are historically valuable, hence the UNESCO listing, but they are quite repetitive in what they show. Obviously they are of more interest to people of the Buddhist faith, but worth a look for all visitors. Do remember to buy tickets at the base before you climb, or else you will get all the way to the top and then not be allowed in!

Its a series of 5 cave temples that have hundreds and hundreds of Buddha statues. if you are in the area than you should see the place otherwise I don't think that its any special to visit hundreds of miles to see it. its a bit of a climb, 280 steps to be exact so make sure that you are wearing comfortable clothes and shows.

It was a public holiday after a Friday full moon when we visited so particularly busy with locals and tourists. Caves were amazing to see- we had read somewhere to go to the one furthest away (cave 5) and work towards the entrance as they get more amazing... I liked 2 and the rest, first one has a long reclining budha and was quite small so very warm but locals were very impressed with this one. Lots of Buddha statues, remember to look up and see all the paintings on the roof! We had a woman working out a possession (as locals described) and smashing a coconut which was all rather intriguing... not sure how much was for the crowd. It is a bit of a climb up, you need to dress respectfully and leave your shoes outside. Amazing views!

Definitely worth seeing and part of the great cultural triangle in Sri Lanka. We went late afternoon and it was very quite. Interesting frescoes makes this place very different from other Asian Buddhist temples.Spent about half an hour looking around.

This temple is quite fantastic. From the plaza in front the golden statue of Buddha absolutely towers above you shining in the sun. It has a dragons mouth as a doorway and spectacularly colourful and intricate facade. I loved the figurines to the side depicting monks processions with offerings and of course the lotus flower design is integral to the facade. It has a Buddha museum inside but we didnt go in as we wanted to get to the Dambulla Caves, the stairs to which are to the side of the temple. A really striking and vibrant building.

A simply unbelievable cave complex with incredible statuary and beautiful wall frescoes that I think date back almost 2000 years. The caves are reached by a long, tough rocky staircase so make sure you bring comfortable shoes. Anyone with any level of fitness will go up okay but its the heat that might get you so bring water and take your time! You can start the ascent at the bottom of the hill as the stairs leave the roadside to the side of the main Buddhist temple in Dambulla town or you can drive up to the car park a bit higher up where the ticket office is. It costs 1,500 rupees for foreigners and is absolutely well worth it. The caves are just stunning. Every inch of the roof is decorated with Intricate fresco and the Buddha statues are captivating, countless numbers of them of various sizes and poses. Wonderful atmosphere of reverence and sense of history. There are two enormous caves and they in particular are spellbinding. The first cave is tiny though and has a reclining Buddha. The next two are the largest, most lavish ones. The final two are smaller and renovation work is ongoing but you can still go in. Stunning views of the surrounding countryside from the forecourt before you go in by the way. You have to enter without shoes but socks are accepted. It costs 25 rupees to leave them with attendants outside. You need to cover shoulders and above the knees. Go early in the day as the crowds can be thick and if  course it is cooler then. An absolute wonder to behold, definitely the finest monument to Buddha I've ever had the pleasure to see.

Be prepared to walk up steep stairs to get to the caves. Once at the top, you will be asked to remove your shoes. Also keep in mind that you cannot enter if you have bare shoulders or knees. There is a place that lends men and women sarongs right next to the cave. The caves are something to see. I was amazed by the handiwork of the beautiful Buddha statutes. Definitely make time to visit these caves.

Charming place, so full of history! The interior of the caves is beautiful decorated. We also hired a guide and it was a good decision because he knew some cool facts about the temple. They have a place where you can rent a sarung to cover your shoulders and knees.
Don’t miss this attraction it is a world heritage site. You will visit four caves foiled with Buddha’s and amazing wall and ceiling pairings. The place is awesome!
The ancient frescoes, and many golden statues of Buddha are well worth a look. The background provided by our guide was a help in understanding what we were seeing.

This is one of the best places that you must visit if you are in Dambulla. Ancient rock carvings and much historical significance. Make sure that you dress to the occasion by covering your knees (for gents) and covering your knees and shoulders (for ladies). Need to buy entry tickets but is really worth the visit. There is a bit of a climb but it’s not that strenuous as Sigiriya. Make sure that you spot the monkeys and also the water fountain inside the cave where the water spring goes uphill before dripping.
This is a bit overrated as it’s man made golden temple in the current era. There is not much historical significance here.

This sightseeing has 2 moments: 1) visit of the Golden Temple: immediately, in distance, a 30meter high golden sculpture of Buddha can be seen. The giant Buddha sits in position of “the teaching”. Under him, there is the particular entrance to the museum: it looks like to a dragon mouth. Around the sites there are many flowers and holy trees (for Buddhism). You can walk around the golden sculpture, above the museum. 2) visit of Caves Temple: after climbing several steps you arrive at the entrance. For respect of the place, it’s recommended to take your shoes off, to have long pants (men), to cover shoulders and legs (women). There are some caves inside which you can find many sculptures of Buddha. Some are colourful and som white. There are also some pictures on the caves walls. Important: you can not take photos of you beside Buddha sculptures Very cheap visit
Nice to do, a bit a climb, upstairs you have to give your shoos in a guard house cost 25 r. inside nice Relics. The view is good.

Cave temples with beautiful Buddha's. Serene and peaceful atmosphere. It is more expensive for tourists. You will have to climb steps to get to the Temples and will also have to take off your shoes before going into the Temple. Overall, it is worth the climb.

After climbing Lion Rock in the morning the 300 or so stairs was no difficulty. The caves are well worth the visit and it pays to have a guide who can explain the various caves and differing ages of the paintings and statues to gain a full experience.

This is just a gem!! The statues, frescoes, paintings and location make it all so spectacular and just wonderful. We had not planned this as part of our tour and our driver insisted on taking us. A true gift as the children really loved it and we found it enchanting!

We climbed Dhambulla rock to reach this historic Budhist Temple, where King Walagamba organized his army to reunite the country. The old paintings and status are still protected and has stories behind each statue. One of the wonders is water travels upwards on the rock (roof) and it drip drop by drop on to a huge pot placed on the highest point.  Unable to video due to poor lighting, however their are youtube clips describing this.
Went in the early morning with a cool breeze. Very calm relaxing place with not to many tourists. The budas are well preserved and are five rooms are very beautifull.

We loved the serene atmosphere of this place. Not too many people around midday luckily. Maybe beginning of July is less busy. Take shoes that aren't worth too much as you have to leave them at the entrance.

Okay so this is a bit of a trek up a hill with steps, but you are rewarded at the top by a world heritage site.  Photos on the internet will give you a flavour, but to be in the site which isn’t overrun with tourists in the way that other places are, is a truly amazing and humble experience. On the hill up, you will likely see monkeys, including babies which are adorable. There are some sellers around, which you may have to politely decline a few times. Other thing to note is, at the top before you enter the temple grounds you have to remove shoes.  Legs must be covered by men and women and shoulders as well. You may take photos so camera and water or drinks are a must.

Okay not very amazing.Have seen better monestries. The ticket counter is in hiding .The nearby Cave temple is not at all promoted well.Their ticket counter is not even visible the staff at the entrance is very rude,since we missed the sign board for ticket he asked us to go down 300 mtr again and get the ticket for entrance,when we asked our children cant go down again n climb back he said they could go n we could watch them from the entrance , but he then said to stand further outside from where we could not see our children.

A few steps to climb before enjoying the wonders in the caves.  5 caves in all with different statues etc to look at. A very impressive formation Don't forget to cover knees and shoulders. 1500R for adults - kids free. ok to take pictures in the caves too.
Go this temple on the morning or after 5 pm. You have to go up a litllebit. In this temple you can take photos. We did really like this temple.
Once visited Sigiriya rock fort everything is second choice. Worth a visit. Beautiful 360 degrees view from the rock is worth every effect to climb
Worth the visit to see the wide variety of images and the local paying homage. The prostrate Buddha was quite amazing

Its very peaceful place and with idols of Budha around. Its on small hill so you will have to climb up a lot and beware of monkeys. Make sure you carry your own water bottles uphill. There are some rules to follow for clothing and you shouldnt be wearing revealing clothes here like shorts, Bermuda, skirts etc are not allowed.

Amazing Temple on the top of the mountain. By climbing to this temple you will see amazing views and if possible chose time in the morning or later afternoon because on daily hour it could be very hot and then it is hard and difficult to climb it. Also check where is the ticket office before you take the visit in to this place because it is located a little bit far away from main road to the temple.
Another climb, up to these cave temples at Dambulla was well worth the effort. The whole place has a tranquil respectful aura and the insides of the temples are just fabulous - do go
Very interesting temple. Well worth the trip. Note theres no short pants permitted, but you can rent a sarong for 200Rb.
Well worth visiting. Loved the atmosphere. Paintings on roof were incredible. Long walk up 400 odd steps but worth it

the golden temple is situated on the climb back from cave temple , the place doesnt offer much in terms of history or architecture , there is giant lord buddha statue, a small museum, there is no entry ticket for the venue, u can give it 10/15 minutes on your way back , nothing special though
Amazing place, easy access by public transport. Lots of monkeys around. Foreigners have to pay extra but if you really wish to get some quite time or meditate this is a must go place!

There is a lot of steps to climb up about 300 in total. One place you hand in your ticket to be stamped, you are allowed in to see the feet of Buddha and the alfresco paintings, after that if you want to go in to another section of the cave will cost you 2000 rupees plus the I think 1500 rupees you had already paid. Must have arms and knees covered, Was not really impressed with this place charges for tourists are very expensive.
a place of god should be clean and revered, but it was dirty and musky. insistance on not showing knees and elbow takes priority over cleanliness....

It's quite a climb to get to the top where the entrance is located. 1500 each entrance fee. There are a few caves which all look very simular. It's nice to see but a lot of the same. 30-45 minutes inside will be enough. Afterwards you can make a short walk to the museum.

The caves are nice but it is rather touristy - making it up all the stairs there’s people waiting for you to sell necklaces etc. The place doesn’t feel “holy” but rather like it’s falling apart. The caves itself with the Buddha’s are impressive but not a must see (it’s not really a cave system but 3 caves where you enter from the outside).
This is endorsed by unesco as a world heritage site. There is lot of history and details in the ancient temple. Must visit for people go pass dambulla area.

Our son loved the Buddhas and enjoyed visiting each one. The caves also provide shade from the hot sun. THere is so much culture and history in these caves. If you want to know more, best to hire a guide! I'm glad we visited, it is a family friendly place even kids can enjoy.
Lovely place to visit (was quiet when I went) and interesting 'caves' with great history and many differing statues/paintings etc.
This is worth a visit, very interesting. A guide to tell you the history is a must as there is no information on sight.
This is worth a visit, we had our own guide who was very knowledgeable on the subject, it does depend on your own interest in these things.

In itself it is not a single temple but there are five, in different caves. Climbing the mountain where the temple is is a good exercise and the views from above are very good. The price, expensive. The buddha statues lying spectacular, as well as the decorations in all the caves. It is also funny to see the monkeys on the side of the mountain.

There are steps to climb to get to the top not that bad just watch out for the monkeys. At the top take your shoes off and there is local who places them on a shelf and you pay to get them back, not alot if money but I guess you could put them in your bag. This is undoubtedly a must visit heritage site in Sri Lanka which ages back to 18th century. There are 5 natural rock caves and each consists of various forms of lord Buddha statues. We felt the authorities are not properly maintaining the place. Foreigners are charged but locals are not. If they are charged, consider providing a guide or at least someone who can speak and give a proper presentation of these caves. Locals are mostly aware of the background story so if you are a foreigner, please spend some time googling before visiting.

In case you are wondering if this place is worth it and should you go here as well as all the other UNESCO sites I would strongly recommend that you not miss these 5 caves.  They truly will take your breath away but do read up about the history and the impact will be much stronger. I overheard one gentleman saying loudly to his guide "I'm going back to take photos".... He also stopped for us to see the Herb Garden and do not get sucked into the whoopla of the Ayurvedic herb seller, he was a hard sell.  We did have an Ayurvedic massage and overtipped for the 20 minutes, but felt very good at the end. Our day to Dambulla Caves will remain as a memorable time.
This is a really nice place to visit. There are lots of Buddha statues and paintings. If you go there around 5PM you can see a nice sunset.

We paid Rs. 1,500 each to climb up the steps to the caves. We were given receipts but no instructions as to etiquette, etc. When we reached the top, we were told to leave our shoes at a kiosk a distance away from the entrance and to pay Rs. 25 per pair of shoes. The rocks had worn smooth over the years, but there were flecks of paint and gravel in some areas which reminded us we had pretty pampered tenderfeet.  We had to avoid a low fence in order to deposit our shoes and everybody had to avoid it again in order to enter the complex.  Each small cave had an entrance and often an attendant who had limited English vocabulary. There were signs saying not to sit on benches that were meant to keep people from touching the images.  We were told variously by guards that we couldn't take photos of people in the caves and that we couldn't take photos at all. But on the other hand we saw families taking moving pictures in the caves. In the absence of official advice, we assumed they meant you shouldn't turn your back to any Buddha image. A lot of work went into the construction and painting of the images, most of them from the 18th century. It would have been difficult to imagine much of a religious feeling in any of the caves with people continually entering and leaving and often receiving instruction by the guards.  The location of the caves atop the mountain affords a good view of the other mountains and the plain below. On the way down tourists are approached by beggar monkeys.  One person was helping people down because some steps were broken.  While it could be improved greatly, the tourist experience is probably worth Rs. 1,500 per person, but it is not worth much more.

A magnificent sight and well worth the visit, Buddha's everywhere but notice that some are different to others and that's based on when they were made, some early others later. If you can get a guide, the stories of the different tales are worth it, there's plenty to see, if you like Buddhas.... Don't forget take some socks, the stones can be VERY hot. Also halfway down the stairs is a little  t shirt seller, selling quality t shirts for 1000 rupees, well worth the money. Sorry to do the tourist bit but Sri Lanka isn't full of people trying to sell you something and this guy did sell quality stuff as good as the shops.

For Dambulla caves, you have to climb a bit. But if you have climbed Sigiriya Rock, then trust me this is a breeze. The caves are beautiful, one can find Lord Buddha in various postures, like sleeping Buddha, resting Buddha, meditating Buddha etc. The temple will take 45 minutes for a complete visit. Though look for frescos in the ceilings, few have been distorted by nature, but many are still intact. Don't give this place a miss.

Very well preserved Buddhist temple. It is situated on top of a rock, and is built around a series of 5 caves. The oldest one dates from 10th century and it is extremely well preserved. The newest is only 150 years old. A must see if you are in Sri Lanka.

A must visit if you are in the region. Absolutely worthwhile taking time to visit this UNESCO world heritage site that has over 153 Buddha statues and thousands of drawings spread across several caves. There's a small climb from the road level to the top of the mountain to reach the caves, where you also get a nice view of the surrounding area.

The header for this webpage is a bit confused. There are actually two separate sites. One is a modern Golden Temple featuring a gargantuan Golden Buddha statue, quite an eyesore on the landscape. The other site -- not far away but up a slope --  is a cluster of caves. Nothing golden about the latter. This review is about the caves. Not about the Golden Buddha which I didn't bother to visit. The "caves" consist of five spaces under rock overhangs that have been adorned with countless statues of the Buddha and related personages, backed by patterned murals. The paintings are old, but apparently most of the statues are only from the 19th century, and not particularly great examples of sculpture. Some look amateurish. It’s up about 200 steps before you reach the ticket office, but the caves are adjacent to each other, so there isn’t much walking within the paid area. There are some nice views over the surrounding countryside. The whole area is considered sacred, so you must remove your shoes before you enter. There is a booth that keeps your shoes for you for 25 rupees per pair. Good for a one-hour visit. As I was staying in a guesthouse not far from the area, I walked to it.  From the centre of Dambulla, the cave complex is about 1.5km south along Kandy Road. Entry was 1,500 rupees. Information about how to get to Dambulla from Colombo Fort: There is no railway station in Dambulla. The nearest station is at Habarana about 20km away, and even then, trains are infrequent. The day train to Habarana departs Colombo Fort at 6am, arriving around 11:15am. You cannot make advance reservations, so you have to go to the station early (like 4:30am?) to ensure you get a seat. The night train departs at 9:30pm, arriving at a ridiculous 3am. There are buses from Bastian Mawatha bus station in Colombo to Dambulla, but it will be a painfully cramped five-hour ride. After asking locals, I was advised to take a train from Colombo to Kurunegala. On a typical day, there are several trains, e.g. departing 8:50am, 11:50am and 1:45pm, for the two or two-and-a-half hour journey. Kurunegala is a major transport interchange. From Kurunegala’s railway station, take a tuktuk to the bus station near the town centre clock tower, and hop onto any long-distance bus heading north-eastwards and passing through Dambulla. There should be at least one bus per hour, probably more frequently. It’s only 90 minutes by bus from Kurunegala to Dambulla. You can't get lost in Dambulla. It's a two-street town.

Calming prayer halls and temples of various Buddha statues in varying incarnations is a must visit site. Added thrill is the steep climb uphill on the rugged stairs to be blessed by cool mountain air and lovely views of countryside. The 2nd/3rd century BC temples are well maintained, cool and have a blessed, calming environment. Do watch out for monkeys. Walk downhill from a different route to visit the Golden Buddha temple and Golden stupa on the other side of the highway.
Great views and the hike wasn't too bad either! would recommend the trip to the top. Peace and quiet and something different.
Worth the hike, temples in caves or caves with temples? who knows.. it was a great experience and the view are amazing.
A fascinating visit to the caves which hold well preserved carvings and murals.  Bit of a walk up a hill to it but not too arduous.
One of the the place you have to see during your stay in Srilanka. 5 big caves and many of Buddha statues, beautiful wall paintings inside the caves
Great sculptures, wonderful colours, it’s a tough climb if you’re not very active.  Monkeys plenty, stay careful of your belongings.
It is a Buddhist temple famous for paintings of Kandian kindom period, Art lovers should visit the place. The paintings need preservation for future

My self traveled with my family many more times of this miracle buddhist holy place in srilanka. it's plesure to see wonder of kandyn arts & culture of buddisht civilization. The location & amazing view have to protect to the new genaration. I love so much to visit again & again this miracle holy place.
The cave temples were beautiful. The hike up to reach the caves took us by surprise. Full moons in Sri lanka can be usually criwded. Worth a visit still- these are mesmerising relics- ethereal.

There are around 400 stairs,so carry water,dress modest. You need to take out &submit your shoes.The 1st,2nd & 4th room were built by King of Sri Lanka 2100 centuary back,the paintings&statues are old but in very good condition.3rd room was built by a king 300yrs back &5th room was built by villagers of dumbulla.

Bit of a walk up the hill to the temples but totally worth it (and good views as well). There are several different caves with Buddha's of various sizes and ages. The reclining Buddha's are really beautiful. You need to be covered up (knees and shoulders) and you have to leave your shoes at a stall for a small fee. The temple is situated about a 15 minute climb upwards at the top of a small mountain. So get yourselves in the mental state to tackle that. When you get to the summit, you will need to remove all head coverings and also remove all footwear. There are is a shoe store but it will cost you 25 rupees to store it with them; a cost that i think is also an opportunistic thing to do albeit a trinket. The temple has 6//7 rooms, all having various depictions of bhudda in different states. And thats pretty much it tbh. I'm not sure how else to describe the temple. On a final note, i would remind the readers to dress modestly when visiting this temple, so no shorts/mini skirts etc. Standard stuff tbh.
Visited these impressive caves yesterday. They are truly impressive and well worth a visit. Abit of a hike up the hill but the steps are well maintained. The climb is well worth it.

Another temple but not the most beautiful or most interesting in my view. I think we would have happily missed it but it was part of the obligatory tour stops. We did not climb up to see it all and perhaps we missed something.

The best time to go is either very early in the morning or by evening say 5 pm. We are all required to take off our footwear, deposit it for a fee of SL Rupees 25 per pair and then walk barefoot. Since its all rocky terrain , the rock becomes hot during the day making it difficult to walk barefoot. Secondly need to have your shoulders and knees covered before entering the complex. Third, we cannot take selfies or photos with the buddha idols , as a mark of respect to Buddhism. Having note all the above three , the area comprises of 5 caves , the last two being smaller. The caves contain various idols of Lord Buddha which is over a few centuries old and have been restored in the 19th century. These caves are located at a mountain top comprising of a friendly climb up the stone and cement stairs to reach the complex. A must visit for those interested in Heritage / Religious tourism. For others it is an adventure.  We entered from the gate close to the car park.

Visited here with my partner and our three youngest. Our guide drove us to an entrance which he said cut out some of the climb, so we did not have to do much walking/climbing!   You have to remove your shoes so we took little ankle socks to put on to protect our feet from the heat and the stones! You must also cover your legs and shoulders (they were turning people away who did not obey this).  It is very hot, so make sure you take water with you. The caves themselves are full of amazing buddas, in lots of styles, sizes, poses and colours - but you are not allowed to take selfies (as you must not have your back to the buddas - having said that, as there were several people there some of my photos have other people in who have their backs to the buddas!! In addition they have posters up telling you not to sit on the walls and in their own photos are people with their backs to the buddas!) But you must respect their culture and they do patrol and if they see you taking selfies they will make you delete them.  Outside the caves are also some great photo opportunities - in particular the view, which is  worthy of a few photos. Plus, on the walk back to our guide we encountered many monkeys who came up really close to us making for some great shots (which the children loved) but make sure you don't have any fruit or food on you, as they will try and steal it from you.  This place is definitely well worth a visit.

Gorgeous cave temples, most of them 2 thousand plus year old. Buddha statues carved directly into the rock, old paintings surviving after centuries, more recent ones deteriorating. Nice view from the yard. A place not to be missed.
This temple was well worth visiting as it was in such good condition. Our guide explained all about it.
So far this has been our tour highlight. It was a long walk up but fortunately we were early so it wasn’t too hot. The caves were spectacular and everyone was so interesting.

We arrived mid afternoon which means the heat of the day but also fewer people. For the majority of our time in the caves there were only a handful of others. The cave temples are really interesting and well worth the visit. Start at the back as the largest and most impressive caves are to the front.

Standing in caves with artefacts over 2,000 years old gave me a sense of awe and calm. I've not ever experienced anything like it. Golden Temple of Dambulla is the most impressive and, one of the eight UNESCO attractions. Dambulla Caves Opening Times:Officially, the cave temples are open from 7am-7pm but sometimes around lunch time and the ticket office might be taking a ‘taking a break’. There are five caves inside, each with a different interior and statues. These statues and paintings are related to Gutama Buddha and his life. These caves include a total of 153 Buddha statues, three statues of Sri Lankan kings and four statues of gods and goddesses. The latter include Vishnu and Ganesha. The murals cover a wide area. The  depictions on the walls of the caves include the temptation by the demon Mara, and Buddha’s first sermon. It is said that pre- historic Sri Lankans would have lived in these cave complexes before the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka as there are burial sites with human skeletons.

Golden Cave temple was really nice surprise for me and my boyfriend. We decided to climb there in afternoon which seems to be the best time. Caves are beautiful and stunning, definitely worth visiting. After visiting caves we watched sunset from top of the mountain and enjoyed view over the jungle.

The temple is located at the top of a mountain and in several caves. The walk up consists of quite a few stairs (some are uneven). There is a place for you to keep your shoes for a small fee. Both men and women need to be modestly dressed  (No shorts). Near the bottom there are a couple of vendors selling scarves and elephant pants though if you need something to cover up with.

The walk up to the temple does involve quite a lot of steps but if you’re not distracted by the beautiful scenery on the way up then when you get into the caves, the forget about the steps.  When I saw photos of this place I thought, yep another temple with Buddhas in it but it really is quite special.  The temple is built into the side of a rock and looks out over lush greenery.  All surfaces of the rock have been hand painted with such precision that you’d be forgiven for thinking it’s a flat surface.   Good news too - once you have finished, there is an easier route down from the temple but you need to make sure your driver meets you there and don’t forget your temple socks!

The guide books are right, start at the top in cave number five as they get better moving down.  As usual you have to leave your shoes at the entrance but they will allow you to wear socks.  Watch out for the monkeys which are plentiful and a bit of a nuisance.
A lovely look into the history of Buddhist beliefs in Sri Lanka. Lots of steps to climb and some great scenic points along the way. Very interesting and worth getting a guide.

Stopped to take photos and just quickly wonder around. Very impressive efigies. You don't need to cover up and you are allowed to take photos. We didn't pay anything to just go in and photograph. I don't think there is a charge.

Quite a easy place to visit compared with some sites in Sri Lanka. There are 5 sets of caves containing loads of efigies. Cool caves. Our of the heat. We were able to take photos inside. Take a look at the ceilings. They are painted and they look like material as the paint flows over the uneven rock ceiling.

The series of five temples carved from the side of the mountain here are very beautiful works of art and well-worth the side trip to Dambulla (which doesn't have a lot to offer otherwise). The caves themselves are very dimly lit (understandably), but you can get very close to the art, so the low-lighting does not diminish the experience. We came up the path from the ticket booth, rather than the big golden temple at the roadside. The steps up this way are not too steep except for a short bit at the end, and if you are lucky you will see monkeys sitting on the hand rails near the top. It is well-worth it to have either a good guidebook or a knowledgable guide, as the temples themselves have no information plaques. Also, wear socks! You must take your shoes off outside the entrance to the complex (as it is a Buddhist temple), and the rocks paving the courtyard get very, very hot as they are not shaded.

The trek up the steps to this Temple in the heat really highlighted to me how unfit I am! But it was worth it in the end. The caves are amazing. It is hard to beleive such a place exists it is quite an ominous feelimg being in the caves with all the statues. There are amazing views from up there and lots of monkeys in the vicinity. We went late in the evening so it was not too crowded. Be prepared it is quite a long walk to get tickets and up to the temple so bring a cold drink and wear light clothing

Quite a climb to get up to the site which is fascinarting but you need to read up on it or take a guide with you as there is very litle information at the caves to explain the context of the exhibits. A good tip is to start at the top with cave 5 as cave 2 is by far the most impressive.

First and foremost, read the other posts below and heed their advice regarding socks, covering up your knees, the stairs, wear sunscreen, etc.... A few things to add, based on my visit in late February: First, "go" before you go. There are no restrooms at the top, where all the caves are, and for all intents and purposes, there are none (or none that most westerners would consider appealing) at the main base/parking area either. I heard a rumor that a new restroom facility was being built at the base, but nothing at the top. So be prepared. Also, these caves are hot, humid, stuffy, and crowded. Especially the smaller ones.  It's hard to spend a lot of time really appreciating/enjoying the contents of the caves, which is too bad because they're actually pretty impressive. If you're in the area, you really have to see the Cave Temple, but just be as prepared as possible. Go early to beat heat and crowds as much as possible.

We tend to find that if you do too many temples there is a risk of them becoming just another temple. This one however stands out given how unique it is in the sense of all the buddhas being within 5 caves. And they are impressive. 1,500 rupee entrance fee (£7.50) not unreasonable either.

This is a serious climb and especially on a hot day so take that into account.  We went up with a 5 year old and he made it up ok.  It really is worth the climb to see the Buddha carved into the rocks. Of all the temples we went too over the years this seemed the most peaceful.  Views from top make for some great photos.

If you climb from the back ticket office , you have an option to get down to the front of the temple.Some funny monkeys will amuse you on the way. Carry a water bottle with you. Great visit. Cave markings very impressive. Worth the climb. Monkeys are also an entertaining bonus.

i think this is the best temple in sri lanka because of the caves its really nice and peaceful place. keep on mind everybody want to cover their legs before enter here.

Its something that you can not find somewhere else. They are 5 rooms into 5 different caves full of status and colours. Its not dificult to get there. the only disadvantage is that its always full of people

Buddhist places of worship can be outstandingly special and spiritual and this is one of the finest examples for that. The setting inside the hill, the view from up there and then of course the magic caves with huge reclining Buddhas and dozens of others - fantanstic.

We arrived a bit early in the region and therefore visited cave temples in the afternoon - which turned out a good choice as it wasn't too crowded. Tickets are pricey as in most tourist places in Sri Lanka. There is a long climb to get to the actual entrance. Once you get started, you quickly realise the uniqueness of the place: Each cave is special in some way and not like anything else I saw before. I thought it was particularly remarkable that many of the caves were changed and improved over centuries but still kept the impression of being one holistic oeuvre.
This place is really worth a visit but some people may find the antiquated step (approx 300) a bit of a challenge . Don't feed the numerous monkeys!
The Golden cave Temple is a must visit on every itinerary to Sri Lanka. It is one of the best preserved cave temples in Sri Lanka. The mural paintings are very important and so too the statues.
This temple isn’t like any other I’ve seen. It is serene & respectful without feeling oppressive in any way. The statues are fascinating - so many of them! Well worth the climb to see them.
Beautiful Buddhist temples in the caves - very reverential, and peaceful. It is a bit of a walk up to the temples - not for the faint hearted! Definitely worth a visit.
Something very magical here - definitely take a guide so that you can understand the richness of its history
Compared to Internet information, there is no free access to the Dambulle cave temples for foreigners. Admission is 1500 LKR.
Worth the climb up to the caves. It is active temple so NO SELFIES or pictures with statues! Shoes must be removed. I cannot comment on washrooms as I did not use them. Amazing art on walls!

I first went up from left of the Buddha and arrived on top was asked for ticket ....it is sold down the hill:  I should have  gone DOWN  MIDWAY on the  LEFT to the ticket booth... the orange roof you see down below...:-( Yes there is a very discreet sign posted left From bottom I recomend taking a tuk tuk walking is a good 20mn  A MILE AWAY ...! see  the picture were to take the path That's way after the white arch TICKET BOOTH really HIDDEN I left a claim but pretty sure the page will be torn down... RESTROOMS ALSO HIDDEN DOWN there or paying 100Lkr at the foot completly right of the Buddha

May be because a stayed a while in Kandy before, may be because it was the fifhteenth laying Buddha I saw , may be because I visited Aluweharaya before.. .I was NOT impressed at all Lot of tourists, pilgrims, caves smelling old  socks... PLUS the ticket booth is way down behind, take a tuk tuk or ask your driver to bring you there DO NOT START TO CLIMB !!! From Dambulla, pass the golden Buddha take the first path on the right  it is a good  20mn walk! I really prefered the natural atmosphere of Aluweharaya  on your way to Kandy, under the white big buddha on your right NO tourist...

A temple in the rocks, full of statues and images of Buddha. This statement doesn't really do it justice. It is in an incredible location with a beautiful view of the surrounding area. There are multiple chambers full of representations of Buddha in various forms (reclining, standing, seated). It is incredible to think of the dedication shown by those who created the statues and the paintings. Well worth a visit.
A must see when in the area, preferably with a guide to explain the history behind the king how built the temple.

This is famous for its recumbent Buddha carved from solid rock and the many statues of Buddha in the five caverns. It is a bit of climb to get up to the caves. I would recommend walking up the fairly steep ramps and coming down by the stairs (400 steps). This is an active temple so usual rules: leave shoes at the kiosk (bring socks, the rocks can get very hot), no hats, long trousers/skirts etc. Inside the caves it is very warm and were crowded when we visited - have patience and go with the flow and it will be fine. You are allowed to take pictures inside. Beware that they close the actual caves briefly for ceremonies at various times e.g. 10:30 while we were there.

This is a beautiful temple but I didn't really need to see them all whilst in Sri Lanka, we saw this as part of our guided tour. There are a lot of steps to climb initially, inside the caves it is hot and humid and when we went there were lots of people. You will need to cover knees, shoulders and to take of your shoes.

We went here as part of our tour of Sri Lanka.  If we had to pay I'd probably give it a miss as it's not really my thing.  However it is very beautiful and very inspiring.  The caves get very humid during the day - wear very light clothing.  Shoulders and knees must be covered as with all temples.  There are quite a few steps to climb to get to this temple - I saw some of the older people struggling in the heat.  Take water.

This whole visit won't take massive amounts of time. There's 5 caves of varying ages filled with Buddha statues. It is interesting to see how it's been made from the rock but we didn't really find it thrilling. We didn't hire a guide, maybe that didn't help? We used our guide book description of each cave to know what we were looking at. The steps up to it take longer than the site itself and are pretty steep, be warned! They are the only reason we've put more than an hour to do this. Nice to see but not a highlight of our travels by any means.

Evrer seen anything similar on my trips. If you are around Sigirya, do not miss this place. You can see several caves with Buddha statues from different times everything being very old. And, it is still on operation having seremonies daily. Good shoes recommended to clive up. And, there is very hot.

The statues and paintings in the cave are pretty impressive, but this was my least favorite visit of all throughout Sri Lanka because of the staff. >No one was present at the ticket building as I walked up, but when I got to the top they insisted I walk back down anyway. I did, and had to wait for someone to show up to sell me a ticket. >At the top, everyone is forced to pay to store their shoes by three guys who have no clear connection to the heritage site. There's really no need for a shoe storage service at this site, but unofficial guards nearly threatened a man who left his shoes at the bottom of some stairs, and I was jostled by their needless hostility. When I went to pay for my shoes, the attendant took my money and walked away. I had to wait and insist on change for the large bill I'd supplied. He knew what he was doing. >In the caves, my visit was made thoroughly unenjoyable when a guide lost his cool and screamed at a man he suspected of tagging along without paying. He reverberated throughout the cave. The man left, and the guide actually chased him to keep yelling at him. When he came back, other visitors said it wasn't necessary to do that, and the guide then yelled at them. I'm sad to say it, but the Dambulla Caves have become a racket.

I felt that the temple is unique in terms of having made out of cave. There are quite a few buddha statues, highlight being the sleeping buddha. The entry to the place was slightly overpriced.

I have seen a lot of negative comments about this attraction but our visit was great. We went with a guide, entered via a back road (avoiding the gaudy budda at the museum at the bottom of the hill) and already had tickets. The guide gave us a great history and the caves themselves are pretty spectacular.
Amazing. Some steps to climb. Can buy flowers to offer across the road from the temple. Can see monkeys wondering about the grounds.
One of the nicest Temple in cave as a Buddhistic place. It is very interesting to see the very old Buddhas statues and the awesome pictures on the walls!

we hadn't planned for this trip but very happy we went. during the walk you have quite the views, and when you get to the top you will be rewarded. 5 caves, with different contant, history very large lying buddha in the first is amazing, but the 2nd cave with some 150 statues...wow we took our time and enjoyed the stories from our guide, great visit. we wat around 1600 when it is more quite / less crowded. alternatively go very early as around 10-14 things seem to get very crowded o, bring something to cover your knees and shoulder
It is a very nice temple if you haven't seen anything like this before it is worth to climb up there. it is very funny to see all the monkeys around. You will like it.
Well worth the effort to get up here. Fabulous icons and moving atmosphere once you enter the shrines. Socks will make it easier.

AUD 22 per person, quite expensive like the many other places in SL. Some of the statues are nice but some of the wall painting has faded away! The place is crammed with bus loads of tourists and with all the money they collect, there should be some maintenance to the property!!

Well worth the climb! Bring a good camera! Don’t forget to see the blue Buddha behind the curtain! Take photographs of the steps going up and the carving above the entrance on the stone rock! Shoes must be removed to enter
Not just another temple/image house/pagoda. But atmospheric caves stuffed with fine Buddhas and detailed wall paintings. A must visit.Steps and bare foot as expected.
Great place to visit and learn a bit more about the history of Buddhism in Sri Lanks and appreciate a great sunset.
A totally awesome heritage site Magnificent architecture and decoration A really enjoyable experience Allow time to soak up the atmosphere of the place as well as marvelling at the art

A dramatic temple in Dambulla with a museum and a massive golden Buddha At the bottom of one set of steps up to the cave temples My advice is to walk to the cave temple up the kings steps and then to come down to the Golden Temple

Just back from Sri Lanka with my boyfriend and we visited Dambulla Caves for ~1 hour. We bought tickets at the bottom then had a long climb up the staircase to the caves. Several of the statues were very beautiful and impressive and the ceiling paintings, although fading, were fantastic. It would have been a great trip but there were too many tourists, which made it unpleasant. You have to remove your shoes before entering as it is sacred ground for Buddhists and, in the smallest of the caves particularly, this resulted in being trodden on by multiple sweaty tourists. We went at ~10-11 am, which perhaps was just a busy time so if going I would recommend being there first thing to avoid the crowds as I feel like we would have enjoyed it considerably more had it been quieter.

Perhaps it was ignorance on my part, but the actual entrance to the 'caves' is at the top of a very long, step staircase, on the summit of a mountain.  That alone wouldn't be a deal breaker.  However by mid day, the sun has been baking the stones at the top for hours, making them all excruciatingly hot.  Since al temples require the removal of footwear, its a painful experience walking around outside. The caves themselves are somewhat interesting, but honestly he entire feels like a gimmick.  They're not real caves, they're walled off cliffs.  The figures and art work are not significantly better than what you;d find in many other temples throughout the country.  Also currently an entry ticket is 1500r which is quite expensive for a site that isn't in the best of condition.

The entrance fee to this tourist attraction is 1500 ruppees. I was expecting a working temple with monks but instead found an exspensive busy, crowded tourist attraction. There are around 6 small caves with Buddhist statues inside each one which are hot and jammed packed with sweating, smelly tourists. If the temple is going to make this in to a tourist attraction which it is then they should provide fans to circulate the air and at least some information boards to what you are seeing! This place should be called Buddha land . Be prepared for the very long steep stairs to the entrance and also the fees you have to pay for taking your shoes off and checking them in.

I would best describe our experience of the caves as underwhelming. My first tip is to wear socks! That’s because you have to remove your shoes and between this area and the entrance, as well as inside the compound, the sun makes the stone floor very hot! My wife came away with scalded feet. The climb to the top is quite arduous but as you get near the top the views back over the countryside are impressive. The caves themselves are small and even hotter than outside. Ok the frescoes are quite impressive but once you’ve seen one Buddha you’ve seen them all! My advice would be to save yourself for the climb at Sigiryia and spend some time exploring the area around the Sigiryia rock which has some impressive caves which were inhabited as far back as prehistoric times.

Our stop at the Golden Temple was well worth our time and money. The walk to the top is nice, the cave temples are amazingly beautiful and we got some intimate time watching monkeys - perhaps a bit touristy watching the monkey business, but not something we see in the wild at home! I would highly recommend a visit - just remember to dress modestly as you are visiting temples.

An appx 100m climb brings you to the rock cave temple. You can choose between steps and slopes to climb. Steps are easier to climb up and slopes are easier for coming down. Though there isn't much on the top besides some statues of Buddha and some fresco Paintings on the ceiling. You can also see water trickling in a vessel kept in the cave which automatically goes back up into the natural rain water reservoir. Worth a visit only if you have spare time

We really enjoyed our experience at the cave temples however this could have been improved if there was more information on the history of the caves. Perhaps we should have paid for a guide as we would have liked to understand how they came about. Advice - both male and females HAVE TO cover their shoulders AND knees. It's a long walk up steep steps to be told you can't enter due to wrong clothing!! Overall a very good experience.
Caves with amazing statues and paintings. Full of funny monkeys asking for food Price for 2 persons 14€. I think is too expensive as a lot of attractions in Sri Lanka but was nice to go there

Really enjoyed the sites and the temple. Amazing statue and well worth seeing in person. JUST REMEMBER TO BRING SOMETHING COVER LEGS AND SHOULDERS. We didn’t so had to find alternatives otherwise you can’t go into the temple of the caves. Well worth a visit.
If you are in striking distance of this you must visit and make sure you have someone with you to explain its significance and history. Quite a steep assent but worth it.

This was an easy tour you can do independently without a guide. There are steep steps to overcome, but easily done! Entrance fee for foreigners were 1500rupees, not too much. The climb is worth it, the views, the cheeky monkeys and the statues are great.

I am writing this on behalf of my husband , we both had tickets to go to see the Cave temple but I am afraid the steps were too deep and too many for me to climb, approximately 300 steps , some I would not have managed as very short and not a young fit person.My Husband really enjoyed the visit . So go if you are fit enough. Remember this is a Temple, so long trousers, no bare arms No shoes or hats, Photo's can be taken.
it's a nice cave with lot of buddha statues. you can see so many monkeys as well. small hike to the top of the rock.

There are seven caves to explore, each one having extravagant Buddha statues. The climb up the back side we fun and a great view of the sun setting. We finished after dark and returned toward the main entrance.

We just did the caves, not the new temple. A good climb with extensive views, and a peaceful environment at the top, despite the numbers of tourists. Each cave has different statues of the Buddha and wall painting which we found fascinating.
Golden Buddha statue is a place to be at early mornings and evenings , have a good meditation and start the day well.

We arrived in the morning and the crowds weren't to big at all. We didn't find the climb strenuous at all. The caves were very interesting, we spend about an hour in total at Dambulla and felt this was enough.

There is different way to access the golden temple cave Follow the way after the golden Buddha as the ticket office isn't at the entrance of the cave You have stairs to access it so take your time it can be done easily but you might struggle if you never excersice
Well worth a visit if only for a short time. Free to enter but a donation is always acceptable but not harassed.

Go really early and be prepared for a climb. Steps are a little hazardous with some big and some little. Street sellers on way up and at top. The caves are amazing and you can hire a guide or alternatively buy a very cheap guide book. Very hot and busy. The toilets are very basic so be prepared. Well worth the effort

As others have said make sure you get a ticket before you go up all of the steps to the complex.  It is odd that they have tucked the ticket office round the back. Once you get to the caves the carvings & statues are amazing and well worth it. A guide (1000rps) is worth paying for to tell you all about it.
A temple built into a huge rock and hillside shared by the Buddhist and Hindu religions.A huge amount of Buddha statues and fresco's dating back to B.C.(I think)

Another must visit sight when touring the Cultural Triangle.  The caves are situated nearly 200 metres above the surrounding countryside and give some amazing views. This complex has 5 main caves, which date back 2000 years plus, though the frontage was built much later.  They contain over 150 Buddhas and figures of various other gods, and the ceilings of the caves are covered in countless murals. To reach the complex, you either climb some 500 steps or take a much easier route which has fewer steps and a lot of short inclines.  At the top there is a stall where you leave your shoes,few rupees needed and I would recommend taking a pair of old socks as the rock floor can get very warm and uncomfortable to walk on.Lots of monkeys about, so keep a close eye on your belongings and don't take food with you. Place is quite touristy, so lots of Hawkers about also.  Nevertheless, a World Heritage Site and should not be missed.
Historical tempal in dambulla .situated Kandy dambulla main road. Wear appropriate clothing as visiting an Asian temple.

The appeal of an ancient cave temple with statues and frescoes has been spoilt by modernising it with new entrances and buildings (corridors). I feel the originality has been lost with these new additions. One does not get the feel of how the monks must have lived there hundreds of years back because of the new additions.

Be sure to get there early to miss the crowds.  We got there for just before 9am.  Loads of steps to climb so make sure you are not hung over!  Worth the effort though. Such a wonderfully peaceful place.  Never fails to amaz how sculptures of such fine quality were carved out of the rock so many years ago. And the views aren’t bad either.

WOW. This place is incredible. It's a lovely walk up to the top (lots of steps but worth it) and the view is stunning. The caves themselves are just magical. I've never seen anything like them. I would say start at the furthest away one...then build up. The only thing that made it slightly less spiritual was that a lot of tourists were very loud and rather disrespectful. To me, it seems the perfect place to be quiet and take it all in. I've never been anywhere quite like it.
We went on our first day in Sri Lanka and loved it. We didn’t use a guide but would recommend as listened in on others and regretted not using one cause there was so much to learn.
We went on our first day in Sri Lanka and loved it. We didn’t use a guide but would recommend as listened in on others and regretted not using one cause there was so much to learn.

Beautiful gave temple: the walk uphill is doable, wear the appropriate shoes. Note: this is a temple, so cover your shoulders and knees! They do charge an entree fee, and about 25 Rs to store your shoes when you are up the hill. Note: monkeys will take your shoes! If you don’t want to pay for storage, put them in your bag. The temple is beautiful and impressive, several gave temples to visit. And take some time to view the sights around you.

This is really a must see if you are in the cultural center of Sri Lanka. The cave temples are very old and they are still very finely preserved. In total, there are five caves. Start from the fifth one and then move towards the first. Third and four caves are magnificent in terms of their scale and grandeur.

There is a lot of confusion in people about Golden Temple and the old Cave Temples of Dambulla. The Golden Temple (one with a giant Buddha golden statue) is a very new addition. The old cave temples are very old. The Golden Temple does not have much. Hence, it is better to go to Cave Temples which have huge caves and are spectacular.
It has a lot of history and worth a visit. The stairs are not for the faint hearted. Wear appropriate clothing as visiting an Asian temple. Carry water with you.
The caves are remarkably well cared for and are being lovingly restored. The walk up is not too long and there are some lovely views at the top. Enjoyable visit!
These caves and temple are seen to be believed. Truly magical and the ceiling paintings were awe inspiring....strict on dress code so shorts have to be below the knee and shoulders must be covered.

A bit of a climb and quite busy with tourists however well worth the effort to see these large and memorable caves with their many Buddhas and painted ceilings Lots of monkeys around scaling what seem to be sheer cliffs

Our trip coincided with a group from South Korea who started chanting. It was extremely moving and they were very friendly and welcoming. My wife was so moved she left in tears. We had a really good guide who was very knowledgeable.

A very impressive rock temple with beautiful carvings and tens, if not hundreds, of Buddha statues. It’s not difficult to find the ticket office unlike some reviews mentioned. Just, make sure you follow the Ticket Office signs before you start climbing up to the caves from the Golden Temple side. It’s very hard to miss the signs. It takes about 5-10 minutes to walk to the ticket office, which is on the back side of the rock but good thing is you start climbing right from there. It’s better to walk back down from the front side though (the Golden Temple side).
Actually it is nice reflection about buddha and buddhism. The location also really good. Climbing the small rock to reach the cave temple very enjoyble.

From the back car park (not where the new golden temple is), it’s 250 steps to where you leave your shoes (including signs saying not to put shoes in your bags, no doubt to give them more business), then it’s easy after that. Except that it’s full of tour groups and their noisy guides. The first cave has queues to squeeze yourself down to the end (the size of many tour group members makes it worse) to look at the faded gold reclining buddha. The other caves are much better, with big chambers, lots of statues and nicely painted walls. It’s a good attraction but it’s much more a tourist attraction than a temple and the 1,500 price is excessive.

The outstanding carvings into stone represented the amazing history of the Buddhist religion. The caves were surrounded by monkeys. The views were amazing and the history of the caves was so interesting. The only thing was you had to wear covering clothes and go bear foot but the carvings took you back in time.

It takes some stairs to climb before you reach the temple (tickets sold downstairs just after you leave parking lot!) but you will be rewarded by great views. It is very interesting set of buildings, very unique. Inside many many statues of Buddha. If you are not an expert or do not have any special relationship to Buddhism it can start to be a little bit boring after two rooms. Tuk tuk from Dambulla city center (clock tower) for 200 LKR one way.

If you've been to temples around the world, I would say don't attempt to compare this to those!  It's dark and atmospheric (as another reviewer wrote) but makes you feel as if you are in a place that should be revered.  The climb up must have made me feel that way as I would hardly do that for just anything *smile* And being required to take off your shoes before entering and forced to walk on the burning hot sidewalk will give you an appreciation to the thousands, perhaps millions, of visitors or monks that have come before you. The monkeys that move freely about the grounds are a tad aggressive and since I didn't have a scarf with me I had to rent one that probably hadn't seen soap or water since I was in high school but life is an adventure ;-) But once inside, the statues and artwork on the walls and ceilings are unforgettable...I don't want to spoil it for those lucky enough to see it in person but it is breathtaking! And this includes the views from the top of the temple! All in all, definitely worth a visit so please make the time to go!
Be prepared for a big climb, but worth it with great views and some neat historical artifacts at the top.Very interesting.
If you come from the side of Gold budha, you must go up turn left and down around the hill to the ticket counter. You must buy before hicking!

The Cave Temples are located on the hill top above the famous golden temple so it's quite a hike for uninitiated tourist. There are two approaches to the temples, the main stairs leading to the temples start beside the Golden temple and consist of wide paved steps but before you do any climbing be sure to get the tickets to the temples at the same counter as the Golden Temple tickets near the entrance or else you're in for a surprise when you get to the top (as we were). The paved route is lined with various vendors selling local handicrafts as well as beverages and snacks. Be sure to pick up a water bottle and something to nibble but watch out for the monkeys (more on that later). Anyways half way up, we buy a water bottle and the vendor asks if we bought our tickets, we hadn't so he told us we'd need to go back down the way we came. Confused we wondered what to do until he told us there was a second ticket counter down the other side of the hill which might be closer. Intrigued and up for a little walk around we took his advice and started down the other side of the hill. It was a deserted track and i started feeling suspicious of the way especially when it ended on a closed gate. A street hawker on the other side noticed us, realizing we were lost, pointed us to follow a track along the border wall which soon led to an opening in the wall. About 1000 meters down that back road led us to two small tourism buildings that looked hardly used where we purchased our tickets. The beauty of this adventure started here, for we had come to the little known and little used King's Staircase to the temples. Weathered and overgrown with tree roots in places it was a thinner and slightly tougher climb than the main staircase, but the views were worth it. Once we got to the top we had a long breather as the temples were temporarily closed for prayers (a gong was rung and food in trays was being taken into the temples so we assume it must be a ritual). We spent time admiring the view and the water lily pond until they opened again and we had a tour of each cave. I'm no history buff nor particularly spiritual in nature but for those who are it must be quite a site (and if you are one, get a guide although we didn't). Centuries old statues of Buddha added over years and years donated by different kings and different follower groups. Leaving down the main stairway we encountered more vendors and also had a chance encounter with a monkey. I had been holding in my hand a disposable plastic water bottle when i felt a sharp tug on the bottle. Turning around a cheeky little monkey had grabbed my bottle and tore a hole with its teeth into the bottom of the bottle. I'm not sure if the monkey knew that i would give up the water bottle after that or not but it got what it wanted and i walked away with a funny memory of it. All in all, i think the place is worth a short visit if you're moving by road between Dambulla and Kandy and want to get a dose of spirituality/exertion while in Sri Lanka.
Expensive place to visit. For younger people easier to climb all those stairs! Lower the fare and do not ask for too many donations as well

I went early in the morning and spent time alone in the caves. They are gorgeous.  Wall and ceiling paintings are some of the most exquisite in Sri Lanka. The sculptures are from various periods. I couldn’t find the image of Nissan????, the vainglorious, but since he was such a boaster, maybe the fact one cannot find the only extant image of him is fitting. This is a very different place than the other Buddhist sacred places.  Well worth the time

We really enjoyed our visit. Make sure to start the caves from the furthest away and work your way back so they get more impressive each time. The paintings and the Buddhas are amazing. Just remember that the ticket office is at the very bottom - it’s not remotely clear (the only sign is printed on a piece of a4 paper and stuck to the wall!) and we didn’t enjoy making the climb twice when we realised at the top that we’d missed it!

1 of the 8 UNESCO world heritage sites located in Sri Lanka. It's fairly easy to combine this with Sigiriya which is the main reason people come to this region. To get it you have to climb a fairly large staircase. A slight complaint is I found it really hard to find the booth where you buy the entrance tickets, 1500 lkr. You need to come here first, if you go to the top without a ticket you are coming right back down. I left my footwear right at the bottom so it involved me walking on a road in bare feet and getting a bit lost before I found, some more signposts would be appreciated. The complex is 5 rooms full of monkeys and Buddha statues. It's impressive but tbh I didn't find it that spectacular. Some of the Buddha statues are pretty big though. I wouldn't go out of my way to do it but if you have come to Sigiriya and some time to kill it's worth checking out.

The Cave Temples are for sure the highlight in Dambulla. Not only the temples are a great place to visit, you have also good views on the area around. Avoid going up during the mid-day heat and choose the afternoon: It's not as hot anymore and you the sunset light is beautiful. I'm not sure if it would be worth it to go make a long trip just to see the temples as there's not much else around (except the quirky Golden Buddha Temple), but if you are in the closer region then you should have a look.

Dambulla rock temple. There is an atmosphere inside where the buddhas are and you can’t miss that . You need to walk up some steps to get to the entrance and then leave your shoes . As usual with the foreign rate it’s much more to pay at 1500 rs than it’s worth as a exhibit You can also see the huge golden Buddha where there is a Buddhist museum . Just about worth 200 rs to get in .

A place of real magic! We cam here in the late afternoon, climbing the mountain from the backside. There are various caves carved into the mountain which open up to your eye once you enter. What an amazing array of Bhuddas everywhere, but most amazing are the paintings all over the walls and ceilings. After we've seen all caves, the sun was already getting low and we went outside of the temple to watch it set behind the sweeping landscape that unfolds to your eye. This was when real magic streamed all across the place! Good thing, this temple is a lot less crowded than many of the ohter more famous places in Sri Lanka so it was possible to really enjoy the sunset mood in a very peacful way. Highly recommended! Walking down the other side of the mountain towards the Golden Temple at the foot of the hill in the dark was easy. The Golden Temple itself is the opposite of what we experienced at the cave temple on top of the hill: This one is more like a Sri Lankan Disneyland. All too colorful, restored with a lot of bad taste ...

Short tuk tuk from Dambulla, then climb the stairs to the cave temple. Shoes off then pay entry fee (can't remember how much, a lot cheaper than the other WHSs). Five caves to visit, with multiple Buddha statues in each one. Dark and atmospheric. As we finished our tour, a group were worshipping, and sitting and listening to the chanting was quite relaxing. Walked down the other side of the mountain past the much newer Golden Temple and museum, then a short walk back to Dambulla.

These caves are beautiful and well worth the climb, which is not as bad as we thought it would be! If you don't want to queue and pay to leave your shoes outside, just pop them in your bag and go in. Remember to take socks as the floor gets extremely hot and will burn your feet.

We visited here today on our tour, the climb was steep however there were little areas where you could stop along the way to catch your breath and have a drink. The view was fantastic and there were plenty of opportunities to take some pictures and get right up on the edge of the mountain.

Wonderful sight!  There are quite a few stairs to walk up (we saw many monkeys along the way) but definitely worth the effort.  Each of the 5 caves is a bit different, all wonderful, in excellent condition.  You will be mesmerized!

Amazing temple set in hill top caves. The photos tell the story of what is inside this cave. Well worth the climb and spending some time here.
Very beautiful, defiantly worth seeing. Its busy though so try and go in the morning rather than the afternoon

Of course it is a Buddhist temple thus almost all the statues represent Buddha and some of them are huge. Impressive place that shouldn't be missed.
If you want only to see 1 temple in Sri Lanka than this is the one: 2000 Years old and fantastic statues and paintings!

The temples are very nice, nothing I have seen before. The caves are also hot, I thing I did not expect
A 2100 years old temple in natural caves. The 7 poses of Lord Buddha captured in natural stone in all the 5 caves. Fascinating, Awed by the historical architecture and ambience.
