The climb to the top which is about 1,000 feet above mean sea level is rather exhaustive but you could enjoy a bird's eye view of the surrounding scenary of jungles, mountains and the lakes on your way up. The temple comprise of several caves and all have numerous reclinging, seated and standing statues of Lord Buddha and His disciples. You could observe the famouse water sprout which does not go dry during the entire year, dripping water from the roof of the main cave. The Golden Cave Temple is of very high religious value to the Buddhists in addition to being a place of great historical significance in the country dating back to 1st century BC to the times of King Valagambahu who unified the country following a period of turmoil.

This was a great surprise when I first entered the cave temple. I was blown away from all the frescos on each wall and ceiling. What I love about wall paintings, is it tells you a story. Within the cave temples are many Buddhas in different mudra positions.

There is quite a long set of stairs leading to the Rock Temple, which is partially doubled by a stony slope. The ascent is quite long but not tiresome. The Rock Temple itself consists of several caves, each containing impressive statues and paintings in a very atmospheric environment. The whole place is surrounded by a fence with barbed wire, presumably, against monkeys, which created a funny impression that I was an exhibit in a zoo for monkeys. The place is really great and impressive, but as for me, considering the amount of people crowding the place, and quite a steep entrance fee of Rs 1500 per person, there are some much more secluded and not significantly less impressive temples in Sri Lanka.

Best to do in the afternoon, not in direct sunlight as can get hot. Wear socks. You have to take shoes off before you enter and the stone is HOT!! The caves are lovely, but there is no information about what anything is, if you want a history lesson read up on it first! We were in and out within an hour. TIP; there is a man in a shack next to the temple entrance where you put shoes. He got very angry about us and our shoes as we wanted to put them in our backpack. He charges 25SLR p/p to look after them for you. Either take your shoes off before he sees you. OR just be firmer with your 'NO' than we were. His lack of english threw us and we ended up giving him money, but other people didn't take any of his nonsense and hide their shoes/put them in their bag.

The climb to the Temple is challengingly steep but well worth it to see the way in which the temple was built into the rock.  Take your time and carry water with you.  We did it on the same day as climbing the Sigirya Lion Rock so we sure knew about it the day after.

Don't be put off by the steep initial climb to get to the caves. It's a stunning place when you get  there, not to be missed. Both our daughters 2 and 5 climbed up with some carrying for the little one. You must take shoes off at the top so if it's a hot day, plan some socks or the slab stones are burning hot.

One of the must see in Sri Lanka is the Golden Temple in dambulla. Although we planned to climb up the evening, but since we reached late we climbed up the next morning. Not much difficulty. The scenes from the top of the hill are amazing. The paintings inside the caves are amazing. Worth a visit

A few of the (5) cave temples are spectacular, the others are nothing that special. The sunset view from the top of the hill with the temples is supposed to be great but it wasn't the best weather when I was there, so I can't comment. The temples don't take very long to visit, you'll probably spend longer walking up and down to them than you will at the temples themselves. Shoes must be removed at the entrance and modesty observed. Be careful to make sure you buy a ticket before you start the climb to the temples - the ticket office isn't obvious or well signposted. The other attractions at this site probably aren't worth bothering with. The towering Golden Budda is worth a quick look but it's contemporary and very kitsch.
The temples are built beneath granite caves near tge top of the hill. Some of the temples are very old. All are beautifully done and show great reverence for the Buddha.
Visit this Temple innovember so pretty and well conservated.yo can spend maybe 1 hour and half, need  to use stairs , comfortable shoes.

We made the climb up to the Temple complex fairly early and spent a lovely hour or so looking around the 5 'caves'. They were all fairly similar although different in size, though this is not a criticism, as they were all worth seeing for the subtle differences. You need to wear long pants or a sarong. If you forget this there is a stall outside which will hire you one for 200/rs. They look after your shoes for 25/rs a pair too so both reasonable rates.

The cave is beautiful and reserved well.  It is quite a long walk to the cave.  But remember it's worthwhile.  You need to remove shoes to get in .   Bring socks to protect from the heated floor.  Wear long shirt and pant.
Sunset is beautiful Paintings in caves A lot of buddhas But some Chineese tourists were too noisy in the temple

Typical of most Sri Lankan attractions, this requires an effort to get up to it, and some of it is bare rock, but the steps (which is most of the way) are well graded.  The temple and caves at the top are very impressive, with five caves of varying size and all offering something different.  The two larger caves have multiple statues which are amazing, but don't miss the painting of the ceilings as they are not to be missed.

So we arrive and follow the signs to go pay....the office is closed and no staff around to ask so we decided to walk up as we assumed you must pay at the top. Upon arrival we were told to go back down as they did not sell tickets and the office was open and must be mistaken. Then to be told we must be lying was hilarious - after arguing for about 15 minutes one of the workers decided to call down to the office to see if they were indeed closed. Alas! No answer - the look on his face was pretty priceless and I have to say that alone was worth the walk up the stairs. His reply was simple - he's gone for lunch, go back down and wait. Fantastic service - high fives all around....not. Upon our descent down from the unseen caves the office was opening back up again. The sign showing opening times isn't displayed on the outside of the office..oh no the clever person assigned that job decided to put the sign very intelligently I might inside the actual office. So if one was to close the office, the sign would be unseen unless you were actually locked in the office! To add more positives the guy who had gone for his lunch and closed the office just shrugged his shoulders and laughed. lol is the only word that comes to mind?

I love Buddhist temples and this one is very ancient and inspiring. BUT. If you have limited time, just go on to Sigiriya, the real must see. AND. If you go when it is very hot, you MUST take some water along for the long stair climb up and down. AND socks too, so that the very HOT path into the final part of the temple when you have to go barefoot doesn't burn your soft feet!

The Dambulla cave temples are a great attraction for those interested in the cultural heritage of Sri Lanka. The statues, paintings and other relics are beautiful and very interesting. The cave temples are also great for photographers looking to capture some interesting shots which include the surrounding landscape and the cheeky macaques. It is a bit of a climb to get to, but any reasonably healthy person can make it. It only requires a short visit so I would recommend this attraction as stop along route between the ancient cities and Kandy.

Historic Temple Caves.  You have climb for about 20-25 mins steps... quite steep...but worth the effort.  For foreigner please buy your ticket at the lower level .. otherwise a hassle at the entrance. Beautiful Caves.. very well done up and all historic.. makes one wonder how they could have done it

The Wandering Yank here again.  It was a hot day, and we had already climbed Sigiriya that morning, but after recharging at lunch we ready for another climb, although not nearly as taxing.  The caves are loaded with beautiful Buddhist statues and paintings on the walls and ceilings, something we had never seen before.  Very well worth the visit. Note:  apparently you will get in trouble if you pose for photos with the Buddhas, so don't do it.  There are CCTV cameras in the caves.
A place that definitely have to visit. When we are faced with the logo of Buddha gold statue. You can take great photos. I recommend

A place that definitely have to visit. When we are faced with the logo of the world's largest Buddha statue. To enter the caves you need to pay to get in and to get there we have to climb a bit. We will finding algumcomércio and some monkeys to reach the entrance. Before entering you must take off your shoes. In the caves we found many rooms and each room has the Buddha statues. Be aware that there is a period where we have to wait to visit the rooms. It was 1PM and had to wait a while to get into the rooms. There is a certain mysticism around the site. I recommend
It does look magnificent. It's apparently the biggest Buddha statue in the world...but boll nothing extraordinary...

This is truly a must see. A magnificent temple set into the rock face with a splendid and impressive outlook over the surrounding area. The climb is not for the faint hearted but get there if you can its worth the climb. Must have a bottle of water and remember to cover up to comply with the local modesty requirements. You will have to remove your shoes but socks are permitted and in my opinion required.
Rich in historical and religious background, the Golden Cave temple is a sacred place of workship. It has a vast Buddha statue collection and the most intricate cave ceiling paintings.

It’s a hot climb up several hundred steps or a steep pathway.  Don't be put off by the giant, gawdy golden Buddha haunting the entrance – the actual cave complex is beautiful with the various caves housing reclining buddhas, intricately painted rock surfaces and various stuppas.  We have visited many Buddhist sites in Asia and this one contains some of the best preserved Buddhist art we have seen.  Well worth the visit.

The Golden Temple & Golden Cave Temple are in one place. Also known as Dambulla Rajamaha Viharaya. Entree fee is US$10 / LKR 1,500. Free entry to sri lankan people. Cave temple is very unique & worth visiting. Place is around 1-2km walkable distance from dambulla bus stop. You will find this temples in main road so easy to find them. You can cover this place within 2-3 hours time. Perfect time to visit is after 4 pm. Check the pictures posted with this review.

I respect the reverence that a place such as this cave temple has for hard-core Buddhists but after seeing one, the rest all look the same. The climb up is not too strenuous for the moderately-fit person.

We went here as part of a three day tour. We really enjoyed it. It does get very warm the smaller the caves go so take plenty of water with you. You are surposed to see miracle water running up a wall and across the top of the cave. We believed it to be an optical illusion. Lots of great Budas to see. Not sure about all the orange budist 'plastic looking' monks you see when you go to the bathroom and the plastic molded fence I think this takes some of the specialness from the temples.

Get ready for the hike up the steps, but the art work in the caves are unbelievable. It is just am amazing site to see and does not take much time visit. You can complete your visit here in one hour unless you really hang around for more experience.
Stunning and unique site - some of the best ancient Buddhist art in the world. Be aware that it is over 900 steps if visiting in the middle of the day.

Reading some of these reviews - the 240 steps were nothing compared to Sigiriya Rock Fortress.  If you are in half decent shape = no problem.  I thought it was over-priced to essentially see one buddah statue after another.  No criticism about Buddah, I admire the reverence, however for about $80 (entrance fee for 2 people + a guide) - it really wasn't worth it. What makes the walking, steps cumbersome is that as a man or woman - you have to wear long pants or a sarong wrap to cover your legs (knees).  This is a hot place March to August, so be prepared to sweat (a lot).  Inside the caves there is no air movement, so it's like a sauna.  Being outside in the open sun is a bit of a relief. Other words of advice - you will be constantly hit up by locals to buy this trinket or that.  We felt like broken records = "no thank you".  Bring a pair of socks you can afford to get dirty because you will need to take your shoes off to enter the temples which traverse very hot stones.  You WILL experience pain bare-footed if 1) you aren't used to walking on rocks in your bare feet, 2) if you don't have thick calluses to take the very hot rocks, 3) if you combine 1 + 2 where you will be walking fast to get to the shade. About an hour and a half tops to take this in.

The cave temples were beautifully fascinating but at the same time were ruined by the constant interruptions by 'tour guides' who just targeted the tourists and asked for money for basically pointing at a Buddah. It made us feel on edge and nervous about talking to people as eveytime we did we were asked for money, very odd considering we paid a good amount to even enter. These people approach you with their love for Buddah but clearly just want your money. Im glad we visited the temples as we learnt a lot and the views was fantastic however the museum was extremely poor and the toilets.....well.....no comment.

One of the finest Buddhist temples In Sri Lanka, that I've seen. Be prepared - there are around 240 steps to climb, but it is absolutely worth the effort. There are 5 caves (the oldest being 22 centuries old) that show dozens of Buddha statues. Local guide will gladly share his knowledge with you for any small gratuity - do not hesitate to hire one. And don't forget to cover your shoulders (truosers or skirt have to be knee-lenght), because at the entrance they charge you for hiring sarong. Visit  to Dambulla Golden Cave Temple was half-day excursion for us, and we all loved it.

Be ready for a very steep climb up 250+ steps to a large complex of a number of budhist temples in caves. Each enclosure contained different Buddhas. We thought it was quite impressive and worth the effort in the extreme heat.

This is another punishing site as far as access goes - lots of steps and quite hard work. The five caves contain 157 images of Buddha and there are 22,000 square feet (about 2,200 square metres) of wall and ceiling paintings. We enjoyed our visit, but the toilet facilities are dreadful - very smelly!
This temple is magical with many Budda figures and wall paintings. Dambulla is a World Hertitage site and is the most impressive of the Sri Lankan cave temples

I went to Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa and Sigiriya, but the rock temple at Dambulla was by far the most impressive of the 4. A steep climb in the heat, but then you are treated to 5 caves of intricate carvings and paintings. The caves are a welcome relief from the heat. There are also good views from the hilltop across to Sigiriya. Well worth a trip.
A good trek up. View as you go up and at the top is quite nice. Some nice Buddha statues in the temple but not really worth the entrance fee. Spent 30-45min here.

These caves are pretty spectacular!  This is easily one of the most amazing Buddhist sites that I have ever visited and well worth going out of your way to visit.  It has been a pilgrimage site for 22 centuries and has over 100 Buddha statues.  This was one of the most memorable experiences from my trip.

Stunning, we climbed up in the late morning, and it was VERY hot! Plan water, and good shoes (not flip-flops, doable but makes the climb trickier). Stunning caves, make sure you don't pose next to Buddha for the photos as it is forbidden. Take some flowers for offerings, always nice to get closer to the local culture and the people. Wear decent clothes as it is after all a sacred place and people go there to pray... The paintings are gorgeous with stunning colours. It's a must during your journey!
---> Buy your ticket before getting to the top (I know that may be strange but we met someone who has had to go down to buy the ticket)

The climb to the caves is about 350 steps, but worth every step.  What awaits you at the end are five spectacular caves, which I considered the highlight of my trip to Sri Lanka.  And this was despite the fact that we climbed all the way up under pouring rain, which made ascending and descending a bit tricky, but gave it a charm of its own.

A steepish climb up stairs on the mountainside to five rock caves dating back to the first century BC, but which continued to be added to up to the mid eighteenth century. The caves contain incredible murals, every inch is painted - the ceilings are particularly impressive - and there are hundreds of Buddha statues in various poses. Another huge Buddha overlooks the centre at the bottom, and the bright colours are really something! We went on a clear day and had a good view of Sigiriya rock in the distance from the walk back down. It wouldn't be accessible for those with mobility issues as far as I am aware.

This series of five caves dating back to the 1st century BC is filled with a large number of statues of Buddha in various sizes and postures as well as mudras.  The array is quite startling, as are the paintings and frescoes adorning the walls and ceilings, though these are of a somewhat later date.  Across the front of the cave entrances is a long white building erected by the British during the Colonial period to help preserve the caves and their contents and, from the terrace in front, one can see across the surrounding temperate jungle.  It should be noted that the caves are about 300-350 ft above the car park area and the climb is quite steep, but easily manageable by anyone with any degree of fitness, despite the high temperatures!
the many Buddhas in different postures are most interesting, all set in caves, with fantastic paintings on the ceilings , being the oldest and largest in South Asia.

amazing site, renowned as the temple of the infinite Buddhas. it was the place of religious worship when the capital was at Anuradhapura. it was donated to the monks by royalty. The paintings inside the shrines are the largest and oldest in South asia. A no-miss!!

If you're visiting the impressive Cave Temples, you might as well make a small detour into the Golden Temple.  The 100ft high golden buddha is hard to ignore, as you enter directly beneath it (and through the mouth of a slightly pretentious dragon), and the interior, which contains statues, manuscripts and paintings, is interesting, without being stunning.

One of the oldest Buddhist shrine in Sri Lanka. located in the heart of dambulla...easy to locate and reach to the site. The interesting site is the caves which consist of Buddha's statues.. its apprx. 300-350 ft to the caves from the ground level. Concrete steps available to climb to the peak of the rock. Its ban to climb to the top of the rock and travelers can climb only up to the caves. The rock surface (inside the caves) entirely covered with paintings...
Significant buddhist site. Beautiful reclining buddhas and very peaceful.  It would be good to visit early in the day.  It's a hot walk up the hill.

It deserves the visit in your tour by Sri Lanka. The history of Rock Temple goes back to the first century B.C., commenced by the King Vattagamini Abhaya. Within these caves is housed a collection of 157 amazing images of Buddha
i liked to walk and the stairs to reach the temple, very interesting to walk especially when the monkeys pass by all the time,,, don't be scare don't won't harm

We arrived on a Sunday and were able to see 'Sunday school' with the children dressed in white National costume listening to a monk. Unexpectedly a steeper climb than I had expected but worth the effort to get to the top even if you need stops to 'admire the view'. We knew shoes have to be removed at the entrance of the caves (10p a pair from memory) and had taken thick non slip socks to wear as we had read the entrance was quite dirty.  This was not what we found and we would have happily have walked round barefoot. The frescoed caves are beautiful and a must see.
You will reach the caves after a climb so get prepared! The frescoed caves are very beautiful with more than 1000 statues of meditating buddha. View from the top is interesting too.

Access to the cave temples was via a fairly step climb in, which was very hot in the daytime, and there was little opportunity to stop on the way up for our guide to point out things of interest. Incredible when you get to the top though! A guide is vital to get the best from a visit, as tours added a lot of interesting information that I had missed on my previous visit, 12 years ago. One thing that I did remember from my previous visit though, was to make sure I carried a pair of socks with me to use when I had to remove my flip flops to enter some of the outdoor areas. Last time, I nearly burnt the soles on my feet!

The site is accessed by walking past a very large golden buddha and up a number of steps. Although quite high up it is not so strenous a climb and worth the effort. At the top there are 5 caves built into the rock hillside each containing old reclining buddhas.
You need to climb up and up and the paintings and statues in the caves open up. Amazing paintings, still well preserved and the statues take you back to the period in history
Excellent location and a site worth visiting, even if you are not religious type. Buddha statue is really big and imposing.
The ancient temple was carved out of a rock facade. Some of the statues of Buddha were carved out from the rock inside the cave. The statues were beautifully painted with natural paints.

While not a real culture addict, I really did find these caves fascinating.  Try to go in the early morning, as it gets pretty hot here.  There are Macaque monkeys everywhere, they were really fun to watch too.

I can't comment on price as that was included in the tour costs. The entrance is fantastically, um, yes, I'm going to say tacky again, although the huge Golden Buddha is impressive at night. The caves, frescoes and statuary are really, really worth seeing. Go late afternoon and you may get treated to a fantastic sunset.

The caves are really nice. Loads of Buddha's and awesome paintings on the ceiling that look like velvet. Go there so you exit the caves before sunset, the view is great in the company of the monkeys! Only downside is the price. As in a lot of places in Sri Lanka the entrance fee is rediculous. 1500 Rs is absurd.

I would definitively recommend a trip to the caves if you are visiting Dambulla. Really interesting experience. We went early in the morning as it can get very hot in the caves and hiking up the steps to the entrance. Watch out for the monkeys that wander round and even in the caves. Don't carry food.

We decided afterwards that we probably wouldn't have bothered with this if we did our trip over. It is very overpriced (about 15usd). The caves are interesting and the walk up is fun with lots of cute monkeys to be seen. The view from the top isn't that fantastic and the site itself is not maintained very well at all, so I cannot understand how they justify the fee. Take socks with you because you must remove your shoes and the ground is scolding hot from the sun.

This popular temple charges an outrageous US$15 for foreigners to tour, but nothing for Sri Lankans. It dates back to the 3rd century BC.  Its frescoes are most interesting but the many statues of Buddha become repetitive when one has viewed a few. This temple must be raking in millions of $A a year but has only a mud carpark, while the toilets at entrance level are squat type.  There is no acknowledgement of how Western visitors are only used to cistern type seated toilets. In wet weather, the steps and alternative granite equivalent of.a ramp are dangerous.  While we were there a Buddhist monk and a Western female visitor fell. Charing R25 for safekeeping of shoes is a ripoff that the entrance charge should cover.  The shoes were poorly protected from the rain with visitors being forced to take them off and put them on again in the open.  Not much good if the heavens have opened. There is an attached Buddhist museum that due to its even more slippery steps I did not visit.

Breathtaking art: cave painting and rock carving. If one takes the time and has the benefit of a good guide, the subtleties of each of the four caves are most interesting.  We weren't sure what to expect - it was simply billed as "on route (from Kandalama to Kandy), visit the Caves at Dambulla" so it far exceeded our expectations! A steep and quite long climb from the car park, but needless to say, worthwhile!

Interesting place but I have visited something similar in Dunhuang (China). The Chinese one is at least 10 times the size of Dambulla. At 1500 rupees, it is a bit pricey for the size of the place. We left our shoes near the entrance but some guy manning a kiosk collected them and was asking 25 rupees to get them back. Not much money but I dislike people trying to take advantage of me.
4 caves with similar statues and paintings...visit only if you have plenty of time.

There's quite a few steps leading up to the caves, but take your time, they're not hard steps so plenty of resting places along the way. The view on the way up is beautiful and lots of monkeys across the path providing entertainment. The caves themselves are preserved well, some have been restored so colours are brighter. The lives and Buddha is documented in the caves, there are 4, one big main one. It's definitely an interesting site to visit and I thoroughly enjoyed it
Located close to Dambulla, It was an interesting temple complex, very large and a long walk up the hill to the temple caves but easy to find with the very large Golden Buddha next to the highway.
Even on a cloudy day the climb up the stairs to the top were the caves are is a decent workout. Worth your while though.
This is one of the best temple i've ever seen, its worth the trip up, ascending by the stairs are all worth it once you see whats inside the temple cave.

This is an absolute awesome place to visit. One of the beautiful attractions. The location is in central srilanka and takes about 4 - 5 hours by car from colombo. I think the best way to visit is like we did - we got in srilanka early morning and it was a good decision to directly drive to Dambulla. We slept on the way and got breakfast too. Going to colombo and then out again would have costed us about  2 hours more! There is a bit of climb but it is certainly worth it. Beautiful place to visit and make sure you take your camera and water along!

This is not, as some told me, simply a walk up hill to get to the Cave Temples.  It's fairly strenuous if you are not a hiker or accustomed to such, so don't say I didn't tell you!  I'm in pretty good shape, but was huffing and puffing toward the end. When you get up there, enjoy the view, it's pretty awesome.  Also, be prepared to take off your shoes before entering the temple area.  It's perfectly safe to leave them with a guy who will charge you a few rupees.  But, if being barefoot bothers you, bring socks. The caves are pretty amazing and wondrous.  Our group hired a guide to tell us more about what we were looking at and I recommend it.  It will enrich your experience and it doesn't cost much.  After all, you climbed all that way didn't you!?

Dambulla Cave Temple is - as many temples - situated on a top. There are quite many steps, but it is worth to walk up. The different rooms are fantastic - very colorful - and it is much different what what we have seen in other places. We recommend to use the shoe stand before the entrance - it costs almost nothing and your shoes will not be taken by the naughty monkeys. The toilets at the entrance need a serious update.

It was a hot day when we visited the Golden Temple and a hard climb up the many steps to reach the shrine caves at the top. But it was well worth the climb to see this Buddhist Temple that dates back to the 3rd Century BC. The paintings and statues are magnificent and our guide was excellent relaying to us the history of the five caves.

The entrance is a bit touristy, but massive in its scale for your attention in not the gaudy way.  You must climb multiple stairs, and then some more, to reach the top.  Two things before you begin you ascent: bring water and buy your ticket at the bottom.  Oh, and realize they close at 12:30 for lunch.  It is only 30 minutes, but it can throw are schedule off especially if you did like me and just stopped there to continue on to another location.  The vendors will badger you, especially if you are a Westerner.  Once you stop, you will be stopped by all. The caves themselves are quite nice.  Rooms, small and large, filled with Buddhas and Stupas of varying size and position (well, the Buddhas in the latter respect).  For me, it was the atmosphere and the incredible views that made it worth while.  Definitely worth it.

Great place to get out of the sun! The cave temple is different than the other temples we have seen throughout the country. It is quiet, serene, and has 5 different rooms to walk through. Its a bit of a hike up to the top, so be prepared to sweat a little!

Cave is a relative term, but the Golden Cave Temple was really interesting to see. In my opinion a guide is worth it to explain everything even though you will only be here about an hour or so. I will note that though it might look like it you do not need to pay the shoe stand to keep your shoes, you can just leave them by the entrance a few meters away.
The Golden Cave Temple complex is another must visit and experience while in Sri Lanka. Everything housed in the caves is most inspiring.

The "hike" up the mountain was pretty cool as we were entertained by a family of monkeys who were swimming in one of the pools. The caves are pretty cool too. There was a gentle man who works at the temple who offered to show us around and explain us the history of the cave. I would suggest you take this service as you get a very interesting history lesson, rather then just going and taking a bunch of pictures. A good place o visit for 2 hours.

I have seen many stupas and buddist temples and I thought this was just another one in the row. I argued with myself whether I should spend the 1500 rupies for the ticket or not. Luckily I decided to enter, and what a magnificent area. I can very well understand that it has a place on UNESCO's world heritage list. After climbing a number of steps you come to the top of a hill. You have a wonderful view over the region. Here you have to leave your shoes and walk through the main entrance. In front of the temple there is a nice yard from where you can see the monastry cut in the steep mountain walls. From the yard you can easily enter the four caves, one by one. I have never seen so many buddafigures in one place before. They were mainly situated along the walls. A special atmosphere is around the whole place. A little funny when one of the monkeys saw his chance to eat some food that a worshipper had sacrified on an alter.

Established as a temple in 1st century BC and continuesly developed by various Sri Lankan Kings until 18th century. There are 5 caves with beautiful paintings and Buddha Statues. Tickets will be 1500 rupees per person. Nearly 1 hour climbing but not steep so any age can do this place with reasonable timings. Best time to go is in the morning or evening as you can avoid heat. Please do forget to wear long cloths which covers your shoulders and knees. Please don't take pictures 1,holding statues, 2,showing your back towards to statues or 3,with sitting on benches in caves. You will be in trouble,if you make any unproper behaviours in the caves as there are CCTV cameras in action.

This series of caves and temples gives a real insight into Buddhism. An amazing place.  The enormous golden Buddha is visible from Sigiriya (about 20km away). We loved being able to lay an offering of flowers in one of the caves. Don't carry fruit or other food up with you - we watched a group of American tourists get terrorised by the monkeys as they stole their food.

See my other Sri lanka reviews as they come on line Don't forget to buy your ticket before you start climbing any steps .... When we entered we were immediately approached by a guide offering his services, this was an invaluable source of information and without him we would only have known what we had read and looked at a large number of Buddhas in ignorance. I would definately recommend one. The caves were amazing and well worth a visit, like anywhere in Sri lanka take lots of water, and a suitable shoulder / leg covering for women. Funny Monkies to photograph too
Steep climb so go early or late. Well worth the climb as impressive and spiritual. Don't moan about the 1500 rupee entrance one 25 rupee shoe protection money - all good value!
We did not have much time to spend here so viewed the temple only from the outside. The temple building is heavily decorated in colorful objects. It is a sight to behold.

site is definitely not to be missed! one detail: mind buying your ticket before ascending the stairs and hill! ticket counter is right from the big buddha statue, note that staff will send you back all the way down if you haven't got a ticket yet....

The view of the Buddha looking down on the entrance is strikingly imposing. As one climbed the steps and flat rock to the left hand side, one couldguage how large the Buddha statue really was. The climb to the caves is not easy for those over a certain age but if done at a slow pace, then the summit can be reached. The caves are most interesting and as with most tourist attractions should be viewed with a guide. A bonus was the view of the surrounding hills and countryside.

The first sight of the Golden Buddha statue - rising in the distance from among the trees - is awesome ( much over-used word, but in this case justified). The precincts are remarkably quiet for such an attraction, even though we went in the late afternoon. My guidebook says the climb to the cave temples takes 10-15 minutes. Are you an Olympic athlete? It takes 20-30 minutes unless you are very young and very fit. And anyway the views on the way are worth a stop!! The temples are quite overwhelming, with so many different images of the Buddha and his disciples. It's worth either going with a guide or having a good guide book to appreciate all the differences between the caves and the images. It's possible to take pictures, but in the end I bought some postcards as it's not possible to take good photos without some tourist's head, arm or back suddenly coming into view! This place (like Polonurawa) is essential if you want to understand the history of Sri Lanka and how it is tied in with Buddhism.
The climb to the Dambulla cave temple is quite tiring and their are monkeys along the way who snatch things from ur hand. They have 5 temples with good paintings on the walls and budha statue.
Its a nice and huge Buddha and we went around sunset time so the climb wasnt too hectic. They have a charge for foreigners and the temple is open till 9pm

Price 1500 rupees. Same price in Taj Mahal, but ticket in Taj Mahal include Red Fort, free shoes service and free toilet. Place of course interesting, but with not adequate price and service. Enough one hour for visit. To more expensive Sri Lankan places we don't go. We saw more interesting places with adequate prices.

I always have to confess that these type of places are not big on my agenda. These caves have a great feeling of reverence about them. The climb up is a little steep but nothing serious. The monkeys are particularly cheeky. Not advisable to carry food. They will grab. There are five caves, fairly similar. It is easy to see how they have been cut out of the rock and it is hard not to be impressed. There is also a small Hindu temple within the complex.

The largest golden statue in the world is very tacky and gaudy, apparently provided by Chinese money.  We didn't go into the museum.  NOTE - schoolboy error, the ticket booth for the caves is located at the bottom of the hill, not in the museum, but to the right of the statue in the car park.  Do not do as we did, and climb the hill, only to have to return to the bottom to purchase a ticket!!! It is a steady climb up, lots of trinket sellers and naughty monkeys.  At the top, you have to leave your shoes and it costs 25 Rs for their return.  I saw someone try to bypass this, by leaving their shoes under a nearby bench, and avoid paying 25 Rs!  He was foiled because the shoe keeper, just picked them up and placed them on his shelf anyway, and he still had to pay the 25 Rs for their return anyway.  This was a highlight of my visit.  Again, lots of scabby dogs and puppies around. Inside the caves there are lots and lots of buddahs.  Some standing, some recumbent.  Some painted, some not.  The cave roofs are painted also, some are very vibrant.  It was just a bit touristy for me - although some people were praying, it just wasn''t quite there for us.  There are beautiful views from the outside, but lots of rubbish, thrown over the fence and just tumbling down the mountain side.  Cost about £7.50 each so worth a visit but not our favourite.  Much preferred the Aluvihara Temple we visited at Mathale.

We enjoyed this temple. We are relative novices when it comes to Buddhism.  The temple was a good place to start our learning journey. The caves are very interesting as are the various statues of Buddha.  It is worth having a guide to explain the site to make the most of it if your knowledge is on a similar level.  Our kids of course enjoyed watching the monkeys that are there.

After reading the mixed reviews on this site, we decided to give it a try and we were so happy we did!  There are alot of stairs so I'd recommend that you do this in the AM--we did it in the afternoon and took advantage of every shady spot!  Also-another good reason to do this in the morning is that you must remove your shoes and the stones get very hot during the middle of the day.  The temple is built into a cave with amazing ceilings, Buddhas...It is really amazing!

I dunno why they have to charge $10 to see this, its kinda steep. The caves are cool to see, but nothing that will blow you away. Add in hordes of tourists shoulder to shoulder in the caves, and a really sweaty 15 min uphill walk to the caves, and i give this place a so-so review. Certainly not a must-see.
Worth a visit if you enjoy culture and art. The rooms are similar but all very beautiful. The climb is steep and remember to cover your knees!
Set in natural caves, many Buddhas carved from the stone.  Be prepared to walk up steep hill and take your water bottle with you.  Guides at the top to take you round, very hot though!

Worth a visit if you're going north/south from/to Kandy and want to stretch your legs during a 4 hour bus trip, but not really worth a detour. Though of historical importance, cave temples alike (and probably less crowded) can be found all over the country. Unless, of course, you're a temple/Buddhist enthusiast and really look forward to seeing the beautiful paintings inside. Ignore the kitschy golden Buddha at the entrance of the staircase. Also, I wouldn't recommend the climb up to the temples to people with poor health, especially during the warmest hours of the day.
It was a steep walk up to the caves which were filled with old statues of the Buddha. Lots of cave paintings on the roof. Worth a visit.
There are other places worth spending time such as the Sigiriya Rock Fortress. If you are a Buddhist then I am sure this would be fascinating.
I thought the statues and paintings were well worth the climb which wasn't very hard.  The time frame on these paintings was impressive.

During our visit to Dambulla, we visited this Golden Temple of Buddha. This is a World Heritage Site in Sri Lanka, situated in the Central part of the country. This Golden Temple is located at a distance of  about 150 Kms,  East of Colombo and around  75  Kms North of Kandy. It is said that this Golden Temple  is the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka. The gigantic statue of Buddha in Golden color, gives a  gallant appearance at the entrance. In the Golden Temple,the paintings and statues are related to Lord Buddha and his life. There are about  more than 150 Buddha statues and  3 statues of Sri Lankan Kings. The history says that King Valagambahu had plans to convert these caves into a temple in the 1st century BC, but exiled from Anuradhapura and sought refuge here from South Indian usurpers for 15 years. After reclaiming his capital, the King built a temple to worship and many other kings added to it later.  The caves had become a major religious center. Further King Nissanka Malla gilded the caves and added about 70 Buddha statues in 1190. The caves were restored and painted by the Kandyan Kings.in the 18th Century. It took us about 45 minutes to go round the temple and we enjoyed our visit to this temple.

We went here on a rainy day so the walk up here wasn't very pleasant. Entrance fee 1500rupi p.p Shoewatch 25rupi p.p The temple is under a rock, but calling it a cave-temple is a bit exaggerated. Would recommend this temple for buddhists and those who love visiting temples. Not a must when in Dambulla!
For enjoying the whole thing take a guide! There a some guys in front of the temple. Its worthy when you know so mich about that Religion!

After reading about the place, I was excited to see 150 Buddha statues in different caves. Since this was my first visit to a Buddhist temple, I quite liked the aura around it. To reach here was a steep climb, so one must wear comfortable shoes, and wear fully covered clothes since its required as per the customs. There were lot of monkeys who wud come rummin to you if you had flowers for offering as they ate the inside of the flowers. If you have been to Buddhist temples, you might it copy paste similar Buddha statues.

If you are not a buddhist that place will probably really bore you out of your mind. I don't remember the exact price, but it was hefty for what you get. You also have to climb up a very steep hill to see a bunch of copy-paste buddha statues under a ledge (not caves!!! Come on!). Don't expect to see some remarcable works of art, do expect to see lots of donation boxes. If you do feel like wasting your resources, my piece of advise is: go there early (so that the hot floor doesn't burn your feet in the middle of the day), bring water with you and don't leave your shoes to the shoe watchers (you can always carry your shoes with you).
dambulla cave temple old place.i think 1300 years old history have.musiam and 5 temple in the top.cave temple make only rock. wonderfulla place

This series of five caves is astounding and the amount or detail and colours on the statues, walls and ceilings inside are amazing particularly as they've been in existence for 22 centuries.   Although we understand that there are steps from ground level, our guide/driver gave us a lift partway so we just had to negotiate a steep slope to get to the entrance to the caves.  A very memorable visit.

I think I was expecting these "cave temples" to be more like the ones in Thailand that were built in actual caves, verses carved out of the top of a mountain.  They were definitely nice, but very popular and crowded.  Beware all the vendors as you walk to the top....

We visited with our tuk tuk driver. He came inside the booth when we were buying tickets and they made us buy a ticket for him - a whopping 15$ ! when normally locals are free. Once this was done, even though the other check points knew this was wrong they still ripped the tickets and stamped them, making it impossible to go back. Basically, they were happy to rip us off, like many people in Sri Lanka who seem to see foreigners as walking money purses only. The cave temples themselves are pretty nice, would have been a nicer experience without the scam.

Amazing cave temple complex that dates back to 100BC. Some of the older buddhas and especially the old paintings are jawdropping. We arrived in the evening which just added to the setting and meant that there were less people there then normally. Spent maybe 2 hours in total.

The walk up as others indicate may take a quarter hour but is not difficult.  One can stop along the path as well.  We found these caves with their statues and paintings to be one of the most interesting things we did in our 18 days in Sri Lanka.  It is best seen with a knowledgeable guide.  Our guide was very well spoken and could explain a lot but unfortunately rushed us along so he would finish in an hour.  I guess many would feel that is sufficient time but we would have enjoyed another half hour or more.
My personal delight: the unbelievably beautiful contrast between the delicate white forms of the temples and the black rock on which they are built.

Buddhas and paintings are superb, one of the best places I have seen in the country;  although the entrance fee,as in most of the Srilankan Cultural Triangle, is quite high. Be fitted for it, it takes 20 minutes up to the hill. Monkeys will entertain you along the way. For a little fee you can leave your shoes at the entrance.
...when I saw the paintings. there is only one large cave and few smaller once, but worth the visit. Great Place. i could spend hours looking at the paintings, but we spent only 45min up there.

Nice temple with 5 rooms, each with different sizes and different positions of Buddha. Listen to your guide. He'd have many stories to tell you in here. Better take socks with you in this visit, because you'll have to walk barefoot and the ground is very hot.

As the first sight of the (new) Buddha statue may be a bit grotesque, with the big open mouth of the figure surrounding the entrance to the new temple, the ascent to the actual historical site is quite pleasanet. The caves itself are not big, but the Buddha statues collection insude them is very interesting. Don't miss the view from the entrance to the caves of the planes and jungle to the west of the site. If you are lucky, you can be joined in your ascent by buddhist monks. Worth a visit.

Superb historic temple made more enjoyable by our tour guide . The steps up to the caves could be a little testing for less able people but when your up there it another stunning view and imaging history,.

One of the main attractions of our weeks tour, our first day out and what a climb, our guide Mahendra made short work of it, we are fairly fit but did struggle with steps. And steep inclines. No footwear at the top and floor was hot and stoney, socks would have been very useful. My legs ached two days after! Not for those who are not used to physical exercise. Watch the locals in bare feet go all the way up, even elderly - amazing.

It is a 12th century AD lovely well preserved caves and temples, after climbing 1202 steps of Sirigiya Rock Lion this one was a piece of cake, but you have to deposit your foot wear at the bottom of the caves for some charges, so thick socks will be very handy especially the paths and steps are all made of rocks. the caves are very interesting with  statues of Buddha in gold with  different sizes and positions, some cave ceilings are covered with more than one thousand paintings of the Buddha.. don't forget to see the bucket of the holy water which never got overflowed..spare some time and observe the monkeys and their monkey activities..  enjoy.

There is a huge gold Buddha at ground level which claims to be biggest in the world, but it seems it is only the second biggest in Sri Lanka. As it was built in 2001 I would suggest forgetting the modern frontage and climb to the historical caves. I would guess there are about 300 steps but they are in flights and wide enough so you can catch your breath without inconveniencing others. At the top are 5 caves with statuary and murals aged between 900 and 200 years old. Very impressive and try to get a summary say from a guidebook. Well worth the puffing to get up and a very interesting insight into Buddhism.

The outside of the attraction is a little unusual - it's a bit 'modern' and plastic looking which doesn't do justice to the lovely paintings and statues in the caves.  Most alarming was the long line of mannequin monks at the outside of the entrance on the hill!  Ignoring the entrance, the climb up is fairly easy and the paintings well preserved.  Quite atmospheric. The hawkers are not troublesome if you are just polite and say no without engaging.  If you're an animal lover like we are, the monkeys are good to watch here.

We called in here on our way from Sigiriya to Kandy. Although perhaps not as special as other places we have visited on our amazing tour, it was still worth the short climb and coping with the normal hassles mentioned by other reviewers given the historical significance of this site. It was particularly interesting to compare the workmanship in the last 2 more 'modern' caves with the older ones - they knew so much back then!

You walk up the side of a mountain (stairs or road) which is not too exhausting. Then you leave your shoes and cover any bare limbs. After that you are ready to enter the cave temples. There are five of them with lots of excellent statues of men of varying holiness. They are beautifully painted, mainly in gold. There are also a number of reclining Buddhas, some of them dead depending on the position of the toes, others just resting.

The caves are very impressive with statues and paintings so well preserved.  It was very interesting.  The view from the top is quite stunning of the surrounding countryside. The steps to the top were quite exhausting!

Interesting history around the caves of the Golden Temple. There's quite a long walk up to get to see the caves (though nothing compared with Sigiriya) but it's worth it as there is a special feeling around the site,if you ignore the hawkers, monkeys, etc.

It is a very nice walk up the hill especially in the morning before it get's crowded. Once you get closer to the temple you will find a lot of monkeys playing around. Nice view as well. Paintings in the caves are well maintained and nice to walk in each of the rooms. You need to be there before 4-5 in the afternoon in  order to have enough time to see the paintings.The walk up to the temple takes about 20 min.

Dambulla caves was an interesting stop on the way from Sigiriya to Dambulla. It is a 15 minute walk up a hill which is not too taxing. There are terrific cave paintings and some statues of the buddha inside of the caves. You can walk to the caves for free but you need to purchase a ticket to enter. Unfortunately entry prices are steep. You must wear pants or a sarong to cover your legs.

770 steps, really hard steep climb for me and I was absolutely exhausted when I eventually reached the top, but to look in the caves and see carvings and paintings from before Christ was pretty impressive!! Be careful on the way down too which was hard going in the rain...
very old .1300years old,many budda ,onthe way kandy road gamagedara resort to 2km.you can working.opening 8.00am close5.00pm

Dambulla's Golden Temple is as described in the guides, it's a cave temple with several rooms filled with statues of Buddha. It's worth a visit if it's on your way or close to your hotel, but I wouldn't do a detour just for this place.

After climbing the hill behind the golden temple you came to 5 amazing caves full of Buddha statues. We were fortunate enough that our driver had a lot of knowledge about these caves and could talk at length of the significance of each cave. This is definitely worth stopping to have a look.

Before visiting Sri Lanka I didn't know much about Dambulla, I guess it is not advertised well, but the place was amazing. We had great guide for very reasonable fee and he told us all about the cave and little more about buddhism.The Temple was may be the one of highlights of our trip in Sri Lanka.

You will see a lot of Buddhas inside the temples, but in a western view they are not very beautiful temples. We found it worth the visit to see the magnificent view from the top, at the entrance of the temples. As people has pointed out it is quite expensive to buy the entrance fee, but if you go here you easily get the feeling that you have seen enough of temples for the rest of your journey and dont have to bother to see any more temples with entrance fees (and that is a comfort at least...). You have to take off your shoes before entering the place (there is another fee for leaving the shoes) but the ground is not clean so you will get pretty dirty feet walking around the sites (a lot of bird poo on the ground for instance). The place outside the temples and the stairs are filled with sellers trying to rip off stupid tourists, as in most other places where the crowd goes.

Recommended for a visit, the statues and painting ceilings are fantastic. It's jus a pity that they don't have more information for a nonbudhist audience as I couldn't properly understand the relevence of some of the art work

The five caves are beautifully preserved and a must see for those interested in learning more about Buddhism. As with all Buddhist sacred sites in Sri Lanka you will need to remove shoe and head coverings and be respectively dressed. For a nominal fee you can leave you shoes on rack for a fee of around 50c. A tip you can come in through the local back door and save a lot of stairs rather than use the entrance on the main road.
This is a must see.  It starts off a bit naff (like the Museum) but the caves were a surprise and just jaw dropping.  take a tripod if you want to take pics and a 21mm lens

The climb is very steep and slippery, especially on the way down and when it is raining. The caves are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a must see, even though you might not like the repetition of Budda's in various positions. However, keep in mind that each position has it's special significance and that everything in those caves has an explanation and a reason for being that way, even if it is just symbolic for some people. As in every sacred place in Sri Lanka, be careful not to turn your back on the statues when taking a picture and not to pose with the statues in general. You have to take your shoes off before entering and pay the fee of 25 rupies.
If you are in Sri Lanka and Dambulla then you simply have to visit this place! After all it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

We visited this after climbing Sigiriya. There is a large golden Buddha at the bottom.  There is a museum inside which is frankly pointless and I stress don't waste your time.  It had dioramas that looked like school children had made them. You buy tickets at the bottom.  Again disappointed with the pricing and signs.   1500 for non-Srilankans is the cost (It actually says this on the sign - I took a photo of it). You climb up many steps and at times just a steep concrete hill (which can be difficult in thongs/flipflops) or if you are unsteady on your feet, more so on the way down.  There are people selling rocks/carvings/scarves, etc on the way up (they weren't too much of a hassle, but I felt the prices were much higher than everywhere else - maybe just me).  At the entrance at the top you have to take your shoes off and they actually have a service here to look after your shoes for a fee!!! Really disappointing that they force you to take your shoes off then charge you for it. We put our shoes in our bags and carried them round.  If you go during the day, you'll have to walk in the shady areas otherwise you will burn your feet. The temple itself is impressive as a whole.  Given its history and architecture. There are 5 caves with each 'cave' is full of paintings and hundreds of statues of Buddha.  But to me they were all the same and without any signs/panels explaining the area, it was a bit pointless.  There are many monkeys around eating all the flower offerings. Summary - Overpriced, no information panels, no signs, nothing. - It was a nice visit and is actually quite impressive given the history - Don't need to spend much time there. - Don't bother with museum at the bottom. Literally the worst museum I've ever been to. - You do not need a guide. If you want to know more, read up on it before hand.

Been there in the afternoon when the sun wasn't that strong anymore. Beautifull views all the way to Sirigiya Rock. Stairs are doable and the caves are ok. Someting I never saw before. Paid 1500 rupee pp and 25 pp for "guarding shoes" at the temple on top.

The temple is at the top of the steep climb, but with shadow and occasional pauses, it shouldn't be too much of a problem. Tickets have to be bought at the bottom, the guy selling the tickets was rude and gave no information whatsoever. The tickets are also very expensive (1500 Rs). The temples itself are nice but with no explanation of the things seen. Guides are charging at least 500 Rs for a short guide. Museum at the bottom is just a laugh. If you are not really interested in Buddha and you are tight on budget, you can skip it.

I really Enjoyed visiting this place ... the whole area is just great scenery ! exactly what i was looking for ! even if it was heavily raining over our head but we really didn't care ! The walk up to the cave temple was little bit hard if you don't exercise ! i really enjoyed feeding the monkeys ... i was giving them mangoes ! but you got to be careful as if you don't give them food they might snatch from your hand ! Up there you will witness a peaceful atmosphere inside the temple with the big lying Buddha statue ! and some other small statues ! Also the view from the top is worth the walk ! you will just enjoy it i promise .

Compared to the 3900 Rps in Sigiriya, the Dambulla caves are 'cheap; just 1500 Rps (€ 9,-). We liked the cave temples very much, but unfortunately there are no information panels. The walk up to the caves is strenous, but OK. There are some peolpe trying to sell you some touristic stuff, but they were not too persistant. The place is clean (no rubbish), but when you look over the wall with the fence, you will see all the rubbish. We also liked the macaques eating the flowers! Overall, we had a good experience, but because of the rubbish, the lack of information and the high entrance fee we give it a 4* rating and not a 5* rating.
Very interesting and a cheap attraction with no bother from people selling things etc but it can get quite repetitive.
The caves are interesting and pretty cool to look around but I would recommend you just visit for an hour or two instead of making a day out of it as its pretty repetitive.

These five temple caves were truly a sight to behold. It is well worth a visit and is much less money and effort to see than the Sigiriya Rock Fortress. It was also the first time we saw wild monkeys so we spent a few minutes taking photos of them on the stairs. Beware that the descent can be very difficult in adverse weather conditions!
We enjoyed looking around these temples, but I wouldn't recommend spending lots of time there because it becomes a little repetitive.
The temple depicts the culture and the Buddha statues are just never ending.. Also one gets to realize the types and the differences in those various statues..

The statues are great and the paintings on the cave walls are interesting. I have to give this 2 stars just because it's too expensive for what it is. But if you don't mind spending the money (1,500 rupees as of December 2014) then go ahead and visit it. There are few plaques anywhere explaining what you are seeing. The paintings look in surprisingly good condition for how old they are suppose to be (several hundreds of years old). My guess is that they are reproductions, but there are no text or signs explaining anything so who knows.
The paintings in these caves is gorgeous. Our guide book suggested starting with cave 5 and working backwards and that is good idea Don't bother with the golden temple, just go to the cave temples

Located at the base of the rock temple, there is a huge Golden Statue of Buddha dominating the entrance. The temple is a revered place for all Buddhists.  The rays of the setting sun seem to bathe the statue in a golden liquid to enhance its majesty.  A splendid sight and a must see for all tourists.

Visited with my fiancee on a rainy day.  Unfortunately due to the weather, it was very difficult to see anything. I have been told that the views up there are spectacular on a clear days, but unfortunately we couldn't see this when we visited due to the weather. It costs foreigners 1500 rupees for entry to the temple and museum. The temple is about a 15 minute climb to the caves. There are steps along the way and handrails, it could be a difficult climb for older people or people who may have additional needs. Nonetheless, the caves were impressive and worth the climb. May be worth noting that comfortable walking shoes are required. All shoes must be removed prior to entry and can be stored by a local vendor for 25 rupees per pair. You also must wear clothing that is at least knee length. We were able to "hire" a sarong as well form the same store. The sarong rental was not publicly advertised, my fiancée being local, knew to ask and the vendors were happy to oblige for a negotiable fee. Overall a reasonably good experience.

Bit of a climb up to this temple, which has a multitude of Buddha's in 4 different temples cut into a rock overhang, usual 1,000 lkr for a guide plus admission, plus 50 lkr for someone to look after your shoes, must have knees and shoulders covered. Some temples close for a short while for offerings, but an interesting site.

The view from the top must be great, but the rain and clouds made it quite impossible to see a thing. The temples are certainly worth the visit, 5 different caves, but the content looked very similar to me (you've seen one, you've seen them all...). The climb to the top is not too hard,  but slippery when wet, so be carefull. The museum at the entrance is not worth a visit. Very basic, most of the displays only in Singhalese, very little in english. William, Senta & little Ella

Both adults and children will enjoy the cave Temples. The climb up the hill takes a while, I am happy it was a grey/rainy day otherwise it would have been exhausting in the heat. Beautiful surroundings, nice view and monkeys makes the climb worthwile in itself. The caves are marvellous, absolutely beautiful. It's a wonder and don't miss it.
Caves made into temples , this was new to me. 155 Buddha. Statues in different postures inside, ceiling with numerouds paintings, really wotrth visiting

The climb is less tedious than the one to the sigiriya rock fortress. There are steps and slopes and i'll advise you to take your time.Along the way there will be locals selling souvenirs and i must say some were very insistent! We managed to catch the sunset at the top;entrance to the temple.You must remove your footwear if your wearing white socks it'll turn brown after your visit. Most of the statues were made around 2600 years ago! The walls and ceilings of each cave are covered with paintings. Very beautiful and magnificent site rich with culture and history.A must go if your in the area. However the public toilets are dark and rather dirty which was a bit shocking for such a tourist attraction.

First of all buy your tickets at the bottom.  As you enter the gate, there’s a building in front of you, the ticket office is at the back of that building (go round the side, not through the building).  Then passing the Golden Buddha and museum (the biggest of its kind in the world they say) start your hike up the hill. The climb is a combination of steps, rock and sand.  It shouldn’t take more than 15 minutes to walk slowly to the top.   Hand over your shoes (pay the 50 KLR to get them back) and then start the painful walk towards the cave temple.  I’d recommend having socks with you, the combination of the sharp sand and the stone flags makes it pretty painful walking if you’ve not got used to barefoot temple visiting yet… Watch where you step – lots of stray dogs and monkeys here and the ground was somewhat sticky (I don’t want to think about it) when we were there.  There are 5 caves to visit, I’d recommend starting in the one that is most distant from the entrance.  Take your guidebook to figure out what is in the caves (or take a guide), as there are features that you will miss otherwise. It’s expensive to visit (US$12), but that’s why you’re in Dambulla right?

We had excellent guide and he made our visit very interesting. The cave and temple are very interesting and location was beautiful. My only problem was walking barefoot that I am not use to and ground wasn't smooth, it was not very convenient for me. I remembered that in Myanmar people were cleaning paths all time and they were very smooth and we didn't have any problems.

The Dambulla Cave temple is a religious Buddhist heritage which tells us about the proud history of Buddhism.There are Buddhist paintings and statues inside the cave and they are more than 2500 years old.The temple is very quiet and a calm place as it is a very common thing in every temple. You can worship Buddha or stay and relax your mind for a moment...I was so proud as a Buddhist to visit this heritage site.Everyone who visits Sri Lanka should come and visit this Buddhist Heritage site...
Stunning views and landscape. Fascinating history and the buddhas in the cave were varied and very beautiful

Beware of guides. Also ask how much they charge up front. The other surprising bit was that resturants charge different rates at buffets for the locals and us! Ask your driver to ask how much upfront again.
It's a great walking through historic place, the cave is more than 2000 years old and the story from it is fascinating, if you are really into historic places this is a must!
The place is amazing, it's a great climb with a great view, the temples inside are amazing, more than 2.500 years old. Definitely worth it if you come to Sri Lanka.
great place to marvel the heritage and the Buddhist heritage. It should be respected as a place of worship.

We did a day trip from Kandy. It took us about 2.5hrs. Definitely worth a visit. Foreigners pay about 2500 LKR. Toilets available next to the visitors centre. They are BAD! So hold if you can... Next to the temple, is two entrances. One to the Golden Buddha and other one up to the Cave Temple. If are going up to the Golden Buddha only, you do not need to pay anything. Tickets are only inspected at the main entrance of the Cave Temple ( at the top!) Remove shoes and pay another 25 rupees for shoes deposit. Climb up can be a little tiring, especially with the heat.  Need good comfortable shoes. Railings not available for certain areas. The slope is easier to handle than the steps. There are many monkeys here. If you are getting the flowers for offerings, watch out for the monkeys. Once inside the cave, you feel like you are transported back in time... there are many Buddha statues, paintings on the cave..is very damp inside.

I don't agree with being left out while an offering is happening behind closed doors. We are there to witness or rather experience an interesting religious procedure, instead we were left out for 15 minutes while an offering was happening. If we did not have a good tour guide, we would not have understood where to go or what was happening. There was no information or guiding.

This temple houses numerous cave paintings and a number of Buddhist figurines. The temple is not visible until you reach the top of the stairs. There is a huge Golden colored Buddha on the exterior which can be seen from the road. Expect to pay LKR 1500 per head for entry.

The Dambulla cave temple is a really beautiful temple carved into the mountain rock. The temple has numerous Buddha statue and has 5 caves in all. The paintings cover the cave completely and are untouched by wind and rain erosion unlike Sigriya. You will need about an hour to explore the whole place. The cave temple is located high up so a whole lot of stairs need to be climbed before you reach the entrance. A lot of vendors can be found on the way up. Expect to pay LKR 1500 per person for entry. LKR 25 per piece of footwear. You can carry your footwear in your bag to avoid the extra cost.

My partner climbed the stairs to the cave temple and found the experience worthwhile. I was feeling too hot for the climb so hung around the complex at the foot of the hill. It was also worthwhile, listening to the chanting from a ceremony, visiting the bodhi tree, and cruising through the largely underwhelming museum. Most interesting was watching the passing show and the frolicking monkeys. Give it a miss if you're on a tight schedule, have been to other cultural sites and have seen a lot of stupas and statues.

The Golden Temple was lovely -- romantic on the exterior and mysterious and sacred on the inside.  The climb up to the top is nice too.  I went in mid-September where the crowds weren't so hectic and the weather was nice.  I like to pride myself on how I edited my first trip to Sri.  With so many relics to see, it can be difficult to choose where to go and what to take in.  The Golden Temple was one of the few I selected and for that, maybe that's why I can appreciate room after room of beautifully preserved murals and Buddha's.  Even if you aren't a history or religion buff, you should go. Great for photos....
You have to climb a lot to up. We went to base with large golden Buddha. Toilet can be more clean as they charge for that.
Great Cave art. Easy to take Photos, but please no flash.  A steep climb, but not too long, 50 rp to watch your shoes.

Overwhelming would be best to describe these 5 caves in the side of the mountain.  Internally they are completely covered in paintings and the statues are quite amazing.    The fronts of the caves have been built to save the paintings and it looks lovely.   You still enter a small doorway to view each cave and the reclining Buddha in the first cave is superb.   Shoes have to be  taken off and a pair of socks is a good idea.   They say over 600 steps, but if you drive up a side road you are half way up AND there is a pathway going up to save climbing the stairs which makes it much easier.

really really worth a trip here. I didnt get to go in to the buddhist museum but really wish i had. Lots more monkeys to see on your climb to the caves and a real cultural experience when you get there. Try and lean a little about buddhism first if you can.
awesome.....place.....u have to climb  a lot...worth climbing..ticket lil costly.but awesom place above the rock.............

This is a temple built in a rock cave which goes back to 1st century BC. The temple has been a monastery first and then with the help of several kings it was restored as beautiful temple with very old statues and paintings. Rightly so it's a free attraction for locals and they charge for foreigners. That's because it's a religious shrine for locals but a tourist attraction for foreigners. If you are a foreigner then I would advice you to hire a guide because there is a lot to observe and see. You can park the car in the car park. There is a walk up the hill for about 20 minutes and then you arrive at the historical caves. You are not allowed to wear shorts or skinnies inside the temple. If you are already wearing them they will be provided a scarf for a nominal charge. Once you arrive at the top, to enter the temple you need to take off shoes too. Beware of the monkeys on the way up. They are very naughty. They try to grab anything they can get hold of. So keep all the foods inside a bag while climbing the rock. No wheelchair access.
For the cost of entry this attraction is underwhelming. If you aren't too into art / history / religion then this can be missed.

For the cost of entry this is an underwhelming attraction. If you aren't strong on your history or religious knowledge / appreciation then this can be missed. The caves themselves are dark and dank - it wouldn't take much to improve the lighting and sweep the floor without taking away from the atmosphere.
While most of the impressive sights are in areas few hours from Dambulla, since Dambulla is a good base to visit the other sights, make time to check out the caves...

It is quite a trek to reach the caves. Not for the terribly unfit, but worth the effort. Can't remember if there were 6 or 8 caves in all, but they were well displayed and maintained. Could have done with an audio tour or written hoardings. Fortunately our guide/driver filled us in.

It's a nice beautiful cave temple. But it's a pity that it was not well protected from flash light cameras and not well preserved from water falling down cave top. History of place and info on paintings should display on board. I wonder why there's a Hindu temple and hindu gods with incense burning rites etc. just next to this Buddhist cave shrine? Isn't this suppose to be a Buddhist temple?

Apart from the downside of a few extremely rude tourists, who don't look at the wealth of stunning religious artefacts in these splendid cave temples at all, but simply elbow and barge through to take photographs without an ounce of appreciation, this is one of the great treasure houses of Sri Lanka. Each cave has its own charm, character and particular treasures and the whole taken together is just mind-blowing. The entire external area set high on the mountain is impressive enough, but the cave contents are intensely beautiful and impressive. Be sure to take enough time here to appreciate the myriad of images and their place in Buddhism at large, as well as the dicreet but impressive setting of the entire complex. Don't miss the museum at the entrance which, despite its cheesy entrance, sets the scene well for the climb upwards and the wonders beyond.

The cave temples are really, really impressive - especially if you think about what you are looking at.   Entering the cave temples I think that the most impressive thing is that everything that you see is actually carved out of the original stone that was there.  It's like they made a reverse mold for lack of better description.   There are so many Buddhas and when you realize that none of them were "Brought" into the the caves but that they are all still attached since they are part of the rock which was carved around them it makes it particularly impressive.  I loved my whole trip through the cultural triangle but this was a particular high point.   While it doesn't take more than at max 2 hours to see and as low as 45 minutes if you skip the museum it's well worth the time spent and it can easily be joined with a trip to Sigirya for a single day outing. I like to address some of the complaints that I read from low start reviews so here are some things to think about if they might be distasteful to you First - it's a steep climb.   They don't add "western" stairs to an active temple that has perfectly usable yet steep steps.   The Sri Lankans are in extremely good climbing shape.  If you aren't then this isn't the place for you. Next - There are monkeys there.  If you don't like monkeys then don't go.  Many people enjoy them even though they are raucous and may try to steal items if you put them down for a minute Next - yes, they charge foreigners and the fee is 1500.   The attraction is not massive and at max it's a two hour visit if you check out the museum slowly.   This may be too expensive for a budget traveler and I really understand this one.  If I were on a very strict budget I would skip this one for something else, still I think "Is it worth $12ish U.S.?" and I think - again - unless you are severely budget limited it's worth that.  You traveled half the way around the world and I can say you won't see something like this anywhere that I have seen even if it's just a small "seeing". Finally - in terms of literature and lack thereof - first of all I am guessing the people who wrote that skipped the museum.  I can only think that they must have.  The museum (included with admission) taught me a ton about Buddhism and the plaques are in English (as well as Singhalese).  Go to the museum first!
Well kept as all temples.Many monkey's around. Very many tourists. Nice walk up and down the stairs.
We really liked everything! We were breathless with everything that we saw! Above all the peace sensation that we could feel in all Buddhist Temple that we visited.

For us this was, once more, something beautiful and amazing! The Temple is simply wonderful! We filled up our batteries and went to the top to see the Cave Temple above and we were admiring all the surround landscape. Our first and real contact about Buddhism was here in Sri Lanka and we really could feel the essence of this religion!
Absolutely beautiful. A real feeling of calm there. My children moaned about having to come here but actually found it to be so beautiful and were very happy taking photos. I am so glad we visited!

Stunning cave temple, a must see!  Don't forget to buy your ticket at the bottom from the office in the Golden Temple grounds, you cannot enter the Cave Temple without one and it is a long climb to the top!

We didn't explore this temple much as we were there to climb to the cave temple above. The giant golden Buddha at the bottom is very impressive though. There is a Bhuddist museum here too but there is not that much to see inside. TIP: you have to buy your ticket for the Cave Temple here at the bottom. The ticket office is tucked away with no obvious signs. Make sure you buy your ticket before climbing as it is a long way to come back down and you cannot buy them at the top!!!!!!!
Not worth stopping for, if hadn't have been stopping for Siguria would have been exceedingly cheesed off. All the Buddhas are very similar.

After the quite long climb of stone steps in the heat to the top, and one or two pit stops to catch the breath, admire the wonderful views (and keep an eye on those monkeys), the goal is well worth the effort.  These are a series of five exquisitely decorative cave temples.  A very emotive experience for me, after first seeing a poster of The Golden Temple in a Buddhist Temple in the UK several years ago, it was an amazing experience to see them in person.  Highly recommended.

A magnificent temple a series of 5 caves established as monestary in 3rd century BC. It is located at the road side Dambulla Habarana. To reach the cave we have to climb about 100 meter. School of friendly monkey make the climb more chalanging and fun.
If there is one thing to see in Sri Lanka; this would be my choice. These cave temples are just awesome. Worth the haul up the mountain.
After going up To the temple crossing local people going there to pray, we arrived in one of the most beautiful paitings i've seen.
