These caves are beautiful. Leave your shoes with the man for 50p but keep your socks on if your feet are sensitive as the rocks get hot in the middle of the day. Start the caves in reverse order as the best caves are numbers 1 and 2- walk the furthest and work your way backwards. Don't look the monkeys in the eyes- they're pretty scary!

You've to climb a couple of stairs to get to the temple, at midway there's a lot of annoying sellers trying to sell you all kinds of things, some of them not wanting to accept no vor an answer. This marked this site negatively since we've to pay to view, sellers shouldn't be aloud along the way. The view from the top is amazing, the caves didn't impress me much apart from the ceiling paintings.

Dambulla is a fantastically worth while short stop around the ancient cities of Sri Lanka. After a short but tough hike to the top of this hill you get rewarded with five awesome (in the true sense of the word) caves. These, as most temples, are best seen with as few people as possible around (easier said than done I know). The sense of isolation and quiet contemplation in the caves is excellent. If the Hindu shrine is open go and see it, its rarely open.
See my 'Golden Temple' comments. The caves will be one of the highlights of your trip to this area with amazing statues, painted walls and ceilings and fantastic hillside views.

We visited this wonderful Buddhist Temple and the associated Dambulla Caves just after breakfast to avoid the crowds and the heat - knowing we had a climb! The experience was awe inspiring. Without doubt the Caves must rank as a 'must see' both in terms of the statues, paintings and hilltop views.

You'll know how good these caves are from other reviews. Here are my tips.... Tips: - Bring water with you, as you will spend time walking up and down the hill, and water might be in limited supply - Don't by cheap: go for a tour guide (who speaks English). The guy will explain the meaning of the different caves and their historical foundations. It will cost you 500 rupees (4USD), and you will walk out more knowledgeable than when you walked in... Enjoy
It's a nice walk, if u don't like climbing stairs u will hate it. Good work out, if your not interested in temples and history it's a waste of time.

Unbelievable but true.. when I saw the cave temple complex on the internet.. I told my family.. "this holiday it's Sri Lanka" and "in Sri Lanka we've got to visit Dambulla" The photographs and memories are forever..

If you step into these caves, you step into a complete different world. Over 150 Buddha's in different sizes, positions etc. Every cave offers you the opportunity to discover various steps of the life of Buddha. Created with so much patience and love and respect to their mental leader, his followers have set up an unbelievable place to meditate, to pray and to get hope again. Without the loudness, the screaming headlines or anything else we have to use in our days, here is an eye-catching highlight hidden in caves as prayers are in us.

Dambulla Golden Temple is a must see if you are visiting Sri Lanka. Fair rates and an incredible atmosphere, like in the most Sri Lankan temples, as they are witnesses of a long lasting trust in the teachings of Buddha. In every fresco, every statue or even stone you can feel that those how have created these places have been inspired by something more important than personal ownership, wealth or so. Theses places were made to honour, peace, tolerance and spirit.
Fantastic location. A bit of walking up hill, but we'll worth it. So many Buddha's. Look at the feet of the first one. Just amazing!
Don't bother with a guide - their incessant prattling will actively prevent you from enjoying what is a really impressive place. Start at the farthest cave and work your way back. Take a good camera.

The walk up to the temples opens onto beautiful views of the surrounding countryside and its worth going up to see the sun set. The detail and the number of the buddas in the caves is amazing - evening was a good time to go as the crowds were thinning out.

The Golden Temple is a multi-storeyed complex that leads to the Cave Temple through flights of stairs.  Inside the complex, you can find the development on Buddhism and see many statues display inside.  The entrance ticket already includes fees to both the Golden Temple as well as the Cave Temple as they are considered as one unity.  Recommend to walk up the Cave Temple for visit at the first instance and return to the complex for viewing after long and hot walk.

Dambulla Cave Temple is also known as Golden Temple of Dambulla and the latter generally refers as a multi-storeyed complex which accommodates many buddha statues collected and donated from different places of the world. Your ticket already includes visit to these two locations but you have to take off your shoes before entering the five caves and different shrine rooms while shorts are not allowed to the caves.  However it is considered worthwhile to pay visit to this spot as you can see many statues and wall paintings in the first century B.C. But this site is not recommended for those with physical disabilities as you have to climb uphill through flights of stairs.

We visited the temple in April, where the weather was really good for such occasion. In hotter days can be slightly unpleasant because you have to take off the shoes before you enter the temple and the stones can be really hot.. But generally there is nice walk on the stairs to temple, with blossom trees around, and at the end you will come to beautiful temple. there will be waiting for you a nice monkey family.
Very nice and huge temple. lots of statues and painting. We have visited quite a few temples in Sri Lanka and this one was definitely one of the nice ones.

Stunningly ugly. Evidently built with donations from another Asian country - it's one of the worst pieces of architecture I've seen in the region, and that includes the enormous gold-painted concrete Buddha. Thankfully, they didn't touch the caves
Seeing this does not take long at all. Worth seeing if you are passing through, but not worth coming out of your way for it.

The cave temples are at the top of a hill which has a steep climb. The kids found it a tad difficult and we had to take couple of breaks. The caves have some good painting and statues to see. The view from the top is also very good. There were lots of monkeys around.

So the cave temples are at the top of the hill and it will take about 15 minutes to get to the entrance. The level of the detail in the paintings in each cave is incredible. They have a small Hindu shrine within the complex. The history of the temple is very interesting, and the views from the top of the hill. Be careful of the monkeys, they will grab anything they can from you.
But of a walk uphill especially in the banking sun but really worth it. Artwork and statues around 1000 years old so very well preserved for their age. Interestinh site all round and great views too.

The Golden Temple is well worth a visit. Boasting the largest statue of Buddha in the World, the sheer size is awe inspiring. The Buddhist Museum is included in the ticket price, then the walk up the hill to the Cave Temples. Again the history you access here is breath taking. Well worth a visit, but be warning, it's a bit of a climb to the top!
Have you ever tried walking in the twilight of a cave and have dozens of Buddha statues looking at you? You should try - an unforgettable experience.

It's a long climb up the hill to the caves. Some parts have no steps and are slippery when wet. To the top you will find your typical vendors trying to sell you all sorts of souvenirs. At the first cave we were lucky to find a guide to explain us the statues and caves. He didn't force himself on to us and just asked if we would like some explanation. He explained us more about Buddhisim as we had no idea what we were looking at. This made it for us the best cultural experience in SL. As with all other sites on the island there is barely an English explanation on what you are looking at. A good guide can make or break your whole experience. The price might be high, especially compared to the locals who get in for free, but I must say for us it was no issue as we found it worth spending the money. As for the complaints I read from Muslim women (not only here but also in reviews of other temples) yes you are required to remove your vail for the Budist temples. Just as non-Muslim women will have to cover their hair if they want to enter a mosque. This information is easily found on the internet or in any travel guide so I don't know why there are so many complaints like it's brand new info. And yes I have the same experience and could not enter a temple in shorts while it covered my knees and had to buy a sarong for 1000rs which is not more than a peace of cloth.

Its a fair bit of drive from Kandy..but well worth the time spent...if with kids...make sure you travel a little earlier...since there arent much places to eat around.. The way the caves have been maintained..the cleanliness.and the history behind it...is really an eye opener. Please do visit. Its a fair hike..on steps..so not advisable for older people and people with disabilities. Also do not visit in shorts...or..sleeveless tops..you might have to rent a dhoti..and a top..or buy it.

If you are travelling between sigirya and kandy, you must stop at these caves that host huge buddha statues against beautiful backdrops crafted and preserved centures ago. Going to the top is not far as compared to sigirya and takes you a slow 20 minute climb. Make sure you get your tickets before you go up! Have some tips ready for the shoekeeper because you can only walk barefooted in this temple.

Went straight from overnight flight to this site. It's wonderful when you get to the top but a schlep to get that far. The statue is a bit gawdy and the entrance through a mouthlike orifice, a bit tacky.

It's a long way before you reach the temple but when you're there it's realy beautiful. Inside the cave's are beautiful wall and ceiling paintings and the statues are also very nice. From the top you also have a nice vieuw over the area. When you are there you must visit this attraction.

It was a great hike up the stairs to the cave temples but once up...the view was breathtaking ! The caves were interesting as it is amazing that the Sri Lankan people had the good sense of preserving centuries old stuff in such a great way.The best thing for me the facade of the cave temples set against the rocks...it was well worth the visit I would say ! Just keep a bottle of water and an umbrella handy !

A sacred pilgrimage site for 22 centuries, this cave monastery, with its five sanctuaries, is the largest, best-preserved cave-temple complex in Sri Lanka.   The rock of Dambulla is the centre of a Buddhist cave-temple complex established in the 3rd century B.C. and occupied continuously to this day.   UNESCO World Heritage

It's gonna take you like 20 minutes to get to the top, you'll find the first cave very interesting but then you'll notice that all the caves are the same only the size get smaller so nothing really special about it.
Unbelievable art in a number of cave chambers, rich in history and religious significance - a real feast for the eyes and like nothing I'd ever seen before.  A beautiful and peaceful place to visit.
This is a decent activity to do while in Dambulla.  Beware as there is a litte climb to get up to the caves but its pretty neat once you get up there.  Lots of monkey hanging around.

Located in the Golden Temple premises, one route goes up to the Dambulla Cave Temple and the other one to the Golden Buddha statue. Its a steep climb (not as steep as Sigiriya) but will take 15-20 mins for sure. The green view from the top is nice and the 5 cave temples are v. interesting. There are 1-2 guides around but if you have enough reading/research material you may not need their service. However, if you havent read enough, its best to take their service or else the importance and meaning of the caves wont be completely understood. Its good to see that the caves are still in good condition and we are able to see a glimpse of art work which is thousands of years old.

Foreigners pay 1500 Sri Lanka rupee per person to visit this temple while the locals pay nothing. Visitors with garments NOT below the mid-calf risk a rip-off at the middle of the climb to purchase ridiculously expensive cotton pants that are usually priced at 600-800 rupee. However, local visitors get away with clothing around their knees. Do note that there is NO free assistance  in this place. Voluntary "guides" demand a minimum fee of 500 rupee for 1-minute information. There are no steps at some part of the slope, so comfortable shoes are required. Visitors are to be barefooted to enter the tiny temple with four rooms. Hence, most  leave their footwear with men stationed outside the temple. Naturally, there is a fee involved. Time taken for the climb is longer than for the temple. The view is spectacular but experience is horrible and the temple overrated.

I was surprised to be informed that we cannot visit the Dambulla Temple with our head scarf on. If we wish to go inside the temple, then we have to remove our head scarf. As a Muslim I would not do that so I did not visit the temple from inside.

Initially a very normal looking cave temple! Then you enter cave no 2, it took our breath away! Words cannot fully described the impact this places will have on you, do not miss visiting here. Very emotional experience.

We really enjoyed our visit, our guide was invaluable to helping us appreciate this truly wonderful place His advice to go early was sound, we arrived about 9am, not too hot and no crowds and we felt very privileged to enjoy this special place almost to ourselves If you are doing the Cultural Triangle - you have to go to Dambulla!

We had a good guide take us through the cave temple.  Worth it to learn about the history of each area.  Many stairs to climb but worth it.  The history attached to the cave temple is mind boggling.  Highly recommended.
Fantastic paintings, but they are in need of conservation. Great that there is not too much lighting inside the caves as these would deteriorate the paintings further.
Visited all caves bit of a climb but worth it. Loads of people about all bringing offerings. In the caves it was quiet and peaceful and cool.Is well worth a visit

We visited in February and it was very hot!!!  Like most attractions in Sri Lanka, we had many steps to climb.  There were monkeys everywhere, which was great!! The caves were amazing.  Truly built into the rock, with stunning murals throughout.  There were a lot of tourists about, to thoroughly enjoy it would be better if not so busy. You have to remove your shoes at the top, which is hard on bare feet, due to the concrete being so hot!!  We noted that some tourists kept their sock on, which made it more bearable!  Would recommend you do that. You also have to have your legs covered, so if wearing shorts you can hire or buy a sarong to go over your clothing. Again, there are locals selling wares along the way. The view from the top is also vast.  I would recommend a visit for the historical experience. Not suitable for people who are not in good health, eg my 80yo dad didn't go up, as it was too hot and too may steps. A word of warning about the toilet facilities located near the car park. They had attendant,so you had to pay, but OMG, they were absolutely filthy and stunk!!!  We only used them because we were desperate, but left an awful memory of a beautiful location!!!

Very windy during monsoons. Modernization has its effects on this ancient temple. New paths has made easy access to the temple but the ancient glory not there. Monkey menace with touts are the negatives. Difficult to enjoy due to over crowding.

For me, this was a highlight of my time in Sri Lanka. I loved the tranquility at the top of the hill, a long with so much history. The fee is 1500 rupees, which is a bit high but well worth it. The trek up to the top is fine, 300 steps, there are water vendors halfway up. Remember to buy tickets from the bottom as they check tickets right at the top of the stairs but only sell them at the bottom! The caves are fantastic, but it is one of these places where you need a guide. We got chatting to one and agreed on 400rupees. He gave us a really good tour for the best part of an hour. Showing us all the caves and giving thorough explanations of their history, talking about the kings as well as Buddhism in general. It was really engaging and he was capable of answering our questions with logical answers which was a treat! It is very peaceful at the top and well worth spending a but of time looking out at the view. We went during the heat of the day which worked out well for us as by the time we were leaving herds of tourists were entering the caves just snapping photos. Get a guide and learn about the place and it is truly interesting!

What a lovely temple! After climbing the stairs to the temple what awaits is special. The temples that've been cut into the rocks are truly impressive. The atmosphere inside is lovely and calming and you feel you could spend hours inside. A MUST.

Right I loved it for two reasons, 1st the history culture colours paintings and the cave temples, 2nd for all of the monkeys that were making me laugh :) well worth a visit , the place is steeped in history , one word of warning if your not one for climbing stairs then be warned.. ps try to go when it is cooler :)

The hike up to the caves & putting up with monkeys is all worth it when you reach the caves.. The site is fairly small, and covering the 5 caves doesn't take long. The caves are beautiful. One could spend half-a-day admiring the painted murals on the ceiling and basking in the spiritual aura of the caves (if only the monkeys didn't come in to steal the lotus flowers!).

Once you had climbed the 300 or so steps on a very hot day it was unbelievable.Has to be seen to be believed the sheer size and numbers of statues carved out  of solid granite would be near impossible todaylet alone hundreds of years ago.

If you make a stop in this small town, visiting this cave is a must. Really beautiful place with three different caves, each one presenting lots of statues in a deep sense of serenity. The only negative point is the price. $10 by the time i went there. But all the touristical areas in Sri Lanka are expensive. Too bad for the low budget travelers. In case you stay in Dambulla for a night, go see the sunset on the lake next to the cave. This one will be for free ;-)
amazing place in an amazing location, I would suggest going early to avoid lots of people. It is a bit of a trek up to the caves but well worth it!
Buddha painting and statues all around this cave. From the outside looks like a temple but from the inside it's a Cave. Please be aware of the thousands of stairs before reaching the Temple.

What a magnificent experience. The entire area just feels so calm and the right place to be. The paintings and the Buddha statues in the caves are breathtaking, a must for any traveller to Sri Lanka. Kind regards Ferdie Liebenberg

This is a chalet located in Dambulla.  This is located on a 15 acre land. Filled with paddy fields, streams, ponds, coconut palms, mango, banana and papaya trees. You will be the only one to occupy Raintree Chalet and to be treated as real guests of the family. Get away from the hustle-bustle of city life and experience true serenity.

We went there on our tourist trip through Sri Lanka and this was one of the more impressive things we saw. The drawings om inside the caves where unreal and all the statues as impressive. It's a bit of a climb but well worth it! Bring some water. Make sure to also wander around the bottom entree as there are some hidden gems!

Be forewarned that the climb to the cave temples may be challenging for those who are overweight, out of shape, or seniors. That being said, the temples are a historic, artistically lovely, and photographically rich treasure. The 46-foot long reclining Buddha carved from a single piece of stone is amazing.
I can't imagine how long it took to built this stone temple. It is a holy place. So don't be noisy.

Beautiful mountain. The temple merges with nature in a unique way. Buda statues are interesting. Nice sunset view. But you can actually walk around the mountain by a narrow path if you want to see sunset without obstacles

You are in the presence of great beauty, history, and culture in these cave temples. It is a solemn and moving experience and absolutely worth every step that might bring you there. For me, this was by far the defining destination of the Cultural Triangle ... far exceeding Sigiriya.
Absolutely loved it , probably the best cave temple in sri laka that we saw , the paintings are stunning as is the location , bit of a swet on climbing uyp the steps but well worth it
The temples themselves are quite woth a visit. However, the kitch figures needed to be avoided, if you dont like random kitchy stuff...

Many steps to climb but the recumbent Buddha is really special. Ladies must have arms covered. There are many statues to view and rooms to view. It does get very hot and you must take water as you could be wandering around for a couple of hours.
The caves are unique. the guide was very good. Nice view on the area. Do not miss if you are in Dambulla. The golden Buddha is also very impressive.

Exploring the Dambulla Cave Temple is a "must do" whilst in Sri Lanka. A few tips before doing so: 1) Ask your guide to take you to the locals entrance (gate) so the climb is less lengthy and much easier. 2) Don't buy flowers or food before heading up to the caves b/c the wild monkeys most likely will grab them right out of your hands. 3) Dress appropriately for the Buddhist temple: long slacks (covering the knees) and long-sleeved shirts/tops.  As you must remove your shoes or sandals before entering the temple grounds, suggest bringing a pair of socks as the surfaces can be hot, sharp, and uneven. Enjoy!

Some great photo shots from main road carpark and ticket office. You can do the walk to top from there or cheat and get dropped about 10 mins uphill and stairs from the top. Only at the top do you hand in your shoes. The temples are amazing and some great area views as well. Check ahead about times various temples closed for prayer and tidyup, (contact@goldentemple.lk) Generally 15-30 minutes where you must just hang around. Inside statues and decoration is amazing and a sight you will not see in many other places. Plenty of friendly touts selling cheap wares.

Whilst the climb up to the caves tested us a bit (including the 9 yr old & 11 year old) it was sooooo worth it. These caves are incredible. Such beauty was remarkable and mind boggling that humans managed this so many thousands of years ago. We loved it!

We went as part of a Hayes and Jarvis tour and arrived about 8.30 and already people were arriving but it wasn't too hot to climb the 200+ steps. The caves have lots of statues of Buddha in different positions and styles. The frescoes are wonderful.

Never seen anything like this. Worth the visit entirely. Not crowded and glad we followed the guide book's advice to begin with Cave 5 (the last one as you walk towards the back) and then work back. They are like nothing else I've seen.

What makes this temple stand out is the fact that it is still intact, unlike many temple ruins we visited in Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa. That's also the reason why we liked this temple the most. Despite its plain look from the outside, It actually has many rooms full of fascinating Buddha statues, with walls and ceilings full of interesting fresco. Be prepared to climb up few stairs to reach the temple and find slightly cheekier monkey (compared to the one we saw in other places). So don't bring plastic bag around! Visited on Aug 2014
I've been there a few times already an will be again! very historical site, original and spectacular view from the top

I loved visiting the caves.  From climbing up the slopes bare footed to watching the monkeys, to studying the beautiful caves.  It was a tranquil and beautiful experience.  I would definitely recommend going.  Although take some change, as typically for Sri Lanka you need to pay for everything - including them watching your shoes.

It's about an half-hour trip up never-ending steps to reach the caves, but the exertion is well worth the visual feast of paintings and sculptures that you'll experience. Go early or late to avoid the worst of the heat/humidity.

Situated up a hill behind a gaudy and cheerful Buddhist museum, are the several ancient caves that make up the Rock Temple. We found the detail breathtaking, and wondered aloud several times as to how the monks managed to  paint perfectly symmetrical Buddha on the ceiling! The entrance charge is far cheaper than government-owned attractions such as Sygiria, and has excellent views once you reach the top. We bought a little explanatory book from the Buddhist bookshop at the bottom for around 500 Rs, which had great pictures and meant we could go through the temples at our own pace. The Buddhist museum at the bottom makes for some great eye candy on the outside, but really little else; there were no descriptions to go with the artefacts and images inside, which was a shame, as we would have loved to learn more about the faith. Nevertheless, there is a good description (complete with pictures) towards the end of the Buddha's life. Entrance to the museum is free if you have a ticket fro the cave temple, its not worth paying an fee to see it on it's own. CAUTION: there are many monkeys that line the route, just waiting to steal your food. They are fearless, so beware!

This is one of the oldest cave temples in Sri Lanka, it's absolutely stunning and well worth the hike up the steep hillside to see it. We went with our children aged 14 and 12, they found it fascinating too. Definitely worth going early before it's too hot for your climb. Despite the fact you climb stairs to get up there it is still very hot work!!

One of the most impressive temples in srilanka and one of my favourites to visit. Very quiet and serene, a wonderful place to find some peace and see something amazing atop and within a huge rock that is over 500steps high. Many of the Buddha's are carved directly from the rock and are truly impressive. A beautiful place to simply see, or to search for some inner peace and serenity. However, the staff are inexplicably rude. My mother, (a Sri Lankan national) was not allowed entry on the basis that she had married a western man. Even when she offered to pay the tourist price (as my father and I had done, not being citizens) she was rudely refused and told that she must descend the 500 odd steps to buy a ticket and re-climb if she wished to enter!!! Now while I understand the necessity for the varying ticket prices in accordance with nationality - I can't help but feel that this is a Holy Place..? Buddhists should not be charged money to enter a place of worship, regardless of their nationality. In reality; nobody should be charged money at all. These are holy temples - and there should not be rude staff at their entrances loudly arguing with people over ANYTHING least of all money. All attempts made by my mother to diffuse the situation out of respect towards the temple were useless. Terribly sad hypocrisy. Ruined the visit terribly for me.

Why are Buddhist temples alway up mountains. I wondered this while half way up the steps straight after breakfast. At the top it's worth it, and to me is the perfect mountain temple. Our very knowledgeable guide, explained all the positions of Buddha, and of the history of the place. The museum at the bottom only has a few exhibits and is not worth going into

This is such a beautiful temple. The golden buddha statue is very awe inspiring. The cave temples are unlike anything we have seen before and definitely something not to be missed! Be aware that the climb up to the cave temples is quite a long one, but it is worth it when you get to the top!

The 500 or so steps are a hot and challenging climb, somehow more difficult than Sigiriya possibly due to the rocks being very hot and lack of shade.  Once to the top you realize it's worth the effort as the cave temples are amazing. Begin in cave #5 which is the farthest and work your way back to see a progression of increasingly large and decorated caves.  Sitting Buddhas, reclining Buddhas, they're all here. Flowers, fruit&veggies and water (also souvenir) can be purchased in the parking lot, and there are vendors midway up.  There are lots of monkeys about but they're not aggressive.  They will, however, snatch your flowers if you're not paying attention.  Be sure to pack lots of water and suggest wearing shoes to the top rather than removing at the base as we did-those steps get very hot.

A must see at Dambulla. The world famous cave temple which was the only attraction there until cricket stadium came up.one of or only one temple that charge a fee for entrance in Sri Lanka. How ever chief prelates have change the place from only a place of historical worship to a complex of modern Buddhist centre keeping the old charm as well preserved as it is separately.

I bought a ticket to visit this temple hoping to expand my exposure to other cultures and to better understand fellow human beings who belong to different a culture. Unfortunately, after climbing the zillion steps leading to the temple at the top of the mountain while taking turns with my husband in carrying our 4 year old baby, we were shocked when a gentleman at the gate of the temple INSTRUCTED me to remove my head vail / cover!! My husband and I tried to reason with him that despite our full respect to the temple's entrance requirements, but nobody informed us about it. No one informed us in any verbal or written manner (like signs or conditions on the ticket) that vailed muslim women are not allowed in unless they give up their vail. Since my husband and I were not prepared to give up our beliefs in exchange of cultural exposure, we went down the zillion steps again carrying our dehydrated child, without seeing the temple. It was a quite disappointing experience where we have crossed thousands of miles to see something beyond 5 star hotels which we are already familiar with.
The 500 steps climb? Please take this and you will find it worth- ONLY when u reach there. This is an unearthly experience! hoooosssshhh!!

A hard climb up to the temples from the modern Golden Temple at the base. Actually found it a more demanding short sprint than the (albeit much longer) Sigiriya Rock climb, maybe as it was exceedingly hot with no shade. The various temple cave interiors are truly amazing. Yes there are dozens and dozens of Buddha statues but there some, together with wall paintings that are thousands of years old. It is useful to have a knowledgeable guide, which we had. I could have stayed longer and wandered at my own pace but a religious ceremony was due to take place and understandably tourists were asked to leave. A must do visit if in the locality

The Golden Buddha is an obvious landmark in Dambula and worth a visit. Even from the car park you get great photos. Remember the dress code, long trousers and covered shoulders, and then proceed to the temple. The real surprises are in the five caves further up the hill. Predictably the caves feature paintings and statues of Lord Buddha and his teaching but also Hindu gods. A guide can add to your understanding.
Loved the caves very beautiful a bit to expensive like everything in this area a lot of stairs to get to the top.

The new golden temple entrance is a little over the top, but the museum is worth a visit. Entrance was lkr1500 per person, children under 12 were free.. A few steps to climb,  it was hot so take water, although there is a water seller on the route. A lot of cheeky monkeys around, but they didn't bother us. The views are great.  Lkr25 to look after shoes. The temples are simply amazing. Stunning Buddhas and painted ceilings. The atmosphere was lovely, serene highly recommended.
Quiet and off the beaten path, tourists are left alone and not harassed. Well worth the cost of a guide who can give you the history of each of the caves.

We visited this place as a part of escorted tour, and as a part of the cultural triangle together with Polonawura and Sigiriya. On the way up we saw monkeys chasing people carrying food or flowers. We were advised about high incidence of rabies between them (and other animals) and must to visit hospital for vaccination after being bitten by them. The place itself consisted from five caves built in different time periods, worth to read about it before the visit. Interesting ceiling's painting, wouldn't spot it without our guide's explanation. We saw group of monks from Thailand praying, confirming that this is living place. Propriate dress necessary and be prepared to remove your shoes. Some visitors were wearing socks, but we felt that they might have lost a spiritual connection with this holy place. Highly recommended place to visit.
It was amazing that this was so old, and the paintings on the ceiling told stories of the time. Ask your driver to take you to where the locals start their climb you will avoid quite a few steps

Some great photo shots from main road carpark and ticket office. You can do the walk to top from there or cheat and get dropped about 10 mins uphill and stairs from the top. Only at the top do you hand in your shoes. The temples are amazing and some great area views as well. Check ahead about times various temples closed for prayer and tidyup, (contact@goldentemple.lk) Generally 15-30 minutes where you must just hang around. Inside statues and decoration is amazing and a sight you will not see in many other places. Plenty of friendly touts selling cheap wares.
Enjoyed the way to the temple very much. Had some fun with monkeys. Dont feed them. Paintings are absolutely gorgeous.

This one of my dream place to see even thought im a catholic, för me its so different ,very interesting , Their are 5 caves temple it was amazing its was thousand years ago when its was built if im right ! When you go up you Will see the beutiful scenery . Its so fun beacuse when you go up thiers a few Monkeys on the steps until you reach the cave i highly recommend this ås a unique part of Srilanka.

The caves were fantastic, but a word of warning:  there are many steps leading to the caves.  Plan on taking water with you as it is a hot climb.  There was a water seller along the way as well as the requisite souvenir sellers. As the caves are a temple, you'll want to dress appropriately.  Women need to have their shoulders covered pants or skirts must be below one's knees.

Beautiful place and caves. While climbing take the sloping way instead of the steps, it is easier to climb. Many sleeping Buddhas, cave paintings and lots of baby monkeys were there in the temple . Don't forget to take water. Very nice place to sit and relax.

Being there in July was fortunate in that the numbers of visitors was not as huge as it does get. The entrance to the temples is off a main road in the town as is to me rather off-putting with a concrete car park and a very garish museum building. Getting to the cave temples involves a fairly steep and continued climb up stone steps to a platform. Because it is a sacred site you need to have appropriate clothing i.e. shoulders covered, long trousers and bare feet beyond the temple entrance. There is a footwear minding service at the top. Wearing socks is an option as some of the floors are uneven and sharp. Once in the temple the whole character of the place changes. It overlooks a view into the valley and the low buildings set into the hillside are whitewashed. The temple is divided into a series of separate caves containing 158 statues of Buddha and thousands of ceiling paintings. This is a sacred, working temple to Buddhists and not just a sight- seeing attraction so you have to be sympathetic to those who are there for religious purposes. This does add to the enjoyment and atmosphere of the place. If you take some time in the dark, cool caves they are a splendid sight. As has been mentioned beware of the monkeys especially if you have food. But they are not a problem - give them some room, they belong there. The only time we were wary was when a family became divided when crossing a path and the male became a bit agitated. Don't fuss or alarm them and they are fine and part of the visit.

A very pleasant place and one I am glad to have visited. Was very tired on the climb up, and the monkeys on the way put me off, but it was well worth it. It is quiet, serene, almost haunting. Impressive. Best to read about it beforehand so you have an idea of what you are looking at.

Private site with lots of monkeys.  Beware of holding flowers that someone might try to sell you on the way to the temple.  The monkeys jumped at me and grabbed the flowers out of my hand to eat them.  They are not afraid of people.  Be careful of how you dress, or you might be refused entrance.  Sometimes knee length skirts are not long enough, if they fly up in the wind.

Did not expect this to be so great. After seeing temple after temple across the country the cave temples were a sight to behold. Artwork and statues in amazing condition. Too many monkeys though - be careful with food.
Steep walk up before you reach the cave temple. Nice to see, but no need to make a long tour to get there. Dress politely!

we much preferred this to Polonawara so don't miss these beautiful serene caves from your itinerary if you can help it. its a fair climb up steps so try and avoid the heat of the day if you can by getting there early there are traders there selling water on the way up just in case you forget yours
A very distinctive temple shaped out of the rock to form 5 caves each with various postures of Buddha.

not to be missed. once you arrive at the caves the many many stairs will be forgotten. Totally spectacular  we could have spent the whole day there. Take sox as the ground becomes extremely hot once you have to remove your shoes. SLR500 entrance fee and 25 for shoes. For some entertainment don't miss the monkey swimming pool at the bottom next to the standing budda

So what's the big deal about a load of caves? First these are old, proper old. They are fascinating and well worth the relatively short climb to the entrance. We took advice and started with the one furthest from the entrance and worked our way back. These are a holy site so behave appropriately and bring some water as inevitably you will be thirsty. Soak in the atmosphere, admire the views and you wont be disappointed.
Visited Dambulla after a long time and it seemed like nothing has changed. I love the temple and monkeys in the premises. Just wish there was a way of protecting the fading fresco.

We had a lovely little man take us round. He was very knowledgeable and passionate. The problem with being a tourist is you will always get people wanting to sell you something. Don't feeling guilty just say no thank you and move on.

A great visit. Totally empowering experience! Loved the monkeys at the top .our guide was very knowledgable and this made our visit all the more enlightening, it's a good walk to the top but well worth the  walk. Not for the infirm as lots of steps,
Do able in an hour, impressive colours and great views from on top, tip , bring flowers to give to buddha

Beautiful and must see caves - the paintings, the statues, the calm feeling inside of the caves are so relaxed and call for a meditation. About 1,5-2 hours for climbing on stairs, recognize the view (Sigiriya is visible), to visit caves and the museum.

excellent once you get to the top amazing views and temple was great however the only down fall was our guide made us walk up bare foot and it was really hot and my mum got insect bite to feet and we burnt our feet the only time you need to remove your shoes is once you reach the temple or go early before it gets to hot
This place is really cool but it is quite a climb to reach it.  If your short on time, it could be skipped.

With an entrance of 1500 Rupees (11.5$) the holy temple is considered one of the oldest temple (1600 years ago) I suggest you'd be in shape, a very long stairs :)  good luck with that P.S. remember to respect the temple. take off your choose, sunglasses, hat

This an ancient Buddhist temple and a world heritage site. This was built by king Walagamaba in during 2nd century BC. Fore more information please visit http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dambulla_cave_temple

A 200metre climb via steps or road brings you to the caves passing groups of monkeys and sleeping dogs. The paintings on the ceilings and walls depict Buddha and stories from his life. The colours are fairly muted with age. We had a guide who gave us detailed information at each point on our visit so made it very interesting. I'm not sure I would have picked much of the information up without him as there was no information at the different points. Not sure if guide books were available but didn't see anybody with one.

Our guide book said to start at the far end and work your way back. We did, but I don't think it mattered. The best one is in the middle cave. All over Sr Lanka they don't like you to take picture with you in the picture with Buddha, so be careful about that. We were so worried about the climb up Sigiriya rock being tough, but this place was tough too, maybe because it was unexpected. There are a lot of stairs.

This Massive Over Hanging Caves r Dedicated to Lord Buddha as Buddha Vihara. Areas R Well Maintained For Meditation & Chanting Manthras So Don’t Make Noise, Take Photos without Flash Means Flashes Spoil The Natural Colored Hand Made Wall Murals Which Price Less Its Really Amazing Hard Work. Once U Entered in Sri Lanka Don’t Miss This. Feel The Spiritual & Humanism For The SAARC Countries Fees 1500 SLR

This is the most important attraction in Dambulla, Cost us 100 bucks per tuk-tuk to reach from the Dambulla bus stand. We paid 1500 LKR per person for the ticket but later found that it may be half of that for tourists from SAARC countries. The temple is great with a lot of Buddhist architecture and there is a short climb to the top. The view from the top is scenic and it is worth the visit. After coming down, we also visited the Buddha museum on the ground It is best to combine Dambulla and Sigriya in a single day after arriving early at Dambulla.

We were on our honeymoon to Sri Lanka. I was really very skeptical about visiting temples on our honeymoon. But as we had too much time to kill, we visited this temple which was very close to our Hotel Kandalama. The temple is serene. I loved the entire premise. The huge Buddha statue, museum, and temple all the way uphill. It will be good if you can pack small sack with you. Sit down during your climb/walk, njoy the breeze, beautiful view and have couple of bites. And then continue your journey uphill at the temple. Once you actually enter in the temple, the peace calm, ad tranquility you witness is truly divine. I actually sat down inside the temple, and absorbed all spiritual offerings. :) In short, it a great place to visit for couple of hours.

There are some steep steps to climb before you arrive on top. Had several small breaks. Important to take water with you. However its worth it going on top and inside the cave. There are a lot of golden statues inside the temple. You have to remove shoes before entering the caves. You can also see a good view from up there.

If you like statues of Buddha you will love this place. Hundreds of them in all different sizes and colours, Some standing, some sitting also reclining and meditating as well as blessing and teaching. It's a bit of a climb to the top of a hill where the caves are but not too bad. well worth it. remember to buy your ticket before you atart the climb. Very tranquil place with lots of good views of the surrounding countryside, lots of birds and of course monkies. On the way up you will pass the golden statue of Buddha which is giant. I really enjoyed the place but i think it's for those who are into buddhism or buddhist artwork.

Ignore the guides (aka con artists) at the entrance to this temple. You definitely don't need them. Cover your knees and shoulders and there will be no problems (capris are fine, even for girls). You'll have to buy tickets at the office across from the mountain's base entrance. Don't forget because it would be really unfortunate to reach the top of the mountain without one. It's a beautiful climb, most of which is a staircase, with about ten thousand peddlers harassing you along the way, trying to sell you ugly magnets and other overpriced trinkets. Don't buy anything from them, either. Things are cheaper and in greater variety in legitimate gift shops. At the top of the mountain before entering the temple, shoes must be removed. We put ours in our backpack to avoid being extorted for money by the shoe-check people. Inside, it is a quiet, beautiful place and you are allowed to take pictures of everything - just not of people with their backs to a statue. Oh, yes, and monkeys everywhere. At one point, I was climbing stairs alongside them, as if they were fellow tourists. Interesting experience.
My wife is Buddhist and we found there to be a lovely, peaceful atmosphere at this temple. This is probably not for everyone but if you like this kind of thing, then a must-see.

We visited here on Vesak (Buddhist 'Christmas') so of course the temple was absolutely heaving with pilgrims and it was a bit of a crush climbing up and looking in the caves once you arrived. To me one Buddha looks much like another, and the highlight were the troops of monkeys that live in the overhanging rocks and come down to eat the lotus blossoms offered by the pilgrims!

The caves were very interesting very colourful it was interesting to learn how they were painted and you could really see the difference with the natural and modern paints, it was a very steep walk and we had to pay to leave our shoes with someone as the monkeys might run off with them.
the temples are still in good condition. a nice setting, with good views of dambulla. the nearby dambulla food markets are excellent - fruit, veg, fish to massive amounts

In the absense of a common ticket for the Cultural Triangle of Sri Lanka, you really have to pick and choose your attractions given the exorbitant prices the Sri Lankan government has set for tickets. Dambulla rock temples is definitely not the one to miss. It's a compact site that's both spectacular, unusual and plan cool and is actually worth the 1500 rupees of the current fare. There's just something awesome about seeing dozens of Buddhas, as if meditating in the cave. The setting is very nice, too, and  you can see rock of Sigiriya very clearly in the distance. Watch out for the spoilt and aggressive monkeys.

As with all attractions in Sri Lanka, the price for entering the Dambulla caves is rather high for foreigners. We paid 1500 rupees to get in, climb the hill and look around. The caves themselves are quite impressive with the number of Buddha statues housed inside them and the artworks lining the walls. And, the hill does offer a pretty stunning view over the surrounding area but it doesn't compare to the view atop Sigiriya.
The most beautiful rock temple, destroyed by newer constructions and the ancient glory not preserved. Use the upper entrance to skip the concrete buildings and to enter the temple.

There is a climb as always in Sri Lanka, to get there. but once you do, it is all worth it. The Buddha statues in the rock caves are unbelievable feat of ancient architecture. Paintings every where is simply breathtaking.
This may well have been the temple that inspired the Heritance hotel I stayed at. The entire temple is carved out of the rockface. It's worth a visit.

When i was planning my trip to Srilanka, one of my must see was the Rock cave temple in Dambulla. Dambulla is a 3 hours drive from Kandy where we were based and the Rock Cave temple is the primary attraction of Dambulla. The temple is a World Heritage Site since 1991. As you enter the temple gate you can see a gigantic golden Buddha statue. Entry to the Rock Cave temple is charged with a concession for citizens of the SAARC country. The cave temple is located uphill and it is a climb of approximately 350 steps. However the climb is worth the effort with a panoramic view of the adjacent mountain ranges. You have to remove your footwear before entering the temple. There are 5 caves which houses statues of lord Buddha of various size. The walls of the cave have beautiful painting which left me spellbound. Visit to the Rock Cave temple in Dambula was one great experience and i will recommended to all to take a dip into history by visiting it.
Are there hundreds or thousands of Buddha? Even if you count the paintings you can not count them all. Amazing and a must during your visit in Sri Lanka.

After the many steps to the top, the temple is quite amazing. Being so close to the paintings inside the cool caves are oddly spiritual, especially when you pass a few people praying on the ground. Worth a visit, just take water!
Amazing history and works of art. And a site of pilgrimage by many buddhists from all over the world. Not for the disabled ....

Stunning cave complex with a lot of history, better read up before you set out. Be prepared for a bit of a climb up to the rock. Don't carry any snacks or fruits in your hands, unless you want them to be snatched up by the monkeys. A tick in teh box if you're in the area.

We visited Dambulla Cave Temple while going from Sigiriya to Kandy. There is a large Buddha statue in front of the museum. Initially I thought it was made out of gold, but later got to know from my driver that it is made from some other metal. The path to the golden cave temple has lot of steps. My wife was totally tired while going to the top. But the climb to the top is totally worth it. There are so many statues of Buddha inside the cave. There are guides available. However I wouldn't recommend using a guide since one can easily learn about the place and and its history easily online, and besides 3G internet is pretty cheap in Sri Lanka. Don't miss this place when in Sri Lanka. Prepare for a tough climb. The price is a bit high for this attraction. I sincerely feel that it can be reduced.
Nice place to look at the caves and Buddha statues, not sure it was worth coming to Dambulla, as it is now 1500 rupees a person, and you only spend about an hour there.
It is a good and inetresting place to visit. Has its spirit even despite the big number o ftoutists.

Dambulla cave temple also known as the Golden Temple of Dambulla is a World Heritage Site (1991) in Sri Lanka, situated in the central part of the country. This site is situated 148 km east of Colombo and 72 km north of Kandy. It is the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka. The rock towers 160 m over the surrounding plains.There are more than 80 documented caves in the surrounding area. Major attractions are spread over 5 caves, which contain statues and paintings. These paintings and statues are related to Lord Buddha and his life. There total of 153 Buddha statues, 3 statues of Sri Lankan kings and 4 statues of gods and goddesses. The latter include two statues of Hindu gods, the god Vishnu and the god Ganesh. The murals cover an area of 2,100 square metres. Depictions on the walls of the caves include the temptation by the demon Mara, and Buddha's first sermon. Prehistoric Sri Lankans would have lived in these cave complexes before the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka as there are burial sites with human skeletons about 2700 years old in this area, at Ibbankatuwa near the Dambulla cave complexes.
Beautiful temple with full history, very charming temple with little bit climb to add extra value to day. shouldn’t missed out if you are in area of this temple

This is a series of caves with statues of Buddha, apart from Kings and some Hindu Gods as well. We visited the caves just after the rains, with excellent weather, and had lovely views from the top. The caves must have been very difficult to build, and the Buddha statues are huge. We did not visit the museum. As with all other monuments in Sri lanka, this too lacked signage / information boards. And our guide gave very basic information. Wish there were audio guided tours.

Good for a one-time visit. Has a lot of Buddha statues, and is known for a tall golden statue too. There is also a museum with some good statues and miniature artsy stuff. Not a very great place to visit, pollanurwa was a much better culturally rich place.

DO NOT START THE CLIMB WITHOUT BUYING TICKETS TO THE TEMPLE CAVES. The tickets are sold in a small non-descript blue building covered by vines- it is to your right as you face the museum. There are no prominent signs so ask around. If you don't have a ticket you will have to come down without seeing the caves. It is a tough climb up to the caves but well worth it- our 5 year old grandson climbed part of it but had to be carried up by his dad. Ask for a guide when you hand in your ticket. You will get much more out of it with a guide than by just wandering around without knowing the history.

Very interesting temples in a stunning location. Recommend starting with the last cave and then working backwards, as cave 1 is the most impressive. Worth reading up on the life of the buddha to make sure you can understand the beautiful paintings.

Climbing to Cave Temple was not difficult after Sigiriya and Lion Rock for me but for my 60 years old Mother it was hard, we stopped lots of times waiting for her. Did not expect to see so many monkeys! Before entering to the caves (5 of them), we took our shoes off and put them into a packet (if you leave your shoes at the entrance and somebody will look after them, you will provide tips for that service). You should be covered and in our case clothes were white - guide told that it is the best when you visit Buddha.  It was a fierce heat - feet burning but tradition and custom is a priority. It is advisable to have water with you, socks or at least wet tissues to clean your feet afterwards (it is quite dirty). So we visited cave by cave. In one of the caves a holy liquid dropped from the ceiling - I was lucky, one drop fell down my left hand. Beware that toilet is downstairs at the bottom and in a terrible condition. (please, sorry) Nevertheless, must see the sightseeing.

Although it takes some effort especially if it is hot, the climb to the Dambulla Cave Temple is a must.  The scenery on the climb up is spectacular and you can stop along the way and sit, take a breather and enjoy the views.  The Cave Temples are lovely to see and worth the climb.  You can also sit and enjoy the views from the top.  This is definitely a must do.

Okay if you have just been to Sigiriya and are just popping in on your way back to the hotel be warned it's another steep climb!! Make sure you buy your ticket before you start, the ticket is in the building to the right of the Buddha museum. If you don't you will be making the climb twice! Once you get to the top with your ticket you have to remove your shoes before going in, there is a nice man who will look after them for you, wether you want him to or not and will charge you 25rupees per pair to get them back. Anyone who can stand being within 5 feet of my trainers and socks after my feet have been in them for a day of climbing is a braver man than me and is welcome to the 10p!! Okay once you have managed to get across the red hot tiles to actually show your ticket and get in the caves are interesting, we had a nice man volunteer to show round. When I say volunteer he did of course expect a "tip" at the end. There isn't a huge amount to say about the caves but here goes, the first one is impressive because it is man made or rather the Buddha is and is carved out of the rock, it was a lesson on Buddhism as well which was interesting. The next 3 caves are all larger and full of statues some older than others but all impressive. The second cave has a fissure in the rock that has water running through it year round and dips into a bowl, it's used for various ceremonies through the year. The guide described the drip, drip, drip noise as a kind of metronome for the meditating  monks as it would help them focus. Caves 2, 3 and 4 were all "built" by kings and other assorted very important people a long time ago 1st century BC in the case of the oldest. Then you get to cave 5 which to be honest has been done on the cheap. Our guide explained that the others were done by master craftsmen under the direction of kings, this one was done much later once the British had arrived and the skills had been lost, so much for progress!! Would I recommend a visit here? Yes as a side trip, would I go back? No, unless I was with someone who hadn't been.

Many tourists come here after visiting Sigiriya- be warned there are 1200 steps to climb so can be incredibly hard work if you've just climbed Lions Rock or are not too fit! Also make sure you get your tickets BEFORE starting the climb or you'll have to go back down - the ticket office is tucked away at the bottom so best ask. Cost was 1500 rupees per person. Initial thoughts were that it looked very artificial - this is due to the large Buddha and museum at the front. I didn't visit this as I had heard that very little of it is in English. After the climb we made it to the rock temple. You must remove your shoes which means that walking to the first cave is not an enjoyable experience for those of us not used to walking bare foot on hot stones. Once inside the caves the Buddhas and paintings are interesting. A guide helps to explain things - this only cost us a couple of hundred rupees. If you like religious artifacts you'll love this place - if you have little children it probably won't hold their attention (though the many monkeys there might!)

I was expecting Dambulla to be full of the nuisance guides that plagued Sigiriya but to our relief, no such issue here.  This was actually probably one of the highlights of the cultural triangle for me, even though it was little more than a stop-off during our drive from Habarana to Kandy. After entering, you are greeted by the sight of the giant gold buddha atop the Museum of Buddhism.  As has been said before, it is cheesy but, unlike most other buddhas in Sri Lanka, they don't seem to mind you posing in front of this one. After purchasing our tickets at the usual inflated 'foreigner' price, we started climbing up the steps.  There's not that many - around 600 or so (half as many as Sigiriya) but under the midday heat (we didn't time our visit very well), it was sweaty business. One the way up, you get a decent view over the countryside and there are monkeys playing all around. At the top, you have to take your shoes off before entering the temple area - note: take some socks!  I did, but my partner Lynne didn't, and her feet were burning on the hot cobbled ground.  The caves are actually quite interesting and our driver/guide told us some of the history of each section as we walked through the caves.  The painted ceilings were especially cool. After that, we took a quick walk through the museum - I'm not one for museums but it was mildly interesting, seeing all the different buddhas from around the world. There's only one thing that lets this place down and that is the dogs.  As a dog lover, it wasn't pleasant seeing so many dogs, many with terrible mange, around here.  Some of the mangy ones looked as if they were scratching their skin off and seeing animals suffer like that took a fair bit of the shine off our visit.  Our guide told us that the proceeds from the foreigners visiting the temple allows the monks to live in air conditioned rooms and eat/live fairly well.. that's great but it'd like to see some of that going towards helping these dogs out (and how about a neutering programme Sri Lanka?). + No real hassle + caves are quite impressive + lot of history - hot after removing shoes! - museum a bit sparse - dogs (mange)

Enjoyed a visit here, it was interesting to see the carved buddhas, and watch local people making offerings at the temple. Watch out for monkeys if you stop to have some fruit/drinks on the long walk up, they're v bold and we saw them take a plastic bag off a child and run away with it!

Started by being dis-appointed as the front looks like something out of Disneyland.  Plastic ricks and priests. After a very hot climb, into the cool of the caves, and they're worth visiting. Truly stunning.  One area was closed for 15 minutes for devotions and of course we had to remove fotwear before entering the whole area, which serves to remind that this is still a 'working' Temple. If you're visiting Sri Lanka and can get to Dambulla, you won't regret the visit

A very nice collection of Buddha statues in a complex of cave temples. Some of the Buddha statues are nicely decorated and coloured. The atmosphere is relaxed and serene. It's also full of these cheeky monkeys! They may look cute, but beware !! Not that they will attack, but they're not really  that sweet.
beautiful place, but it was hard to find were to buy tickets for the first time, so we had to climb this rock twice
Beautiful caves, kids got a little bit bored but I guess I would have at their age. Well worth a visit and can be done in an hour.

Very hot and humid climb to the entrance which needed a few stops for breathe for the oldest member of our party. Monkeys greeted us on the way, allowing for another stop for photos etc. Dont forget to cover up to go inside - knees and shoulders! Beautiful setting, serene and cool and well worth a visit. Lovely photographic opportunities. We watched the monkeys slipping in and out of the rubbish bins too which was fun! Toilet facilities at the bottom of the climb - drop toilets - take baby wipes / paper tissues!

This is a place very worth to visit both for these with religious interests and for anybody interested in history and culture. Beware though – this is definitely not a Disneyland or a labeled exposition, it is an active worship place, therefore you will need either some apriori knowledge or a guide to tell you what is what and what’s all about. We were lucky in this having a good guide who managed to catch attention even in these having no knowledge of Buddhism in general or Buddhism in Sri Lanka. As in many Sri Lankan places, it will be hot, some steep climbing present and you will need to take off your shoes. It is advisable to have water with you, socks or at least wet tissues to clean your feet afterwards (it is quite dirty).

We climbed in the early afternoon so it was really hot, especially to beat the steps up, but definitely worth it! The main cave overwhelmed with peace and amazing aura. It was beautifully lit up. The ceiling had all the beautiful ancient painting nicely maintained. The resting Buddha statues were many. I found it overpriced though, as most of the entrances in Sri Lanka.
I have been to Ajanta caves in India and are really beautiful.. and after looking at this Golden cave temple I can imagine how beautiful thos temples would have been if they had preserved it well..
though its a religious sight but its worth the visit.. got bit tired climbing the place as we were not prepared for another hike after Sigiriya.. but was worth the effort.. must go and visit..

This is one of the highlights of my Sri Lankan trip. Those cave temples are beautyful. Inside you will find a number of different Boeddha's and they are all beautiful. You can also enjoy the silences and the beautiful view from the temple.

We were advised that there was a short climb to the caves. No, it was a steep climb with lots of steps. The caves themselves are more like large niches in the rock face and very crowded and hot. So don't expect to cool off in the caves after a hot climb. Having said that, the statues and wall paintings were very impressive.
The temple is really worth a visit. The architecture is impressive  - the site has a beautiful view over the surroundings and the temple caves very impressive.

After we survived the climb (without shoes) to the little hill, beautiful view to the near country appeared. That was just the first reward. Then we admired several caves with original ceiling painting and many Buddha statues. It was really stunning experience, I definitely recommend to see. On the way back you can watch clever monkeys on the trees.

We were really tired when we got to Dambulla but it was really interesting and well worth the climb up the hill. You really need socks for the walk from when you leave your shoes to the temple entrance. We had learned by this stage that a guide wasn't necessary and instead got on our ipad and learned just as much if not more than we heard the guides telling people. It was great to wander around and the site was impressive, quiet and the most spiritual place we visited. My wife was worried about the monkeys but they weren't a problem at all.

It was a pleasure to visit such a place and appreciate the 'spiritual feel' that you get from visiting the various temples (there's more than one). You don't need a guide so politely refuse offers of help when you arrive and take your time to look and appreciate the majesty of the temple area. I thoroughly enjoyed my two hour stay and well worth a visit if you are in the area.

Overall the temple complex was interesting with a guide and the Buddhas were spectacularly presented considering their age! We weren't expecting the climb or the reward and it certainly isn't 'just another temple'. If it's hot then I would recommend socks as the walk across the stones from the shoe depository is akin to walking on hot coals and take water and umbrella or hat for shade.

As part of  my short historic and cultural tour around Sri Lanka, I had my driver take me to see the Dambulla Cave Temple complex.  Dambulla is situated in the central part of the country,  148 km east of Colombo and 72 km north of Kandy. The very first thing to consider is that these are functioning holy spaces and respect MUST be shown at all times. Shoes are left outside and no photography. Dambulla is the largest and best preserved cave temple complex in all of Sri Lanka. The rock towers 160 m over the surrounding plains.There are more than 80 documented caves in the surrounding area. The main cave attractions are spread over 5 caves, which contain statues and paintings. This paintings and statues are related to Lord Buddha and his life. There are a total of 153 Buddha statues, 3 statues of Sri Lankan kings and 4 statues of god and goddess. The latter 4 include two statues of Hindu gods, Vishnu and Ganesh. The murals cover an area of 2,100 m². Depictions on the walls of the caves include Buddha's temptation by the demon Mara and Buddha's first sermon. Caves 1 and 2 are the most interesting of the 5. Cave 1  is the Temple of the King of the Gods and contains a 50 foot-long reclining Buddha. Cave II (Maharaja Viharaya) is The Temple of the Great King is considered the most spectacular of the caves. It is about 150 feet from east to west and 65 feet from the entrance to the back wall with the ceiling about 24 feet high. It has great volume and the Buddha  within was originally covered in gold leaf. If you have any interest in Lord Buddha and his life, the early Sri Lankan kings or  the Hindu gods, Vishnu and Ganesh, you must visit here. Even if you do not have a serious interest, the Dambulla Cave Temple is a very interesting place to visit and should not be missed.
We had an excellent guide to this beautiful interesting historic site. Hundreds of Buddhas, and a great setting.
We were not going to visit this site but made time to do so, so glad we did, they were amazing. Very colourful and our guide who took us was very well educated on the Buddhist religion.

The Dambulla Cave Temples were the last and the best temples which I viewed during my Sri Lanka's "Cultural Triangle" tour.  Each of 5 caves was unique and colorful with wall to wall murals and an array of statues.  Walking from cave to cave was a study of Buddhist art history through nearly 2,000 years of time.
travelled all through sri lanka for a month and this way by far the most magical place we visited. took my breath away.
Outside the season but still with nice weather the caves are much more quiet during this time of year. Beauty is equal to the nicer caves of the valley of the kings in egypt

It is a bit of a climb to the top and worth it.  We did get attacked by a monkey that wanted our water bottle  - but he let go when we gave him a good shake (he was hanging onto the bottle).  The toilets at the bottom are not good at all -beware and have plenty of tissue and hand sanitiser!

This UNESCO world heritage listed site is absolutely fasinating! There is a reasonable climb up to the caves but it is well worth it. The oldest cave dates from 100 BC. The Buddhas inside are great along with the paintings on the walls and ceilings. Throughly recommend a visit, one of the must sees in Sri Lanka.

Wonderful caves with many Buddha images on the ceiling and statues of Buddhas, very pretty area! Just make sure to wear socks! You have to take your shoes off at the entrance and while the floor is cooler inside the caves, the bits where you have to walk outside are HOT!!

Fantastic paintings and the whole cave system has a great atmosphere. It' a shame there are so many tourists here, but then that's to be expected as it really was worth visiting. We had young kids (ages 2 and 4) and they loved it too, lots of colour and a fascinating place. And a few monkeys help entertain the kids too.

Like most places in Sri Lanka, if you don't have a guide organised by a tour group there are usually people outside who will give you a tour for about 3e. Interesting place. There is a lot of steps up to it though so wear comfortable shoes.

For me this was a far more interesting place to visit than Sigiriya.  Peaceful, inspiring, amazing, how these Buddhas were carved out is beyond me, and the paintings are magnificent.  A must visit if in this part of the world.
Well worth the climb up to see. Remember you will need to cover up when you get to the top and remove your shoes.

Visited Dambulla caves on 8 March 2014. Really enjoyed it here. Many buddhas to see. Definitely look up at the ceilings when in the caves as the paintings impressed me most. The caves were also a cool refreshing break from the outside heat and you could sense a historic feel of relief and calm from the many visitors both religious and tourist who had past through here over the many years before.

Dambulla cave temple was the most impressive attraction in Sri Lanka. I took an a/c bus from Kandy bus station and it goes right to the entrance. ( no need to take a taxi or tuk tuk) . The price for entrance ticket is reasonable. Climbing to the caves is a little bit hard , but it worth all efforts. There are also many drivers who offers a round way to Sigiria.
Some fairly impressive carvings of the Buddha. Keep your socks on - the stone floor out side the caves can get so hot in the sun that you burn your feet!
nice buddist temple with five caves there are lot of steps to climb so dont go in the afternoon and carry drinking water
Be prepared for the climb, some steps which are not all the same level so wear reasonable shoes, well worth it when you get to the top.  Worth going reasonably early to avoid the crowds and the heat!

The bottom of the Dambulla cave temple seems rather commercialised, nice big gold buddha at the bottom, good for some photos. Well maintained area with lots of pretty flowers to gawk at too. The climb up the hill towards the cave temple itself is rather steep with a fair bit of gradient at some points. I'm 21 and fairly fit but some overweight people did seem to struggle. A lot of people have also pointed out that comfy shoes are a must but in my opinion, they're not. I wore flips flops and they were more than adequate. I bottle of your finest liquid is a must though! Sri Lanka does get rather warm. Costs around 1500 rs to get in which is about 7 GBP. Fairly inexpensive which is good especially due to the historical side of things, On the way up, they are a few viewing spots for the view over Dambulla which is nice. Plenty of Brown Macaques too which was ideal for photography (If your into that, which I am). The cave temple at the top is clean and well maintained albeit fairly busy with tourists. There are about 5 caves all with lovely paintings and history buddist teachings on the inside, along with a host of sized buddhas to see. All the caves close for around 20 mins around midday for the monks to offer food to the gods. Again, if photography is your thing, you will need a camera with a powerful low light sensor/high aperture setting to takes photos in the caves. Overall a nice, historical place to visit. You can also get a bracelet tied on your wrist by a monk, for money of course.

It is a very hot climb to this cave complex that has lots of history. The complex at the bottom of the hill is rather touristy & don't bother going in- all rather new. It is worth considering taking a guide for the caves to learn more of the history.

A great historical monument, an absolute must during a visit to Sri Lanka. The Golden Temple is immediately beneath it. Have a good interchangeable lens camera at hand with a powerful sensor for shooting in low light (in the caves). Prepare yourself for climbing many steps - may be tiring in the heat and humidity. But worth every bit of effort.

A must to visit on your tour of Sri Lanka. Ancient caves which contain huge sleeping Buddhas and an incredible number of wall and ceiling paintings.It is a long climb from the car park up a series of steps and steep pathway, so you will need comfortable walking shoes. It is a temple site so normal rules apply about removing shoes, long trousers for men, and knees and shoulders covered for ladies. The only loos here are in the car park at the bottom of the hill.
Yes really worth the hike. A good guide book will do though rather than hiring a guide. Make sure your feet are hard!

This was an amazing experience.  The outside is a giant gold Buddha (modern), and then you climb up a lot of stairs (totally worth it) to ancient caves that were ornately painted (floor to ceiling) with gorgeous Buddhist art.  Make sure you wear long pants or skirts that extend below the knee or you may not be let in.  Otherwise, you can rent a wrap around cloth (donate a buck) at the place where you leave your shoes.

Four of the five cave temples were decorated in the 16th century, and are filled with sleeping buddhas and some standing bodhisattvas.  The walls and ceilings are all painted.  This is  a popular destination for large groups early in the day.  The .   caves close at 10:15  for a 15 minute service, and tourists are asked to leave.  At that point the large groups depart.  So I suggest that you come after 10:30 when the crowds are gone

We stopped at the Dambula caves on our way to Sigiriya. There is an easy path and a harder path to hike up - tons of monkeys on the way up, very harmless. The tickets are sold at the bottom which we didn't realize till we got up the top - a shoe stall vendor was willing to go down and gets the tickets. The caves and the Buddhists statues and alfresco paintings are well preserved and is truly amazing given the art work is so ancient. This definitely needs to be a part of your Sri Lankan relics itineary

We were there in the afternoon after a morning visit to Pidurangala. After climbing half way we realized that the tickets are sold at the bottom, so we had some more excercise :-). We took our shoes in a bag, as I do not like to pay for nothing (and this is for me "storing the shoes"). The caves are interesting and I got some information from my guide book, as no leaflet was attached to the tickets (as usual in SL). Probably, as some people mentioned in reviews, it would be nice to have some knowledgeable guide with us to get more from this visit, but you have to have a really good guide - I heard several of the "guides" telling just obvious things, a budda here and a budda there.... Guides are another story, despite the fact that this is a religious place, and its beauty invites to contemplate in peace,  some of the guides are explaining their stories laudly (and mostly these are the ones that have nothing to say) - this is really disturbing, and takes away some charm of this place. Later on on our trip, we visited Mulkirigala rock temple close to Tangalle. It is quite similar (on a bit smaller scale), very impressive but so much more quiet and you pay only 300.
This is a magnificent boudhist temple. The giant Buddha give you an idea of the enormous temple. A place to go in Dambulla.

After a steep climbing (with sveral stopson the way...), there another huge granite rock full of surprises. There are 5 caves andeach one is a budist temple, full of budas at every position, colour, material, etc etc. It´s worth the climbing...

It was a tough climb with 2 kids and we didn't find anything interesting on the top. Also the entrance fee was pricey for tourists. The steps weren't proper and lots of aggressive moneys through out the climb.
If you want to visit the cave dont forget to buy tkts before walking up all the stairs as the tkting office is at the very entrance!

First remember to buy your ticket at the Golden Temple before you go up. We had to go back to get the tickets. Not a good idea given the steep climb. Once your up there both the caves, the buddhas, decorations and the views are majestic. More then worth the trouble. Also funny to see some Japanese elderly being carried up the steep hill by hired locals. For us it was worth the sweat definately!

the caves were nice with great ceiling art. the entrance price is a little high but still worth paying and going. the only part that is a real shame is the copious amounts of rubbish off the sides of the  hill the temple is on. and a bit more sweeping up rubbish in the temple would have been welcomed on my visit.

LOTS of steps and a lot of annoying monkeys (even a few rabies ridden dogs) on the way up. You then HAVE to pay for your shoes to be 'stored' by a local and you are not allowed to carry your own shoes. The Temple is full of tourists taking hundreds of photographs instead of just taking time to look around and absorb what is here. There are a lot of budda statues in different sizes, shapes, positions. I did not appreciate it fully here as there was no guide and it was not as easy to obtain a guide here as it was for other attractions in the country. I would have liked more information, but unfortunately it was limited. A great place to see though (p.s...there are some times to avoid as the area is closed due to prayers - we narrowly avoided this!).

For sure it is a long climb, but take your time and it is well worth it. The entrance, off the main road, is garish, the Golden Budhha in the front and entrance area is also not that peaceful and serene, but once you are up them loads and loads of stairs, it is awesome.
