To imagine something like this was done thousands of years ago, and which is still going to this day in an excellent condition, is really something.  As you walk the stairs, you come across venders of crafts and also monkeys! But it is a good enough walk. Once upstairs, you have to take your shoes/slippers etc off for the entry, and if it is a hot day, well, you have had it, walking on that rock ground. There is a small charge. But once up and inside, it really is something - I am so glad I went.  The statues are huge, in plentiful, so colourful though faded colour but still looks great. It was clean everywhere, and once feels at real peace.

the 5 cave temples are really a monastery at the top of a long but relatively gentle climb from the garish entrance-way by the road. The huge rock overhangs that create the caves seem to have been little modified by man, except that the surfaces have been smoothed and entirely painted with representations of Buddha, his life and animals. Any spare space has been covered with decorative geometric patterns. Truly awe-inspiring. Get there early in flat rubber-soled shoes: we had a great guide who got us to the entrance just as it opened (7:30?) and before it was too hot so we climbed up the slopes and steps in the shade. When we were coming back down (around 11:00) the crowds climbing were obviously finding it really hard work, especially those with leather soles and high heels! Don't be put off by the strangely over-decorated (almost from a cartoon film set) entrance area - the rest is nothing at all like that. Apparently the long line of aerial model monks dates from 2013, but the really beautiful statues and paintings 150m higher up the hill are 2000 years older than TV! We spent time in each of the caves on the top platform, as they are all different (because of the 1000 year range of their periods of decoration), and enjoyed the huge vistas from the platform over the forests and hills. But it was the explanations of our guide (who is a Buddhist) that made it all come to life. He was so good that other parties without a guide kept tagging along and asking him their questions.
Amazing caves with lots of Buddhas, a must see. Monkeys, lots of stairs and a gigantic golden buddha...

The caves are up a fairly steep stairway that are fine for anyone of moderate fitness. If you are particularly interested in Buddhist temples and holy sites, it will have been worth it, but if you are only reasonably interested in such things, it's quite a long way to climb to see statues of the Buddha when there are much more easily accessible ones all over Sri Lanka.

Unique painted 'caves' (not proper caves, but underneath a rock overhang), filled with numerous Buddha statues of different kinds.   Very beautiful, and we found it quite moving to imagine the people who painted them.   Each cave is different and has its own atmosphere. If you are all climbed out (from Sigiriya Rock, say), ask your driver to park half way up rather than at the bottom.

The temple is definitely worth the climb, but it's not an easy climb. You need to take your time, and water. People of all ages make it up there, so it is certainly do-able. The exterior of the museum built in recent years at the base of it all is certainly no indication of the rest of the site. It looks more like a casino than a sacred place.

This is the only attraction in Dambulla we visited and we were not disappointed. The temple looks beautiful from outside and inside is mesmerizing. There are too many statues of Buddha inside each of the cave rooms. For first time travelers, there is giant statue of seated Buddha near the entrance, before the climb, so don't miss that

Well worth the climb. The view at the top is great and the caves are unique. Amazing how the temple was created and is so different from any others we saw on our trip. The paintings have been so well preserved and the eerie lighting adds to the mystique.
The temple is made inside the rocks and that is amazing. If you can, just leave ur shoes in the car as you have to take them of anyway. Remember respectfull clothing.
The climb was hard, but all worthwhile, bring a walking stick with you, it helps a lot. Photography is allowed with the Caves.

I am not quite sure what & if we missed anything, but we decided to skip this when we saw that the entrance was so Disney-ish. For a cave temple entrance, it was a bit disappointing that it looked more like an entrance to an amusement park. Anyways , maybe we will attempt to enter it the next time around.

Just in case you haven't seen quite enough Buddha statues on your visit to Sri Lanka there's always the Dambulla Rock Caves - 5 caves elevated high above Dambulla stuffed full of Buddha statues and paintings dating back hundreds of years. The entrance to the caves is a newish addition and resembles a bingo hall with it's huge tacky golden Buddha and plastic monks, tasteful it is not. It's a tough climb to the top with various street vendors selling various ... Buddha statues, trinkets, food etc.  If you are an animal lover prepare yourself for the distressing site of many stray dogs in a very poor emaciated and diseased state - truly shocking. The caves themselves are fascinating with many statues both of the Buddha and other Hindu and Buddhist deities. Definitely worth a visit.

Part of Standard Iteneary on the Ancient towns circuit, one can visit the Dambulla Rock temple on the way back from Sigiriya. The complex houses a series of caves atop a cliff housing a series of buddha idols, apart from a museum and a modern vihara. A bit touristy, but fine for a one-time visit. The entrance fee is 1500SLR per head for all foreign nationals.

You need to buy ticket before climbing the hill. There are several caves on top of the small hill. I think the caves and statues may be interesting, IF you have a guide, as there is no other explanatory means there.

There are a lot of steps and slopes to climb up to them (I hadn't realised but even if you a bit old and wheezy like me you CAN do it!) Pretty amazing how they did this so long ago. There are many statues inside.The entrances are quite small so it's a bit of a squash when busy. Nice views from the top. As it's a holy place, remember to bring socks if you like as you have to remove your shoes before going onto the site
Quite a few steps to climb to reach the Rock Temple. Important to remember to have a long skirt below your knees and for shoulders to be covered otherwise they wont allow you in

We visited the cave & museum expecting splendour but were extremely disappointed. The charge for tourists is 1500 rupees each. There are no leaflets to explain what anything means, no information about Buddhism. We spent about 2/3 minutes in each cave and 5/10 minutes in the museum, as without any information we were just looking at things with no idea what their significance was. We were also unimpressed by how commercial everything was and how many salesmen were around trying to make money out of what is supposed to be a place of spirituality. If you know a lot about Buddhism or follow this teaching then I understand why you may want to visit but otherwise, don't bother.

There are so many great temples in Sri Lanka its hard to rank this any more than average. The walk up to the caves was a nice but of exercise and the caves were full of well preserved statues and lots of wall paintings. Its definitely worth a visit.
Cave paintings interesting but expensive.  Rest of temple a bit tacky and not much information about anything.  Good view from the top, though.
this is seriously not interesting! the view is nice from the top though. I wish i did not visit and saved time to spend it elsewhere.
Very interesting place, use a guide when your there. Go late afternoon and catch the sunset on your way down.

Fairly gentle climb up a combination of sloping paths and steps, take it easy and the summit comes in about 15/20 minutes. The essential shoe removal took a few minutes and it was not a busy day. The cave temples are amazing, statues and reclining Buddhas carved from the living rock, colourful and quite sophisticated paintings, many figures and an extraordinary display of roof art. Be aware the benches are not for sitting on. Take time out to savour the atmosphere and vast amount of work to create then Maithili this hallowed monument.

the rock temples (caves) are spectacular, the five caves contain over 150 images of buddha and the largest is 14 meters carved out of the rock. The caves themselves have decorated walls and ceilings. A wonderful world heritage site

The wall and ceiling paintings in this rock based temple are wonderful to look at. With a simple external structure and monkeys running around, one steps out of the sunshine into caves gleaming with red and gold figures, both sculptures and paintings. Well worth a look.

I visited this temple after on the evening after climbing sigiriya. The ticket cost Rs1500 (the ticket counter is in the building on the left side). Buy ticket before climbing. The temple and the rocks above was illuminated  buy the sun as it is setting down and the sight was just amazing. I was mesmerized looking at the outside, but i was blown away at the details on the inside. The cave was painted to great details even on the roof and i cant stop admiring the art and appreciate the effort. The moment continue with beautiful sunset. During holidays, many locals would go to perform their prayer.
This was one of the many temples we have visited. It is one of the well-preserved with so many Buddha statues. Surprisingly no one of them is smiling. Therefore I felt it as a little bit said place.

The caves are truly amazing, incredible structure carved into the rocks. The walk up is nice too, great views - just take it easy and don't rush up (it takes about 15 minutes walking at a quick pace). Say hello to the monkeys on the way up, and make sure to keep hold of any food! You need to pay to leave your shoes outside but it's only a small payment. Make sure you buy your ticket at the bottom before walking up! Great photo opportunities for any photographers.

Cave temples of Dambulla are World heritage site and are located on a hillock behind the Temple of Giant Golden Buddha. The giant Golden Buddha welcomes you at Dambulla Temple . Once you have had a look at the temple you can then proceed for the cave temple for which the approach path is from the left of the Golden Buddha. After a a bit of stiff climb half way point is reached. Here the path on the right is sloping ground and the path on the left is with  stairs . Right path is easier to follow as it is less strainious . But the climb is worth it as . There are 5 caves carved out in the rock face and the overhang  over a period of almost two thousand years . There are more than 150 statues of Buddha  spread in the 5 caves . Two of the patron Kings have also put their statues in the caves The cave walls and roof are painted with beautiful murals and paintings depicting various incidents from the life ov Buddha and contemporary social life . As the caves are situated almost 200 odd meters high the panoramic view of the surrounding area is quite breath taking .

This was our first temple visit in Sri Lanka.  We were a little nervous about removing our shoes.  Also, beware all the monkeys and don't step in any of their droppings. The carvings and paintings in the caves are interesting. To save yourself a bunch of steps, if you are in a private car, have your driver take you up the side road that ends about half way up the mountain.  You can enter there if you have purchased your tickets down below.
We got there an hour before closing time and avoided the crowds - would recommend that. Don't be tempted to avoid the shoe store; the monkeys will get them for sure!

My husband and i visited the rock caves as part of our Sri-Lanka tour with Kuoni. The caves are very unusual, with lovely Buddhas, statues and paintings on the ceilings of the caves. The walk up the steps to the caves could prove hard for people with walking difficulties, but it is worth the effort. The only thing that dampened our visit was the distressing state of the stray dogs that live there. Sri-Lanka have a charity called Embark which is supposed to help the dogs. We saw no evidence of it here.

The Cave temples are worth the visit. But whats better is the climb of some 400 odd steps and the greenery around the place once we climb to the top. I didn't want to climb down, it was that nice on the top of the hill.

It was worth the steep climb up to the cave temples.  The paintings and statues are really beautiful and on an amazing scale.   It's worth getting a guide to give you more information about the temples.  You need to take off your shoes and the stones can be hot, so it may be worth taking socks.

Worth the climb to see fantastic cave temples. Don't forget to look up and see the painted ceilings. Take socks as you need to remove your shoes to enter and the rock can be hot. You can short circuit the climb up by buying tickets then going back to the road and taking a tuttut up a bumpy back road that takes you half way there. Not for those with bad backs however. A folding walking/hiking stick can be useful.
worth a look but not as good as the cave, rather like a lot of the temples, very glitzy but not as good as the cave
Visited the caves. Beautifully carved statutes  carved out of rocks. The colours are reds orange and yellows. The Buddhas are in different poses .

Wonderful sculptures and wall paintings in several caves - it's definitely worth the walk up to the entrance of the caves. Like almost everything in Sri Lanka - the entrance fee is a bit high - but still acceptable.
A very good place to start the journey in understanding Sri Lanka Ancient culture. Shouldn't be missed

Make sure you look in all the caves, each a little different and one...I think it might be Number 2 or 3 is really spectacular, quite unusual and not seen anything like this elsewhere. Very expensive, about $20-25, cant remember exactly, all the sites in this area were...you need to see them though, feels a little like tourist exploitation. You need to cover shoulders and legs to go into the caves...men and women. Quite a climb to the caves...not too challenging but need to be attired for it. Toilets not great...the worst amongst the ancient sites.
I was in awe of the cave temples. The paintings and statues were stunning. I wandered silently and in respect for such a sacred environment. Highly recommend.

This is a must see religious location close to Dambulla. The various caves contain amazing statues of Buddha. If the weather is inclement hire a tuk tuk to take you partway up the mountain. Cost is around 300 rupees per couple.  Just a note of caution. Watch out for the monkeys and steer clear.
Awesome cave paintings - lifetime experience. Remember it's a religious temple so cover shoulders, remove shoes and take your hat off.

If you come from or go to Kandy, get off your bus near the temple. It's a bad idea to walk from Dambulla Bus Terminal. There are a lot of steps up to the temple building. Buy a ticket before going up the steps. The addmission is 1500 rupees plus 25 rupees for a shoe storage use. I understand tourism is an important industry for Sri Lanka, but the high price may make international tourists have second thought about visiting the temple.
Its a decent climb,so be prepared. Saw few celebs visiting the temple, which was pretty exciting.The caves were not that great.Can miss this.

We arrived here based on the suggestion of our driver, during our research we didn't consider this place as a must see in our 10 day trip. However, this was one of the highlights of our trip. We paid a small fee to get into the temple. You first must climb up about 250 stairs to get to the temple, seeing we were exhausted from our red eye flight it took us about 45 minutes to walk up. Normally I would guess it takes maybe 15-20 minutes. When we got up to the top it was truly amazing! Well worth the walk up!! We got up and the temple is literally built in the side of a mountain. They had several rooms full of Buddhas, they ranged in sizes from 35 feet long lying down to some that were in a sitting position that were around 10 feet tall. The ceilings were painted with art in every room. Truly breathtaking to see the ancient temple. We walked back down and went through the museum that was also on location. Very nicely set up. The only thing I would suggest is getting a guide to tell you more of the history, we opted not too, but many other people and groups did.
It is worth the short climb to the top to see the cave paintings and numerous Buddha statues.  Watch out for the monkeys along the way - they will try to steal food from you if they see it.
See the 30m giant golden Buddha statue because you are there for the Rock Temple... What is very nice is the row of statues of buddhist monks in colourful garb.

After passing countless monkeys (all posing for your pictures), you reach the rock temple, a group of room-like caves ornately decorated with numerous statues of Buddha. It is another stunning example of the depths to which Sri Lanka has gone in its religious endeavours. Beautiful cave after cave allow for a wonderful historical visit.

We do not regret visiting the Cave Temples, but did feel that they did not live up to our expectations. The history of these caves is fascinating, but we were not as impressed as we had hoped. There were monkeys everywhere, stealing the flowers that people had bought to offer to the Buddha. Each cave seemed relatively the same (several anyway), and this did not compare to the temples we saw in other countries. However, it is the history behind them that make them more significant, and I am not sure if you will find these kind of reliacs in caves anywhere else in the world! If you have a very basic appreciation for history of this sort, then it may not be the site for you. We felt that at 1500Rs per person, we overpaid for something that we felt was as interesting while reading about it as seeing it. I know that many people love it, so I hope to not skew opinions. It is also difficult for me to go to a religious or religious related site and have someone demand hundreds of rupees for holding our shoes. It didn't really fit with the spirit of the site to have my shoes held hostage for 500Rs.

The rather kitsch Golden Temple at the bottom of these rocks, impressive in a sort of way, does not prepare you for the range, detail, complexity and authenticity of the caves in the hillside above. If your in a large coach, you'll have a fair old trek to the top....but it's worth it! If you're in a private car or minibus, insist that it takes you half way up. It's still a hike to the top, but a lot more manageable. Five cave temples from different eras, all fantastically carved from the rocks themselves. Wonderful statues of the Buddha, of former kings, of Hindu gods...extraordinary frescoes blended into the flow of the ceilings. You need a really good guide to help explain things...or space and time to linger over your printed guidebook. What you really need is to linger a little longer than is probably allocated to appreciate the range and beauty of it all. This place was one of the highlights of our 14 day trip. The temples are still active places for the monks. Be prepared for one or other to be closed for 20 mins at a time.

There is a fee for foreigners of 1500 Rs per person for the Rock Temple, it seems that the Golden temple is free of charge or at least no one was checking the tickets there. For the Rock temple the ticket checking is way on top so if you forgot to buy your ticket… you can probably buy it there too? I wouldn't take that chance. All in all its a nice little complex of cave temple, that look more like storage rooms for old artifacts. So many budha statues. There are a lot of steps to get up there so be warned once you get up you need to of course take of your shoes. A similar cave temple but less touristy Mulkirigala. The entrance fee for that one is just 200 Rs it has about 5 caves and an awesome view of its surrounding on top where a behind the dagoba.

When we saw the Disney-esque mouth entrance to the museum / main visible building we weren't expecting much. This is not the temple. You climb up the side, up into the mountain, it's quite a tough walk, and the temple is tucked away into the side of the cliff. Beautiful Buddha's and artwork, it felt really authentic. Enjoyable visit.

A fantastic sight to see, make sure you buy the tickets at the bottom before the journey up many flights of stairs.. Also, make sure to take an umbrella or rain coat, it can get very wet up the top, and its a long walk down in pouring rain!
Watch out for monkeys. Get ready to pay to leave your shoes. Be ready to be amazed by the caves full of Buddhas and the view.

First we went all the way up to read on top of the hill that apparently we had to buy entrance tickets. After buying them we went back up and at the entrance they did not check them! There were several nice caves with nice paintings and Buddhas in them! Overall worth a stop!

We loved the beautiful view from the top and the caves themselves.  You can really imagine someone living here for more than a decade as it is quite far up and has running water!  The cave temples are interesting but when we went it was so hot that it was hard to concentrate after the climb. Top Tip (which I'm sure must have been mentioned before but I omitted to see it) would be to ensure you buy your tickets at the bottom of the hill  (behind Donation centre) before you notice the signs half way up and have to run back down again! The mango salesman half way up the hill did well out of us as they were very succulent!
Well worth the climb up the hill to visit the caves - the cave paintings and the history is fascinating. Not to be missed if you're visiting this area.
A lot of steps up to the top, to the 5 caves. Lots of Buddha statues in various positions. Worth the entrance fee.

The golden Buddha is a beautiful monument but when you climb the steps to the top is where you will really appreciate the beauty of the whole place, inside the caves you will see painted Buddahs and stories and outside with the views are magnificent. Watch out the monkeys throw mangoes from the trees, they are very cheeky.

Well this temple will never fail to amaze you. At the main entrance you will already be greeted by a giant face of a dragon and huge golden Buddha. Then i noticed some Buddha-like statues on side which actually reminded me of 10,000 Buddhas in Hong Kong so i thought climbing up the stairs going to the cave i'll be seeing more of it but its just on that side. Nways, the hike with the stairs is long and tiring but once your on top its all worth it!  The Buddhas inside the cave is just something to cherish. Truly a must see temple in Dambulla.

After a climb to the top of a peak behind the Golden Buddha, there are great views. Don't be put off by the monkeys, just make sure you don't have any food with you that could tempt them. Once you check your shoes, you cross the threshold into another area where the paintings and reclining Buddhas are housed. Make sure to go early in the morning.

The steps up to the main temple are pretty hardwork  but worth the effort.   There are numerous traders at the half way point and unfortunately some of them were rather persistent.   Probably best to go early or late in the day as the climbing is hardwork in the hot sunshine!

This was our second visit here (our first was in 2002). Entrance prices to all the major sites in Sri Lanka have escalated for foreigners. The entrance fee was 1500 rs each (free for locals - the usual two tier system!). There were not many other people there when we visited, which was fortunate, and we were not hassled by hawkers. However, the toilets were disgusting and we had to pay to use them. Dreadful! Remember to cover your shoulders and knees.

This temple is located in Dambulla town itself. It has five caves which were all made into temples at different periods. The caves are hidden behind a modern temple, and you need to take a walk in front of the newer temple to reach the steps going up. Then it's a good 600 over steps up until you reach the cave temple complex. The steps are broad and not steep except maybe a few at the initial climb. The caves have large Buddha and Hindu deities, depicting various religious themes and events. It will take at least one hour to visit all of the caves, but it's really an interesting place. It's good to visit this temple before lunch, as you can then adjourn for lunch at one of Dambulla's restaurants and the walk up can be the good workout you need before a hefty lunch.
Impressive and worth a visit. The caves are interesting and the view is awesome. Make sure you wear appropriate clothing.

A trip back to history can be encountered in these impressive caves. The walk up the caves have a lot of monkeys loitering around - they can be very naughty and jump onto you. The paintings and statues inside the caves are preserved and impressive.

As you walk up the hill via the stairs and rock path, the views of the surrounding countryside grow. It is now 1500 rupees to be admitted as a foreigner. The paintings on the cave walls give an ancient feel to the various caves enclosed by walls ( I even found a couple of doors worthy of a picture!). You can find quiet places to enjoy as you walk at your pace, look at the view, pray or just settle down.
Definitely worth a visit if you are in the vicinity. Lots of monkeys on the way up! Well preserved statues of Buddhas in the caves
The five caves are an impressive site and one of the few attractions easily accessible.  Careful for the touts near the entrance.

It was a warm and sunny day to go walk on the steps to visit the Golden Cave Temple,and definitely worth it. when arriving on the top you have to put away your shoes in a very hectic situation at the shoe-stand,just pay attention to where they lay your shoes so you can point them out when picking  up. In the Temple it was quite busy but you can walk around everywhere so you'll get your chance of taking pictures. It was a marvelous trip to the top and going down again with all the man who sell all kinds of artifacts,but don't be fooled and bargain with them. The only thing that i was botherd with is that the restaurant was  not open,so no acces to a comfort room or any drinks,small lunch.

The buddhist caves are remarkable, and so is the view from the top. The trees are plagued with monkeys that seem a bit hostile but are always fun to watch. I would avoid going at midday since it is a bit of a walk uphill and it kills you with so much humidity!

After visiting most of the temples in Nepal & Japan I expected something more. Fortunately we were smart enough to buy tickets downstairs, before the climbing part - if you don't do that, they'll not let you in and you'll need to get back all the way down to the counter. The temples are just holes in the slope with couple of monuments inside. As in all the Buddhist temples you need to leave your shoes outside (you can take them with you in a backpack or a purse if you don't want to pay for the storage), expect the stone on the footpaths to be really hot (even in late October, when there is no sun at all and it's raining most of the time). The only nice thing during the trip was a monkey we met on our way up - check the photos.

You pay and they want more for your shoes. Not locals, just you! The caves were ok but after you've seen your one hundredth temple, Buddah statue etc, it doesn't really excite. Go to Polonarrawa for great Statues!

It's quite a stiff walk up steps to the caves and the whole site is a temple, so once you get to the top you have to remove your shoes and make sure you are wearing suitable clothing (shoulders and knees covered).  The buddhas are amazing (there are so many) as are the ceiling paintings, and much of this site is very old. Watch out for the monkeys, they try to steal your food!

nice caves but noting that amazed us. The big buddha and temple in front of the caves looked so much like out of amusement park that all the rest looked very cheap. painting on the walls were nice but maybe some restoration will make them more impressive.

Please be aware before going to this site of the following: 1. It is currently 1500 rupees entry for adults (approx $11 US) 2. If you are wearing shorts/ skirts that do not cover your knees you will have to rent or buy a sarong (200 rupees to rent). Same goes if you are wearing a top that is too revealing. 3. The Buddism Museum is included in the price but it is tiny and not very impressive. The lights weren't even on when we went 4. The bathrooms are some of the worst I had experienced in public places in Sri Lanka The caves are interesting but if you are like us and on a budget while traveling you might want to think twice before doing this site.

This site has earned its designation as UNESCO World Heritage site. You need to first climb some steps. When you get to the top, you enter five different entrances to view over 150 statues of Buddha. The best cave is the third one. Incredible and very amazing how they have lived and have carved all these statues and they used rock colors to color to statues (as we were told by our guide). The climb is well worth it. The caves are full of buddha and even one statue of the king. You must stop and take time to visit this place.
Steep climb up to the cave complex.  Only really one cave was impressive. Rest small and disappointing.  Very tacky new temple area at base of steps.
Go there early and climb the stairs before there are too many visitors.  It is beautiful and deserve to take sufficient time to admire.
Not too diffucult climb, and a lot of monkeys to see. Also not too much salesmen that hassle you. The temple is nice and the view is pretty
This is  good fitness test which I failed miserably. Really appreciated our driver/guide explanation of all the contents of the caves. The climb was worth the effort.

It's a long walk up with kids. The monkeys are generally friendly but one wanted a bit of my daughter for no apparent reason. The view at the top is lovely but the caves were disappointing. I was hoping for something like batu caves but it was pretty boring. Not worth the 10 dollars per person entry. The people are so so so friendly though on the walk up and down.
We paid for a local guide 1000lkr and it was well worth it. We found the guide at the steps walking up very genuine.

fisrt you have to buy a tourist ticket that means EXPENCIVE , too much expencive ! you have to climb many steps and finally you can visit the place is nice , is interesting and you don not need many time

In my opinion,The Cave Temples at Dambulla are the highlight of our trip to Sri Lanka.  Five temples, carved out of the rock face of a mountain, some 500 feet up.  It's a somewhat strenuous climb up, mostly on stairs, but I saw many senior citizens making the effort and succeeding to get to the top.  The temples are quite spectacular and there are no restrictions on photography which surprised me.  It is hard to believe that people were able to carve these caves and Buddha statues some 2000 years ago.  Take your time and make the effort to climb up and you will be rewarded by a phenomenal site.
...but well worth it. To think they have been there almost two thousand years, and so beautifully preserved.
The big gold buddha can be seen from quite a distance. It is so big, it takes breath...but the real important place to see are the caves, which are just amazing.
If you are in dambulla, you just have to visit this. It it amazing. Just spend some a bit longer in the caves, you can feel the energy breathing at you.

The recorded history of the Dambulla Caves goes back over two thousand years to the time of King Valagama (ruled 103 BC and again 89 BC – 77 BC). The king sort refuge amongst the monks living in these caves when he was ousted from power in 103 BC by South Indian marauders who invaded the country. After a grueling 14 year campaign Valagama finally regained control and in thanksgiving built the original vihara on this site. Since then the site has evolved organically into its present state. The beauty of the cave temple is its setting into five huge caverns high on a mountainside. Inside are 153 Buddha statues in various reposes, three statues of ancient kings, and four other statues including those of Vishnu and Ganesh. The eyes on some of the statues are interesting. The ceiling and walls have been painted and repainted over the centuries by the resident monks and contain some interesting juxtapose of imagery including those of royal life. See if you can spot the somewhat risqué scene in one of the large murals. It is a scene of a king holding court. But if you peer through the doorway in the painting you will see a couple indulging in some intimacy. Since the ancient site is located on a mountainside there is a rather strenuous climb to the top. Photography is allowed but don’t offend local sensibility by posing with the statues. There is an entrance fee to enter the site. I found the modern additions at the base of the hill a bit garish and lacking finesse.
I liked Dambulla cave temple even though it involved climbing a  height equivalent to about 300 steps  which is partly steps and partly gradient

I really enjoyed going to this temple and loved the original rock art which has been so well preserved.  We were fortunate that I driver suggested to take us half way by car as it was a hot day.  We then had a relatively easy walk up to the temple from there.  Don't buy the lotus flower on offer, as there are monkeys everywhere along the path.  Even though they are not aggressive, they eat the flower and will try and take it from you, which means you could get scratched. Well worth the visit while in Sri Lanka if you have time.
The temple itself is fascinating and the caves are really impressive. But also the walk to the temple is great as it offers a fantastic overview of the region.

Each one of these temples is a masterpiece. Carved into the side of a hill, each is a different shape and size and contain a variety of Buddha statues and wall paintings. Flash photography is discouraged. (I took pictures with an iPad.) The monkeys on the path up to the temples were so entertaining, the sometimes steep walk was a breeze.

Our guide started the climb from the halfway point so we were saved a series of steps. From there, it was an easy leisurely walk to the top . You can either take the steps or keep left and climb up the slope.  Lots of monkeys running around but not aggressive. Beware if you buy lotus flowers as the monkeys love to eat the "lotus heart" and will snatch the flowers away. At the top, you must take off your shoes and pay LKR25 to the "shoekeeper". The cave paintings are very beautiful and well preverved. It is a series of 5 separate caves ranging from the 5th century to 1970s. Be mindful not to touch any of the statues as a sign of respect . View from the top was very nice. Highly recommended !

A little of a walk up the hill but well worth the effort. Full of history, well maintained, and couldn't be better located. But the most important thing to remember is make sure you keep your shoes on until you get to the entrance of the temple at the top where they have a small stand for you to leave your shoes. You don't want to walk up or down the hill barefoot. Insist on this no matter what they tell you. It is allowed.

This is 200 step climb to the temple.  It is worth it.  Great old sculptures and artistry waiting at the top.  As with Sri Lanka - they are only looking at making money.  I would advise you take of your shoes before you get to the top or they will charge you to keep them safe.

The massive Golden Buddha statue looms over the countryside as you approach Dambulla, and it is impressive.  But on closer inspection, the whole complex is quite modern, gaudy, and just ugly.  The face of the Buddha is not as serene as most of the others you find scattered across the island.

We had a great afternoon in Dambulla, visiting the Cave temples and the religious works of art housed within them.  The climb upto the temples is long and steep, but after sweltering in the sun, the view that greets you from the top is breathtaking.  We were fortunate enough to have our knowledgeable guide explain the caves and their contents, but most of the information can be found in the good guide books.  Highly recommended.
A visit to the five adjacent caves that house these ancient temples is worth the hot climb uphill from the carpark. The vibrant paintings and sculptures inside are awe-inspiring, given their age.

Reading about the temple caves you'd get the impression that it's a massive site with lots of history to digest and sights to wander off to- well it isn't. It's significant and some caves are impressive but it's not sprawled like how guidebooks wrote about it. It helps a LOT to brush up on the site's history before going there to really grasp its importance. That said, it's worth few of hours to see the wall paintings and admire the view from the top but it's not as sweeping as others. Plus the museum has nothing in it unlike the one in Pollonaruwa,

The cave is fantastic - but getting there isn't fun.  Expensive tickets relatively speaking and then an exhausting climb - which at certain times of the day is made worse by the heat.  And the real problem is that in places the steps end and one is climbing on slippery bare rock.  Bearing in mind the cost one would have thought that there would have been safe access.  By the time we got to the top we were close to heat stroke & coming down with wobbling legs on slippery bare rock  - well, not good.  Not a place for the unfit or those of poor balance !

Another important heritage destination in Sri Lanka. The series of statues carved in stone is testimony of highest level of perfection attained by the artisans of that era. But, I wonder why all statues have bees painted and why the caves have been compartmentalized? it has greatly undermined the original character of the place. I would appeal the authority to wave or lower the entry fee which is currently very very high (specially for foreigners). And,please consider providing drinking water fountains at appropriate locations as people of all age group are visiting the caves and they may not be carrying water bottles all the time.

I visited Dambulla Cave Temple after doing Sigiriya Rock which was really challenging. After reading some blogs from travelers that you can do both sites on the same day I decided to do it but it turned out to be difficult and too taxing in one day.
I loved the caves with their very ancient statues intact and the lying Buddha but I didn't like the Golden Temple...too commercial, nor the fees for washroom/toilet paper.

To visit this site was to see someone's vision over 2000 years ago. To be in the presence of statues that were of this age makes you realise what life is about. The walk to the top was a bit of a struggle, but if you take your time it is worth the effort.

These caves are truly amazing, the whole environment is clean & very easy to manoeuvre & because there are many of them together for tourists it's not congested or rushed. The v ll paintings are amazing, beautiful colours & maintained very well. Just show respect for the environment understanding the significance.
A Million Buddha statues adorn this temple. :) Other than that, it has a great location and a great hike to get there. A must stop for most.
A Million Buddha statues adorn this temple. :) Other than that, it has a great location and a great hike to get there. A must stop for most.

We stopped at Dambulla Golden Temple and caves on our way to Sigirya.  The tour bus dropped us off at the entrance to the Temple, almost at the footsteps of the massive Golden Buddha statue.  We were accompanied by our knowledgeable guide Anura.  From here on, it is roughly a 30 minute relaxed walk along the well maintained path and rock steps to the top of the massive monolithic rock  into which these cave temples are carved in/ built over many centuries, dating back to 2nd century BC. (for younger adults in better shape, I suppose this climb can be done in half the time).  The party of 10 of us who were all 60 plus in age were quite exhausted by the time we got to the top.  Shoes had to be removed and stored for a charge of Rs25 per pair before entering the temple complex.  All of us were deeply enchanted by the spirituality of these temples.  Each of the cave temples had many Buddha statues, all intricately constructed, and the ceiling and walls were painted in brilliant colors that resembled tapestry.  The first cave temple or the "Cave of the Lord of Gods" has an enormous reclining Buddha statue, nearly 50 feet long.  The second cave temple is the largest of the caves and is called "the cave temple of the great kings".  This particular cave temple appealed to us the most, by the large number of Buddha statues, all very well preserved. There was a life size standing granite statue of lord Buddha with many seated Buddhas. There were also other statues,of kings and Hindu gods in this temple. The fifth cave temple is the newest and the smallest of the temple caves.  The reclining Buddhas in caves, 2, 3 and 5 are all in very good condition.  The cave temples close their doors to the tourists at 6.30 PM.  We did not get a chance to visit the museum at the bottom of the hill near the entrance.
This temple is a must if you wanna see Buddhist temples the temple is very unique with historical impressive Buddhas. there are several caves with old Buddhas different sculptures inside.

It’s a 10-15 minute walk up the hill if walking at an average speed. When we visited the majority of visitors were local Buddhists so respectful clothing needs to be worn. At the top of the hill you need to remove your shoes so if possible bring socks to avoid burning your feet on the hot floor. The caves themselves are have a special atmosphere and are well worth making a special effort to visit

We stopped on our way out of Dambulla on our way to Kandy! I thought this was going to be a quick stop but ended up taking a good couple hours. First there were tons of steps, so just a word of warning to any one with an mobility issue or who is in very poor shape, you will be huffing and puffing after just a few steps and you will continue till you reach the top... Bring Water and wear cool clothing! However well worth the climb. The tour guide we had was fantastic at the site and the info was very informative. The sights and pics inside the various sections of the temple were very interesting to see and photograph. The temple entrance was very ornate and colorful. Definitely worth the stop (and climb)!

A huge Buddha very colourful unlike the the ancient Buddha statues and stupas in Sri lanka. Nevertheless very impressive , beautiful collection of Buddhas from the world over  more like donations . Attached to this are the caves , indeed an experience to go through  them.

We visited this purely cause we were staying in Dambulla. The entry fee of LKR 1500 per person is very high. Locals get it free. There are 4 caves. All have the same looking colored statues and painted ceilings. Every cave has a buddha lying down and in various sitting and standing positions. The climb is not as high as in Sigiriya. Not worth the entry fee

As Buddhist, Golden cave temple is very important for us. it brings us for our proud history. We showed it to our 4 years daughter and explain it well. she enjoyed it. surrounding nature is unique experience.  many thing to experience. I guess we need at least 1/2 day to fully learn everything.
Each cave is slightly different, but each one is a place for spiritual reflection. The statues are beautiful, and the devotion of the visitors is inspiring.

A modest walk up from the parking area (but wod be easy enough for the vast majority of people) is how the visit starts. The buildings around the parking area are nice enough but IMO are a bit more gaudy than are the caves themselves ie do not be too concerned by the first impressions. The cave temples are a series (5) of natural caves which have been adopted and than adapted for use as Bhuddist temples. The cave temple entrances are sheltered by an arched arcade and an open courtyard lies beyond the screening wall - from this courtyard one has  excellent views of the surrounding jungle-covered hills (plus of Sigiriya to the north). The individual temples have been decorated and filled with impressive Bhudda statues. Although I am not religious, the place still seemed to have quite a spiritual feel to it. One cannot wear shoes in the temple complex (they can be left safely outside for 25 SLR per pair  (i.e. <20p). Also, hats must not be worn and long trousers and covered shoulders seemed to be the required etiquette. The entry fee - paid in the initial parking area - is 1500 SLR (approximately £7.50 in October 2013). The ticket is checked on entering the temple complex itself - which, as above, is at some (uphill) distance from the parking area. Leaving the ticket in the car is thus well worth avoiding! Only a few vendors on the steps up to the temple complex - nothing too bad, though. A guide might have added some value but we managed perfectly well without one. Ours was quite a quick visit - but one that made a very positive (and I suspect lasting) impression.

This was a lovely place, interesting features, and caves. We had a weird experience with a guide, who just approached us and started talking to us about the place when we walked in. He was very informative, but after the first big room we figured it probably isn't part of the ticket price, so we asked him if there was a charge. He ignored is and kept trying to carry on with the tour, until we said 'look we have no money', and he walked off in a huff. It didn't spoil the beautiful place that we were in, but I'm starting to get a bit sick of every friendly face expecting money from me for providing a 'service' without asking, or letting me know the cost first. Oh, and if it's a hot day wear socks or your bare feet will burn on the Rock outside.

The Golden Temple is a beautiful temple containing Buddha idols many of which date back to a long time ago. There are maybe a total of 4-5 caves. Positives: The view from the top is amazing. Negatives: Ticket prices for foreigners is a bit on the higher side. Overall, it is a great monument to Lord Buddha.
Amazing place. A unique temple inside a large cave. The ceiling decorations and the rock carvings are very special. The monkeys on the path up the hill are an added bonus.

Direction : As you enter Dambulla town, turn to your right & just pass economic center. Hard to miss even during a fog!!! :) Parking : Never a problem; unless it's a full moon poya day or any other Buddhist festival day. Location : Well, you need to break some sweat, you are climbing a rock after all!! As most interesting places in Sri Lanka, you need to "climb". Try to make it before sun is at it's peak, as the rock will heat up & your ascend will have an effect on your tender legs, if they are. There are proper steps all the way. At the entrance to the cave you will have to remove your shoes, as it's a venerable location, & proceed to purchase an entrance ticket (sorry, no exceptions). Please do wear modest clothing to cover self, as shorts/revealing clothing is frowned upon. There are 80 odd of caves on record, but only 5 caves are on view. DO take your time & don't forget your camera. In one cave you will find a pot/urn filled with water to the brim, where the water drips from the roof of the cave. A large Bo tree with a small ponds of water lilies are found outside which gives this place serene look. History : It's said a great king from Anuradhapura on exile hid/took refuge within these caves along with the Buddhist monks. On re-assumption to the throne, the king return the gesture by building this monastery with artistic value. Do not miss : The seated Golden Buddha statue, built during recent times. There are these touts around who might try to say that the statue is the largest in world. Well, you should know better than him... :) Avoid : The monkeys!! They are wild & never mild...

A group of caves converted to a series of buddhist temples.  Well worth the climb up.   Good views over the surrounding countryside and Sigirya rock.  The walls of the caves are covered in beautiful paintings and there are many buddha statues.   The wall paintings here are not so elegant as the ones at Sigirya but there are many more of them and there is a much greater variety.
This is a great place, with many beautiful buddhas, set into caves above the town.  well worth the walk up a steep incline.

I visited Dambulla with family in August. It really is an amazing place with ancient buddha statues and wall paintings. The climb up in the heat of the day is quite hard... probably is best to go up when its cool. The tour guide was obviously talking on reel and didnt seem too interested in his job. All in all worth a visit if your in the area.

It's a steep climb to the top where the entrance to the caves are - takes about 10 minutes or so in the heat maybe 15 minutes.....keep stopping to take in the surrounding views and watch the cheeky monkeys!! The caves are fascinating - the paintings are breathtaking. You only need about an hour here but it is well worth a visit.

This is definitely one of the highlights of the cultural triangle. Located close to Sigiriya this is a sight that should be visited at the coolest time of the day. The reason is that the rock cave temples are situated at the top of s relatively steep climb. This may be achieved by steps, paved slopes or a combination of both. Monkeys lie in wait for the unwary, seeking to seize flowers or fruit to eat. There are five cave temples varying in age. The oldest has been dated to the 1st century BC. The first temple that one comes to is the oldest and is filled with a reclining Buddha at para nirvana. It is all one carving into the rock including the pedestal. The image was once covered in gold. The soles of the feet remain painted. It is intimate and had many worshippers inside making the atmosphere very hot. The second cave is in stark contrast with the first. It is immense and filled with Buddha images lined around the walls. Murals cover the walls and should be examined for their intricacy. Cave 3 contains another reclining Buddha image but this he is sleeping. The many images here are carved in wood. The Portuguese influence may be perceived in the statue of the king. This cave is from the later Kandy period. The last two caves also contain images. One point of note is the small stupa in cave 4.

The caves were great and this was one place where it is worth 500 rupees for the guide as the information is very interesting. The painted ceilings and statues are 2100 years old, and are fantastic to see. There are wild monkeys near the caves and we saw two with babies which was delightful, steep climb to the top. You need to remove your shoes before entering. Where sensible shoes for the climb, ensure shoulders and knees covered. One word of advice, find a public toilet before you visit as he ones here are disgusting!

If there is one thing that you see in Sri Lanka, make it Dambulla. The Temple at the bottom of the hill is stunning in itself. But that's not where you're going. You're going up the hill - pretty much to the top. It's a good, fairly steep walk - 10 to 15 minutes probably. Lots of monkeys and great views. Right at the top you come to the cave temples. They're stunning and well worth the walk. Absolutely unique. Lovely frescoes, beautiful Buddhas. Amazing. Make the trip!

it is a Buddhist temple site with caves located atop a small rock which is reached by climbing up around 100 or so stairs a 10 minute climb. the site itself offers spectacular views of the surrounding plains the caves house the statues of Lord Buddha all some 1000 or more years old. the temple closes by 5 or so in the evening. the entire excursion generally takes around an Hours time. worth spending the hour. we felt the tickets for foreigners were a little overpriced.
The cave temples were a revelation with their extraordinary frescoes and statues of Buddha. The colours were bright, vivid, as if they had been painted just yesterday.
I liked the big golden boudha the little walk but then 12 dollars to see a cave with dozens of boudha statues.. that is super boring.. been  in Asia 10 years.. cannot believe it's world heritage..

This is a beautiful place! An amazing experience that must not be missed! We spent a couple of hours visiting this temple with our guide. Once you understand the history behind this place, you can start appreciating why this place is a must if you go to Sri Lanka!

The cave temples are found high up after maybe a half kilometre walk which would be difficult for people with mobility issues. One needs to be careful because if wet the rock surfaces in part could be slippery. The statues in the caves are amazing and there are also great distant views of the countryside.
At first I thought its just another Temple at the top of a large rock, but after a long hot walk up felt it was worth the effort. Amazing effort has gone into this.

The Cave Temple is well worth a visit - the Bhuddas and artwork in the 5 caves are absolutely marvellous. One word of warning though, on arrival our driver directed us to the Temple and said it was only 200 metres. It was all uphill and I think 500 metres or even further!
A guide told us very interesting details about the different caves. It was absolutely worth the money. We were very impressed about the beauty of the various Buddha statues. Excellent!

This site is situated 148 km east of Colombo and 72 km north of Kandy. The rock towers 160 m over the surrounding plains and needless to mention it involves a 40 min trek uphill.  This complex dates from the 3rd and 2nd centuries BC. The temple is composed of five caves, which have been converted into shrine rooms. The caves, built at the base of a 150m high rock are by far the most impressive of the many cave temples found in Sri Lanka. The view is breathtakingly scenic. There is a guided tour available for temple complex at a reasonable charge. The temple entry is quite grand give a typical essence of a Sri Lankan monestary. Overall a good site to visit. Tip "be careful of the monkeys sitting all around the climb towards the temple."
The temple is beautiful and filled with monkeys. The paintings are lovely and definitely worth the money.
A lot of history to this cave. Fantastic views.It,, a temple built in side a cave which has unique architecture.
Nice painting and caves..Very historic place to visit.Don't feed any monkeys around there might be a problem.

These caves cannot and should not be missed on your trip to Sri Lanka.    I took so many photos from this fantastic place.   And I went as soon as they opened which meant I had the whole place to myself for about 90 minutes.   Go early before the crowds come in.   A must!!!
It's location and the religious art that is displayed can take you back to ancient times to experience Buddhism.
Most beautiful cave temples with astonishing paintings. Not to be missed, and well worth the effort of a short climb up.

It is almost unbelievable the amount of designs and patterns painted these caves. Many statues of Buddha but in my opinion the paintings are what stands out the most. All walls and ceilings painted  .... out of this world

I was truly blown away by this place. Yes you have to walk up some steps to get there, but that just makes it all the more rewarding, and if my 13yr old daughter can do it then its not a problem. In a nut shell up on the side of the mountain there is a temple that consists of a number of caves that contain Buddhist sculptures and murals.  When we visited, there was also a troop of monkeys hanging out there. It has a very authentic feel to it, and I could have happily just sat and soaked up the environment  and culture for some time. Highly recommended.

What a wonderful stop on our tour of Sri Lanka.  There's of course that amazing building and the enormous golden budda.  However, the experience is in walking up the steps to the left of the building and going to the small caves that contain a range of elaborate and interesting sculptures, paintings, etc.  (Defintely not handicap accessible without assistance.)  Religious activities are still held there so that while tourists are welcome, a certain amount of decorum is appropriate (e.g., no short skirts, revealing tops, shoes inside the cave, etc.)  An added treat was observing the numerous monkeys who have made the grounds their home.  (Be sure not to bring food with you and don't leave your bag/backpack open and unattended.)   You can make your visit as long or as short as you want based upon your interest.  Suitable for all ages. Note regarding bathroom situation:  Better to go before you get there.  In urgent situations, you'll need to pay a very nominal amount and should bring your own tissue paper.

Well its a climb similar to Sigiria rock, personally i found it more steep than that. Its an fun adventure getting up, i think the journey is more fun that reaching there. On top you have caves filled with Buddhas, there is no explanation why so many Buddhas were made sitting next to each other, the significance etc. i guess you have to pay a guide to learn more. Half way up, there is the option of going up the slope rather than take stairs, slope was better for me. Worth the climb.

A bit of a climb up lots of stairs, well worth it , very beautiful and peaceful no shoes to be worn inside temple, lots of Hindu chanting the day I went with a Hindu Priest tying a white cotton around my wrist and chanting a little prayer(for a small donation) very humbling experience . the 3rd cave where all the Buddhas sit has a large fenced Brass vase which water drips into(no one knows where the water comes from) well worth the visit. Highly Recommended !! watch the monkeys and your bags on the way down.

Very calm and peaceful up top. Lot's of budhha statues in 5 caves. Very good for cultural learnings and expereince. Best time to visit is late in the afternoon. Didn't go to the museum however. The entrance looked like a commercial/theme park type building though with a neon signage saying Golden Temple.

Most of the rooms are Buddha temples from various times. Beautiful sculptors - some of them made of bricks and clay, others are made of wood. Also on the ceiling there are Buddha paintings that look very similar to the sculptures. One of the temples is for a Hindu god - Vishnu. Many ceremonies are going on and the place is rather crowded. To get to the cave it takes a decent climb on steps. Be prepared and take water with you. All in all: very interesting and recommended location.

This is an interesting set of 5 caves at the top of a rock. It is not a difficult climb but to see the Buddhas and the Bo tree is an experience in itself. Do give your shoes to a reputable person and pay for it! I wouldn't want to walk down the rock road without shoes. Start with cave 5 furthest from you and see how they improve. Views are good from the top.
wonderful view from the top of the temple, walk with a lot of monkeys climbing around you, few caves with interesting paintingssnd dculptures inside

The exterior of this place itself is quite stunning....with a 30 feet tall golden seated Buddha statue set against the backdrop of green hills and blue skies. The recently constructed Buddhist museum is nothing much to talk about and can easily be missed. Climb up the stairs (should take anywhere between 20 minutes to 30 minutes) and reach the majestic cave temples. Remember to wear socks as you have to remove your footwear and the ground can get quite hot. This cave complex is quite stunning...nothing like I've ever seen before. Should be of particular interest to cultural enthusiasts and photography buffs. But even if you're neither of the two, and if you're in this area, do keep around an hour to hour and a half aside to visit these cave temples. Truly worth it!!!!
A steep climb but totally worth it! the culture seeped in the place is just amazing. Take water along with you!

A bit of a steep climb esp for us bit chubby people. but surely worth it! The caves are kept clean. And the work on the walls are well preserved! the Buddhas are almost in full form and not destroyed or broken. It is a must see place in Lanka. Dont miss it!

Beautiful and V interesting.saw two but was asked to leave temples as I wear a headband due to radiotherapy baldness. Man mortified when I explained, but I sat out of the last three out of respect. I fully understood why he approached me, and saw photos of the last three temples. Go!

The modern temple at the bottom might put some people off but the Cave Temple at the top is worth a visit. There is a road up the side to the right which saves a long walk up steps. From the road there are still a few steps or a pathway. The Temple is fronted onto a number of caves with a variety of statues of Buddha both standing and reclining. In front to the Temple is a long quadrangle with a lovely pond. There is a large tree sharing much of quad. The caves themselves are very old with some lovely wall paintings. We gave the museum a miss.
Well this was a little treat on our trip. I was not expecting this at all. It's definitely a must see in Sri Lanka.

A must visit historical and culturally significant location. A bit of a tiring climb, but well worth the experience. Please refrain from taking flash photography, though no signs are displayed. It is upto us to do the right thing and not destroy public heritage, intentionally or non intentionally. If you are a traveler, you know such things are not possible inside Louvre or any other historically significant location.
Amazing budha scultures in eerie cave temples and amazing painted ceilings. You can prob give the museum a miss.

Don't get put off by the touts, the crowds or the entrance to the Buddhist museum which looks like a plasticky gate to Disneyland. Bring water and a little patience and stamina and walk up the stairs. Grandmas can do it, so you can too! At the top, behind a gate with more officials and touts there are the famous caves. I suggest you start with the one furthest in the back, and from there work your way back towards the entrance. As you progress the caves and statues get more and more impressive - you will probably share a feeling of enormous respect and awe, regardless if you are a Buddhist or not. In between the 5 caves let your eyes rest. Enjoy the outlook to the countryside below you, enjoy the cheeky monkeys, enjoy some people watching. Definitely  visit worth the climb, regardless of how hot it may be.
The Dambulla Cave Temples are a must-see. The caves are truly remarkable, filled with Buddha statues and beautiful frescoes covering the walls and ceilings. Highly recommended.
This is a must see in Sri Lanka, of the many Unesco World Heritage sites I rate this one as the top.
liked the temple. should have clear signboards in regards to taking photos. apparently you cannot pose next to the statues.
Select this site within your tour...the caves are well decorated and the boudhas are fabulous .Adivice you can access by car to avoid steps to climb .
I found the sheer magnitude of the statues and artwork amazing. It never ceases to astound me how they build these places in the most difficult of circumstances.
Read the history of cave temple on wiki before you visit. Get the buddhism and not the bussiness buddhism!

Our first major attraction of our holiday - a great introduction to Buddhist temples.  like other sites though very expensive compared to the cost of living in Sri Lanka, you get the feel you are being milked, especially when expected to pay extra for shoe minding and other minor additionals.   1 or 2 of the hawkers here didn't want to take no for an answer
Golden Buddha statue e is one of the significant monuments in  dambulla  worshiped by all the Buddhist devotes. This is worth visiting when touring dambulla
If you can be bothered to walk up the steps to the cave you will be rewarded with the amazing caves.

Didn't expect to see what I saw .... was worth the short but steep climb, best time to go was late afternoon... hardly anyone there. Actually.... I was the only one there and the last down. It was great to have the whole place to myself.
Not mind blowing compared to other sites especially if you are in the area.... but still worth a visit. I enjoyed it!
A must if you're visiting the area. Beautiful, peaceful place with a fabulous story behind it. Not too hard to walk up to the caves.

There are plenty of temples but this one stands out for its setting atop a giant boulder and the number of statues and frescoes. Read up beforehand or use the services of a guide. Take your time too to appreciate the views.

This is a wonderful place to visit - pick your time though, we went just after new year and the locals were still in spiritual celebration mode so it was very very busy and you feel a little like you are encroaching on their private moments. But it is worth the trip and all the steps! They do charge tourists an admission fee but as it goes towards the upkeep of the temples you don't tend to begrudge paying it. Would advise you to use the tour guides (additional charge - discreetly paid for at the end) - as they will explain the history of the caves etc

Quite a steep climb up from the car park but rewarded at the top by a beautiful monastic courtyard with lovely views over the valley. The second cave is particularly interesting with over a thousand images of the Buddah.
Make sure you buy your ticket first down the bottom as they don't check it until you get to the top and then if you haven't bought one they make you go all the way back down...

The main highlight of Dambulla (UNESCO World Heritage Site) are the cave frescoes. There're absolutely breathtaking cave paintings on the walls & ceilings. Many buddhist statues can also be seen in the caves. The climb is a little challenging but it's well worth it. Once at the top we took about 20 minutes to rest while watching the monkeys come down from the trees & play right next to us. You can't miss this site since it's on the main road.
Lot of steps upwards (and downwards of course). Hire a guide to explain everything so your visit makes more sense.

The climb up to the Dambulla Cave Temple is pretty challenging but we made it - mainly because our guide told us it was well worth it, and he may have misled us about  how many steps there were ("just a few more", "no more than 25 steps at the end" -- but it took 500 steps to get to the last 25!) Anyway it was certainly worth is, with statues as well as wall/ceiling painting dating back at least 900 years.

There are 5 cave temples on a hill at Dambulla - a UNESCO world heritage site. The caves are accessed by climbing the hill, and there is an option of an inclined path, or 600 plus steps. The caves represent a lot of hard work in days gone by, I am sure. I understand the roof murals aren't the originals - they were repainted from time to time. The tickets are LKR 1,500 for all foreigners now. The Dambulla owners don't accept cultural triangle tickets.
Monkeys were scary & nuisence. You have to climb many steps. It very nicly designed & fantastic tought.

We, having teen agers and little children in our group went there but only elders and teen decided to go up there to the cave temple as it is high and you have to climb about 700 steps. There is an entrance ticket for the cave temple and special discount for SAARC country tourists. I think we paid 1500 LKR per ticket. Up there was cool weather and windy. On the way you can meet with many monkeys.  Many local visitors are there to witness this temple as well. Good place for them who are interested to see historic places. It’s a long cave in which temple has been made and many Budha statues can be seen there.

The Gold plated Buddha statue is a great site to witness! Don't miss it. It was a long drive though as we stayed in Marawila but it was worth it! We didn't go inside the museum so we didnt end up paying any entrance fee.
Stunning location, ancient buddhas inside a working temple. A must see for visitors. Don't bother with the Golden temple, just head straight up the stairs.

The caves are an awe inspiring place to visit. The entrance at the base of the site is by a huge golden stupa (a site for keeping relics and precious offerings) and to our right was an enormous golden seated Buddha towering above the Temple, museum and shops that could be entered through a great, gaping, toothy mouth. A long line of statues of monks clothed in their bright orange robes and carrying offerings led up to the side entrance whilst a huge moulded elephant and baby stood to one side.  The caves are much higher up the hill. After the climb to the top (a tuk-tuk will take you 1/2 way if necessary) we climbed the last few flights and reached a booth where our shoes were collected in as we were to proceed barefoot over a slab pavement worn down by millions of worshippers and tourists over the years. It was warm underfoot and wet from the rain. This would normally be fine but our feet were softened by winter shoes, socks, slippers and soft carpets so those of us from colder climes walked gingerly! There are 5 cave temples at this sacred spot that was first used 2,200 years ago as a refuge for monks. The statues, frescos and murals probably date from 1,000 AD and many had been restored by UNESCO funds. One cave had a 46 foot reclining Buddha, a cave with 60 statues, some Hindu deities and 2 kings not to mention the 1,500 paintings on the ceiling. A bowl in the middle caught water from a fissure in the ceiling – this is holy water. All five caves were filled with statues and had glorious ceiling and wall paintings. We were really impressed with the natural rock cave formation and the portico terrace built to protect the temples in the days of Colonial rule. Walking down the steps we came across ladies selling lotus flowers for the worshippers and Toque Macaques amusing tourists with their antics. Our guide, Priyantha de Silva, http://www.pridelanka.com, a Sri Lankan whose English is excellent, whose gentleness, charm and care during the whole 5 days we were travelling made us feel welcome in his country and I can't wait to return.

My review has nothing to do with the actual beautiful cave temple in Dambulla. I recommend everyone to see it as it really is magical, it could be SOOO much more if not for the corruption. I know everyone seems to love how beautiful it is and it really does move you, however. The fact that is a bunch of monks running a business when its supposed to be a spiritual experience is very sad. I understand attractions need to have a ticket to maintain the historical site and keep it for the future generations. Here, its so clear that a large sum goes to fake attractions and silly statues, all that money should be spent in preserving our wonder and given to charity. i could say a lot more about this place, but it wont change the fact that you do need to go see it, as it is incredible. I just want to warn you, that from the ticket counter all the way to the final security entrance people are so rude and horrible, they completely give the wrong image to people about a Buddhist atmosphere. As a foreigner living here and understanding Buddhism, its very embarrassing. The whole way up to the actual cave, is all about sucking every bit of money they can from a tourist, even if it means doing it the dirty way. Everyone needs to survive, but have a look where you are. The dogs that are in the area are the skinniest i have seen, how are monks not feeding them when they clearly are starving. Not the Buddhist way. The evidence of corruption is very clear. Pleaseeeeeee people, enjoy the beauty of  this cave and your vacation, but don't be so naive and bring to light the flaws of what shouldn't be happening.

It is the largest and best-preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka. Please note that in Srilanka entrance charges differ for Sri Lankans (being the cheapest), SAARC countries (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan) 50% discount on presenting passport & all other nationalites who pay 100%. Tickets: LKR 1500 for everyone. You have to buy the tickets at the bottom. Time: Takes a max of 1.5 - 2hrs with climbing up and down, taking in the views and taking photos. Hence this can be clubbed with something else. Lots of stairs to climb, make sure to wear comfortable shoes. You will be asked to remove your shoes right at the top before entering the temple area, to keep your shoes safe there is a charge of LKR 25 for each pair. Make sure your arms and legs are not exposed, both for the men and women.

Get there early to avoid tours and climb the steps (a few hundred) before noon. The rock temple is the most lovely, astounding place I have ever visited. It's worth having a guide for a few hundred rupees on top of the1500 or so entry. Wear comfortable shoes and cover arms and knees to show respect. Shoes must be taken off so another raeson to arrive before it's too hot. Watch out for monkeys and don't buy crapfromtouts on the steps. Great views. Offerings take place around 10.30 and the temple shuts for 15 minutes but you can relax and admire the fabulous view. Take water, wear a sun hat. You can take photos of the 1000 buddhas inside the temple but not with you in it making faces which seems very fair.

At the top of the hill one finds the caves of Dambulla. The statues and painting of the different caves are all very impressive and beautiful. It is the best historic site I have seen in Sri Lanka. The tip I can offer is about...socks. You have to leave your shoes at the entrance of the complex but socks are tolerated. If you don't want to suffer on the sizzling hot stone pavement and run to the entrance of the caves don't do like me, don't forget your socks.

If you saw nothing else in Sri Lanka you must see these caves. After yet more steps and climbing you are rewarded with the most amazing site.  It is just mind boggling to think how this work was carried out carving these caves and images out of a mountainside.
Leaves all the other temples were saw in the shade because of its location and the beautifully decorated caves complete wwith 150 images of Buddha.

To see these shrines, carvings of Buddha and general paintings are extraordinary. All of them carved from the rocks and the walk (steps) up to the temple were part of the experience. A word of warning - do not feed the monkeys!! If you do they are very mischievous and you could find your bag ransacked for more goodies.
The Cave Temple was very busy due to an impending religious festival. The many historical statues and artifacts were impressive
Just sensational - the most amazing collection of up to 2000 year old Buddhas carved out of 1 piece of rock in 5 "rooms"

I will leave it to others to describe the significance of these cave frescos and carvings/statues. Suffice to say it was for me a very tough climb in the afternoon heat, but very much worth it in terms of the beauty and history within the caves. The surrounds needed a good clean up when we visited(unusual for Sri Lanka). You have to take your shoes off at the top so socks would be useful.

This place has gone up in price, making the entrance 1500 rupees! All of the 'cultural triangle' activities could cost you an absolute bomb so decide carefully if you are on a budget. The nice thing about this place is the Buddhist museum/park you can sit in and look at the statue monks and massive gold Buddha. I think a few hours here would be enough.
go there and visit the great Dambulla Cave Temple. Its a must if you are in Sri Lanka. Very interessting place with a great athmosfere..

This attraction is nearly one kilometer away from Dambulla city and this is a must see location if you visit Dambulla. The secret temple has a huge golden Buddha statue near the entrance and you need to climb some steps to get into the Caves where you find ancient paintings, statues of Lord Budha, stupas. Please note well that you need to wear white clothes and covered body, up to knee roll shorts and etc.

Maybe because we had climbed Sigiriya the day before, but this was a longer, hotter climb than I expected.  I wished I had better shoes and a bottle of water.  The bottom of the site and the stair area are pretty dirty and filled with aggressive monkeys.  Nonetheless, the site itself is beautiful and the cave paintings are amazing.
These caves with the Buddhas and the original paintings on the roof are well worth a look. Short climb and no problems from the merchandise sellers.

On the parkinglot, the giant golden and other statues remind more of some kind of "Disneyland".But once you entered the "courtyard" with the different cave temples, it's totally different. From large to small, the cave temples date from different eras. Let the buddahs "work" on you, with the silence, the smell of the incense sticks, the flowers. And then, go back into the humming life of the small trading town of Dambulla.

Well worth the steep climb to the top.  Traveling as two fit 20somethings it took us around 15 minutes. The view from the top is wonderful, yet when we reached the cave temple we were only then told tickets must be purchased from the bottom! Luckily another Sri Lankan offered to walk up and back for a 'donation' to get our tickets (1500 rupees each). Brilliant views and lots of monkeys. The cave itself has very interesting features. We found a guide to be unnecessary. The best time to visit is early evening, it wasn't so hot and we got to see the start of the sunset at the top - it was also fairly quiet. This unique rock temple site is a must to visit in Dambulla (can't think of any other reason to go!) and though it is quite a long hot climb this can be taken at a leisurely pace.The 5 caves each filled with buddhas of all shapes sizes styles and positions is quite a sight. Entry fees are quite high for foreigners but that is the usual situation.

Another great location to visit if you are visiting the cultural triangle. A lot of Sri Lankan culture involved with the buddhist background. It is surely a must see and you will enjoy this amazing site.

Well worth a visit if you are in the cultural triangle. Amazing structures and clam and quite inside. Could get very crowded specially during holidays but a  must see. Be careful not to feed the stray monkey's as they could be dangerous.

The caves are very small and would be quite impressive if it wasn't for the hassle you get from the locals trying to sell you services or souvenirs.
