The beautiful Royal Rock Temple sits 100m to 150m above the road in the southern part of Dambulla. The hike up to the temples begins along a vast, sloping rock face with steps in some places. The ticket office is at the gate near the monstrous Golden Temple, and your receipt is checked at the entrance at the base of the hill. Cultural Triangle tickets are not valid here. Photography is allowed inside the caves, but you’re not allowed to photograph people. There are superb views over the surrounding countryside from the level of the caves; Sigiriya is clearly visible. The caves’ history as a place of worship is thought to date from around the 1st century BC, when King Valagamba (Vattajamini Ahhaya), driven out of Anuradhapura, took refuge here. When he regained his throne, he had the interior of the caves carved into magnificent rock temples. Further improvements were made by later kings, including King Nissanka Malla, who had the caves’ interiors gilded, earning the place the name Ran Giri (Golden Rock). There are five separate caves containing about 150 Buddha images. Most of the paintings in the temples date from the 19th century. At the foot of the hill facing the highway stands the modern Golden Temple, a very kitschy structure completed in 2000 using Japanese donations. On top of the cube-shaped building sits a 30m-high Buddha image in the dhammachakka mudra (wheel-turning pose). Signs claim it’s the largest Buddha in the world, but it’s not even the largest in Sri Lanka. A museum displays replicas of the cave paintings, imported Buddha images and little else, with only brief labels in Sinhala.

Our personal favourite from our tour of Sri Lanka.  We have not seen anything like this on our travels across Asia – thousands of Buddha images (statues and frescoes) in one place. The cave temples are carved into the side of a 600ft plus high rock.  They are very atmospheric and serene.  The earliest temple dates back to the first century BC (created by a prince who sought refuge there for 14 years until he successfully reclaimed his throne). Temples were added and embellished up to the 17th century Kandyan kings. Approx 2.5 hours from Kandy and less than 30 minutes from Sigiriya.  The site itself is relatively small – it only takes about 1.5 hours to visit. You need to buy your ticket (3,000 rupees or US$25) from the Golden Temple complex on the main road at the bottom of the hill – as others have said don’t be put off what looks like a tacky theme park.  After you have bought your ticket, pace yourself on the climb up – 332 steps or a path which is steep in places (no handrails); or you can cheat and take a TukTuk up to a side entrance which cuts your journey by half.   As for all temples, you must dress respectfully (legs and shoulders covered).  You need to remove hats and shoes once you get to the top - you have to pay a small fee (about 25p) for shoe storage. Also, remember you must not stand with your back to, or have photos taken alongside, Buddha statues or frescoes. At the top there are five separate caves. After removing your shoes and entering through the main gate you will encounter Cave 1 to the right.  There are seven and some nice if somewhat faded frescoes but the cave is relatively small and is dominated by a huge 25 foot long sleeping Buddha carved from single piece of rock. Cave 2 is the largest and most spectacular. It is over 122ft wide and contains over 60 statues of Bhudda (various sizes and poses - standing, reclining and seated); Gods and kings which are made of stone or wood.  There are also lots of beautiful frescoes – one showing the trials and tribulations of Buddha is especially interesting.  Don’t forget to look at the ceiling.  Cave 3 has a seated Buddha in the centre surrounding by 50 other Buddhas, plus a 30 ft reclining Buddha.  Lovely ceiling frescoes.  Cave 4 is over 50 ft wide.  Cave 5 is said to be the newest and has 11 Buddha statues, two with colourful cobra hoods. Tips: Wear sensible shoes for the climb which you can easily remove at the top.  Keep socks on as the stones underfoot can be hot and sharp. Take some water. You will get more from your visit if you have a guide (or at least a guidebook) to explain some of the history and significance behind the statuary and frescoes.  Unless you have a good camera I would recommend buying some postcards from the local vendors.  Finally, even if the weather seems fine, take an umbrella if not a light raincoat!

Take water as it gets really hot and sticky. The caves inside are completely embellished with vivid frescos depicting life in Sri Lanka since antiquity and huge Buddhas are carved in various postures. Non flash photography is allowed and a tripod is a must as there is only natural lighting through the doorway, although i have used a combination of a table,a ledge and high ISO with good results. It is OK to photograph the Buddhas, just not with you in the photograph with them according to custom. Take your time to soak up the atmosphere, support the locals  and enjoy this beautiful cultural site!

If your not too into temples you can walk up here for free and still get a spectacular view of a sunset and the  surrounding countryside. Strongly recommend heading up about 5pm and staying till the sun sets. Time very well spent
During a visit to Sri lanka it is a must to visit and take a Guide it is worth. Lots of stairs, but you will be amazed

Cant miss the extra large golden stupa and then the golden Buddha atop a building that looks like a tacky fast food restaurant. Nothing special about this place and would drive past and go onto more worhwhile sites. Feels like an amusement parks but no amusements

A series of 5 caves which are home to some extraordinary rock art and Buddha statues. Every surface in the caves is covered including the uneven surfaces which have been painstakingly painted in alignment with everything else. The well preserved frescos depict all kinds of Buddhist imagery and is well worth a visit.
Beautifully maintained caves of Buddha imagery - each a somewaht different style It is full of atmosphere
Very atmospheric on a busy local festival day.  Look out for the resident monkeys if you are going to eat outside!

I disliked being hassled by itinerants. Its all very impressive but I have seen an awful lot of buddahs over my years in Asia.  These are a bit special, but if we had not been staying near Dambulla then I would not have made a huge detiour.
The caves are art forms themselves with beautiful painted ceilings, I've never seen so many Buddhas!  One of my favorite sites in Sri Lanka.

A nice place to visit but the price is ridiculous. They charge 3,000 rupees each (about US$25) to visit! In addition there is a charge at the top of 25rupees for someone to look after your shoes. I asked if I could carry my shoes or put them in my backpack but was told a definite no. I have visited many buddhist temples and never had to do this. Its a form of glorified begging. I asked my driver if the money the monks got from entrance fees was put towards charitable causes (as I looked at the stark poverty in the surrounds of Dambulla). He told me no. Apparently however this temple is the richest in Sri Lanka and they use the money to invest in commercial property (of course this is just heresay but...).  Under the circumstances I would not advise anyone visit this place.

Loved the temple when we finally got to the top, there are a lot of stairs but it's very do-able.  Our 6 year old made it on her own with some breaks but we had to carry our 2 year old.  Challenging but worth it.  Try to stay out of the heat of the day and don't forget your water.

The temples are very nice, especially cave number 2 and number 5 and 1 being the least interesting. The rough guide explains more the our guide did, so  would stick to a good guide book instead of hiring a guide.

Been here before and I still love seeing it. Took some friends who were visiting from the UK, and it was awesome. If you don't fancy climbing all the way - there is a short cut - ask your driver once you buy your tickets to take you up the side road to the side entrance, it cuts your journey by half! : ) no - its not cheating!!! particularly if you have climbed Sigiriya that same morning!

This was a lovely experience. Although the site is quite small, we went quite late in the evening (although still light) just before it closed. It was very calm and peaceful and a lovely place to spend a bit of quiet time. Up near the temple there was a lovely cool breeze which was nice after the hot humid weather. You don't need to spend much time here but it's worth visiting.

The climb up is moderately tiring. The caves are interesting and I have never seen or imagined that i would see such number of buddhas and rock paintings of them in one place. Lovely pieces of art, history and showcase of belief/religion all in one.

The Dambulla caves are worth a visit after a trip to Sigiriya. Expect to walk up some steep steps to find 4 caves with beautiful Buddhist & Hindu paintings & statues. Some of the artwork is stunning and it is interesting to see so many Buddha statues in one place. Be sure both men and women wear clothing that covers the knees (or more) and does not reveal shoulders. Also, be sure to wear comfortable shoes and plan to leave them at the entrance to the temple. I would not recommend going too far out of your way to visit, but if you are in the Cultural Triangle it is worth a stop.
One of the various places to see in Sri Lanka. It stands out as something different from the usual stuff. The climb up is a bit steep though. Make sure you buy the ticket below before climbing up
Very uninspiring. Caves are small, dull. Walk of 332 steps gives you a nice view, see cheeky monkeys playing but above else, not worth it.

I hadn't really done my homework about this site, other than knowing there were some remarkable caves with statues and paintings.  So I was a bit unnerved when we parked by what looked like a particularly tacky theme park.  The vast golden Buddha,  huge lotuses, the model monks, the dragon mouth entrance to the museum, oh dear.  I also hadn't realised it was a steep climb to the caves - luckily we had sensible walking shoes on, plus water and, as the weather was drizzly and grey, an umbrella each, plus the big one our guide had.  It is a bit of a climb, but if a rather overweight pensioner can do it without too much difficulty, it can't be that bad.  No vertigo issues, but the usual slightly uneven, steep steps and lack of handrails.  The caves are marvellous, and the paintings and statues fascinating.  I particularly liked the drip line with fishes painted either side, leading to a pot where the water collected for the monks to drink.  It was interesting to note that the much earlier paintings are in far better condition than the later, 17th Century Kandyan ones.  It started to absolutely pour while we were at the top, and there was nothing for it but to walk down (a lot easier than going up) in the torrential rain - but it was warm rain. Being saturated was a good reason for not visiting the Museum inside the Golden Temple - it really didn't appeal after the beauty and serenity of the ancient temple & caves.  These are a must see, and it helps if you have a guide to explain some of the significance and stories behind the statuary.

Caves and Buddhas were very nice, and the climb to there was not as hard as i expected. Fortunately it was a bit rainy, so walking barefoot on the stones was not very painful. But the price is a bit high. There are also many monkeys walking around, so the walk to the caves can also be fun, although the view is not very good from the top, only one direction view. I think walk and caves takes about an hour.

What a wonderful place to visit in Sri Lanka, apart from Sigiriya , Brief Gardens and Kandy this is a definate MUST for any one contemplating a holiday to the island (and all these places are near to one another -easy to plan ). When we arrived we saw a massive bawdy looking Buddha - plastic looking- you get these all over the island- this signifies that you have reached your destination, you pay the fee and then there is a rather steep hillside climb to reach the famous caves.Get there early before the hoards end up spoiling the ambiance - and beware of the pesky monkeys who are cheeky and confident enough to take your belongings if left unattended! You ain't going to see anything quite like this- the resting Buddha, the Golden Buddha, hundredes of images of the Buddha, all the different poses he takes up and the fabulous cave drawings, the frescoes- so historic and old and yet still so vibrantly colourful. You feel as if the cave walls are made of fabric -the detail is so good. There are monks in prayer, it is a very special place. We were very awe inspired and felt quite humbled- it is good just to sit down outside and take it all in. Only drawback was that on the return leg we were pestered by people begging for money- somehow this seemed to spoil the spirituality you had just reached from seeing all the wonderful paintings and statues...still that is Sri Lanka.
Worth it a big climb to the temples who were really astonishing, with lots of ancient Buddha's statues. Don't miss it

Dambulla cave temple is a great place to see this January i went alone there because i stay near to there . I remember my grandmother said there is a interesting story with the  mountain when you climb down in your right hand side , as my grand mother said that mountain has create the peal of rice who ate giant peoples were inthat area 2000 years ago. Dambulla Cave Temple is perfectly located within what is known as the cultural triangle. On one side is the great city of Anuradhapura the ancient capital of Sri Lanka and the other side world famous Sigiriya and on the other side is Kandy, the capital of the Kandyan Kingdom. In 1991 the Dambulla cave Temple was named as another world heritance site in Sri lanka. This Temple is situated in 600 feet high and the rock on which it sits spans 2000 feet in length. When you type visitsrilankaholidays on google you will meat lots of information about this sight and more details about sri lanka. In this cave there is evidence that the people have been living in this area for over three thousand years. These ancient caves have become a grand temple for the monks of Sri Lanka.

The hike up was really really pleasant with a great view.  Especially early in the morning before the day heats up.  Prepare to pay for shoes and entrance.  However, the cave area is interesting with many different sizes of Buddha images.

One has to remember, these are sacred grounds and accordingly no shoes are allowed. The ground can get very hot in the summer. Make sure that you carry some thick socks with you. The Monkeys are well used to humans and can be very cheeky.

Our driver suggested giving us a lift half way up so we didn't have as far as some people to walk!  On the way up to the caves there were a couple of annoying sellers who pestered us, after a firm and final no they backed off!  Of course they tried their look again on the way back down but another firm no they went to pester someone else. The caves were beautiful, the colours on the paintings and statues were stunning.  You can take pictures in the caves too.  We didn't have a guide at the caves but if you are really interested in finding out more indepth information than just looking then this would probably be recommended.  There are alot of monkeys hanging around here which we loved watching, they are obviously use to being around humans but try their luck at every opportunity to grab food, so don't take food when visiting the caves.  Seeing them sitting on the electric fence which clearly isn't ever switched on was amusing.  On the way down there was 2 beggars with limbs missing who I couldn't resist giving a little note to, then of course a lady giving out flowers, she wanted tipping too.  Be aware and take plenty small notes!!!

this is the largest and best preserved cave temple complex in Sri Lanka.There are number of documented caves around this hill area and the cave temple spread over 5 caves. these caves consist of statues and paintings. Mainly the Lord Buddha statues are there from small to large sizes. paintings are related to  lord Buddha and his life. the climb to the cave temple is not that difficult since the path is well constructed though you will have to climb some steps. be aware of the monkeys around and they are not afraid of humans and they will grab anything from you if they feel its edible( including flowers), so be vigilant.at the top of the hill you can see the surrounding including sigiriya rock. entrance is free for locals but not for foreigners.

The caves are very beautiful, with superb frescoes.  Be aware that there are lots of steps and that the path underfoot can be hot in bare feet. Take socks!  And as hats are not permitted in the temple area, think about a sunshade.

An amazing cave temple!! 4 separate caves relating to different times in history, the earliest which has a huge Buddha carved into the rockface within a cave is 2nd century! Bit of climb but well worth it, can always get a tuk tuk half way up the hill! Amazing views from the top as well as the temples. Expect to tip the man who looks after your shoes as all shoes must be removed to enter the temple.

Well worth a visit - large site with a steep walk up to the temple. We had a guide which was useful. He explained the different aspects of Buddha and also the other figures and what they represented. If you've not got your own guide - worth paying for one of the temple guides to get a good insight

The caves are located on the top of a small hill and it is nice to walk a little bit before visiting. I could not imagine a buddhist temple of that kind with several statues and a lot of colours in each of the 5 caves.
The climb is steep but worth it,to see the cave temples.each cave has its own beauty .the wall paintings are very interesting .Loved all the Buddha statues

Yes, you have to leave your shoes. Yes, it is a 10 minute climb. But once you get up, you will not regret it. Carved out of the rock, these cave temples radiate calm and peace. The Buddhas will fill your spirits; they are beautiful, formed by skilled craftsmen. The temples themselves are decorated with such artistic skill. One of the best parts of my trip to Sri Lanka. Worth the journey, worth the climb, and worth braving the rather naughty monkeys who want to steal anything edible from you. Or anything they think might be edible!

Although you must be fit to climb to the top you must! It's really breathtaking in many ways. The view is nice, the temple is magnificent and the feeling it leaves behind is unmeasurable. Together with the tooth relic temple it made our trip.  Some insist you must dress with long pants, I do it out of respect but you will find many visitors that don't follow the hint.

A worthy visit if you want to see the history. Take a guide so you can get the full experience and the stories of each cave and temple. Be wary of bringing a blessing of water lily's - there are monkeys everywhere and they are not afraid to take what they want - the flowers...

For us this was one if not the highlight of our trip! In all fairness, we do like Buddha caves. We did not find the climb tough at all and we did it in the pouring rain. You leave your shoes after the climb, you can collect them afterwards for a small fee. We started with the last cave and worked our way to cave 1. Every cave is different and truly beautiful. The walls and ceilings are covered from top to bottom in paintings. We had a guidebook with us for explanations. If you want, there were some people that picked up a guide but we did not find it necessary. A magical place!

The cave temples at Dambulla are truly beautiful and well worth the climb uphill.There are lots of places to rest along the way and you can buy little snacks and trinkets on the way up. At the top you will have to leave your shoes, a few rupees per pair for them to be stored. Don't worry about being barefoot as it's mainly smooth surfaces to walk on. There are 5 separate cave temples to visit, every one filled with beautiful Buddhas and exquisite wall paintings. They are breathtaking, but you may feel a little "templed out" by the end. Modest dress is required to enter the temples, cover knees and shoulders. There are plenty of monkeys about and dogs and puppies everywhere. It was a rainy, misty day in December when we visited and the mistiness seemed to enhance the atmosphere. It's a mystical place. At the bottom is the huge golden Buddha of Dambulla and also a museum. Entrance fee is 1500LKR.

You need to be feeling fit to visit Dambulla a lot of steep stairs to get to the top but most of Sri Lanka sights are likes this so you should get used to it! We took a guide from the bottom who was informative . It is 5 very very beautiful caves  with great painting and sculptures. Doesn't take too long to see if you are on a tight schedule 2 hours at most.

Well-preserved Buddha relics. A rather long climb up the mountain but a good view eventually. The caves are quite interesting to visit and spend some time looking at the glorious statues of the Buddha mainly in various poses.

To get to the cave there's a bit of a climb but it's worth it when you see the inside of the caves. You need to leave your shoes outside - it seems that locals are able to just leave them near the steps but tourists have to pay and then they are stored in a little cubby.

A must see! The caves are reached by climbing uphill for around ten minutes, and it's definitely a worthwhile climb. You can hire a guide outside the entrance but we used our guidebook instead which recommended that we began with the cave furthest away from the entrance, working our way back to the most impressive, closest to the entrance. Make sure you have something to cover your legs if you're wearing shorts and take some water up with you if it's a hot day.
It was pouring when we went here, and having been to the Ajanta and Ellora caves in India, I was wary of yet another tourist attraction. I was astounded by the beauty and history of these caves.
Its a long climb up and dont bring food as you will be attacked by monkeys but definately worth it.,  Amazing 2000 yr old caves.

Miley Cyrus once said "Life's a climb, but the views great"...this rings true for the Dambulla cave temple. Up the steep staircase you must go..dressing inappropriately is a big no no..seeing the temple is an interesting sight..just don't give the monkeys a chance to bite!!!!
Very interesting temple with caves full of buddha statues either carved into the rocks or brought in - fascinating location at the edge of a mountain too. Beware of the monkeys!
A must on a visit to the cultural triangle. A steep staircase lads up the hill to a series of caves with lovely statues and wall paintings. Lovely views and atmosphere.

Quite a climb but so worth it, amazing cave paintings and the view at the top was great, moody clouds the rain stopped and started. Kept the teenager busy with all the walking, having a photo with a snake a the bottom was their highlight. Wearing crocs ( waterproof) was mine!

Climbed around 5 pm. Nice cloudy day with lesser crowd. You can choose either to go up stairs or just an upward path. Can be very slippery when wet. Beautiful caves and very peaceful atmosphere. One we had seen all the caves, it started to rain. That just added to the beauty of the summit.
Fantastic sight, really enjoyed.  Our guide was very knowledgable so learned a lot about the temple.  Views from the top were great.

You should go there to feel an absolutely wonderful calming atmosphere of this place. I totally enjoyed the amazing landscapes and a sweet aroma of sandal sticks. Beware of monkeys - they can steal your food and flowers. Could be rather aggressive.

Another World Heritage Site (1991) in Sri Lanka, situated in the central part of the country. This site is situated 148 km east of Colombo and 72 km north of Kandy. Really peaceful surroundings. On your way up you'll meet lots of monkeys(+), and beggars asking you some coins. For those wanting to try spicy mango, you have the chance to  buy them there. Water lilies are sold to be offered to buddha- 100 rupees 7 flowers.

It's just a short climb up to the top, but look out for the monkeys on the way up! My wife had pink flip flops on and a curious juvenile thought he'd check to see if they were moving watermelons by poking them. No issue, just a little closer than we wanted to be, to the monkeys. The caves are very beautiful though. Try to go at less busy times as they can get cramped for space, and I'd recommend a guide as there is a lot of interesting information on them.

Dambulla Golden Cave Temple was - unlike most other hyped up spots in Sri Lanka - at least worth the climb.  I wouldn't have climbed much further.  But for the climb, I appreciated the temple.  It was beautiful to look at, but do yourself a favor and get a decent guide, because it's not so beautiful that you want to do it without the history lesson.  (This is especially if you're well traveled, because you WILL have seen more beautiful sights.)

We climbed (and climbed) up the steps and admired the views as we paused to get our breath back. Once we arrived at the top we had to remove shoes and pay for safe-keeping, then pay to enter the cave area. The paintings and Buddhas were pretty impressive but there was no explanation anywhere in anything but sinhala. The area was dirty from both birds and monkeys so not pleasant to walk around barefoot.  My best advice is to wear a pair of socks which you are prepared to sacrifice. The toilet facilities near the entrance leave a lot to be desired.

If you are visiting Sigiriya, make a stope in the nearby Dambulla Cave Temple. From my point of view is worth the way up the caves. The buddist temple is full of interesting paintings and buddha statues. Be aware of the monkeys on the way up/downs to the temple, some of them are really hungry and just grab whatever you have in hands :)

Behind the massive gold statue of Buddha and up a very steep hill are the cave temples of Dambulla. There are five in all, and each one differs slightly from the rest, with numerous Buddha's statues and frescoes. We arrive during a prayer service and so were unable to enter for about half an hour, but this gave us time to soak up the scenery and views. Definatley worth stopping off at for a few hours. Just be warned that you have to walk up to the temples which some people could find difficult.

It's a steep climb, particularly nearest the base, but rest stops can be made along the way to enjoy the monkeys and the view. We followed a group with quite an elderly lady amongst them and with support on either side she managed her way to the top. It was a bit wet when we went so extra care was needed as the steps were quite slippery in parts. Once the caves are reached it all feels worth the effort, the Buddist artwork and statues are truly amazing. Then the walk back down is great as you can really enjoy the view.
It is one of the historically significant sites in Sri Lanka.  And although a bit of a climb the caves can be viewed reasonablly easily.

Very nice temple though a steep climb,  the views are amazing on top of the hill. the peaceful buddha statues add to make it a great visit. We avoided the museum downhill and got our tickets and drove half way up the hill from the back route and climbed on from there.
there is a bit of climbing but it is worth. women need to remember to cover legs and arms. they can borrow some stuff for few rupees if u don't have anything.
Fantastic bit of history tucked away in several caves.  Make sure you have a guide to explain what you are seeing

The rock cave temple in Dambulla was just a wonder amidst the city. The climb was steep and tedious and it was pouring heavily. The climb was worth it, if you find it tiring just turn around and soak up the beautiful view from top of the hill, you will be all energized to walk. On top of the hill is the cave temple with four caves and Buddha statues of all size and postures can be found. Better to have a guide. We did not opt for a guide. there are enough photos but here are some too..
Fresco paintings are stunning.  Be prepared for a long climb up the rocks and hassle from many touts.  The museum is a little sparse but is included in the ticket price.
Very steep stair climb to get to the caves, but it's a very beautiful series of caves showing Buddhist art.  Definitely a must-see if you're in the ancient cities area.

Well worth a visit: five cave temples from different periods, featuring various Buddha statutes, ornate carvings, fantastic decorations. We went late afternoon and it was uncrowded. Bit of a climb to get there but worth it.
Don't bother with giudes outside, they aren't official or that knowledgable and aren't worth the 500rp

This is a nice temple located at the base of the Dambulla Cave Temple.  You can walk around it for free.  They have statues of several monks lined up for their daily meal.  We saw monkeys eaating the middle out of the Lotus flowers from the offerings.

This Cave Temple is 5 small temples with lots of Buddhas.  It is privately run and costs too much for the 1/2 hour it takes to see everything.  The shoe guy would not let me leave my shoes by my self so when I did, he came and took them.  I had to pay him to get them back.

They plastered the whole ceiling of a rock cave and painted it in intricate detail.  Then they carved out the statues with hand tools.  It's impressive.  The golden Buddha looks to me like it is standing on top of an elaborate Chinese restaurant.
It was quite a climb but well worth it to see all of the historic frescos. This is something that you will not see anywhere else as they are so well preserved.
A short hike up to visit the 4 caves, which housed some beautiful religious relics from some 8 centuries ago, which have been amazingly preserved / touched up

We visited on a stormy afternoon and didn't realise that we had to walk barefoot into the cave temple. My mother is a diabetic so it was a really worrying excursion for us. So is you have medical issues, do go prepared with socks.

You arrive at the temple and the place feels like McDonalds.  The neon lights are a bit gawdy, but you are not here for the lights you are here for the ancient caves and their drawings. Be sure to get your ticket at the bottom as they do not sell them at the top. The walk is steep, we did many more steps at Sigiriya the previous day and this felt harder.  There are sections which are sloped rock instead of stairs. The paintings are nice, clear amazing.  The ages of each cave varies from really old to not so.  We did it without a guide and felt we did not miss much of the experience.  Read up beforehand and enjoy.

Absolutely amazing temple. The entrance fee and stiff climb upwards is well worth the effort and the five temples dug into the rock is truly amazing! A guide (with a fee donation) explained the different temples and the importance of the buddah statues. He was also very informative on the religious importance and significance of the rock temples.

Not far now said my guide, as I huffed and puffed my way up yet another flight of roughly hewn stairs, ten minutes later we made it to the top. What a view! What a climb. The Dambulla RockTemple, was donated by King Walagambahu in the lst century BC to Buddhist monks. Dambulla is a World Heritage site and is the most impressive of Sri Lanka's cave temples. These  five caves contain over 150 images of the Buddha of which the largest is a colossal figure of the Buddha carved out of rock and spanning 14metres. Well worth the the climb but be aware that like most bubuddist temples you have to walk around the actual temple bare footed,

It was hot and humid during our trip and we had taken a pass on climbing Sigirya Rock as well as some other sites.  But we "cowboyed up" and climbed up to the cave temples.  It's not a hard climb but the top never seems to arrive when you're pouring sweat.  But once there, it it totally worth the effort to see the carvings and paintings.  In our opinion, this is a must-see.  One note of caution - be sure to let the shoe keeper guys hold your shoes.  My husband left his outside the entry point to the temple area and someone stole them.  Karma's a ........, well you know what karma is.
The many Buddas carved into the walls are works of art, though the climb up on proper paths is a bit of an effort, probably good to work off some of the good Hotel food!

Interesting place - worth to see. You must go up quite high so better in the morning Be carefoul with monkeys - they can be nasty. It is better not to buy fruits offered by vendors around - I saw monkey attack the women who keep fruits in hand

I found the cave temples at Dambulla fascinating, and well worth seeing - It was busy with other tourists, and not a patch on the other sights in the cultural triangle, but definitely worth visiting if you're nearby and have a couple of hours free. I was astonished at the sheer number of Buddha statues and paintings in the caves - every square inch was Buddha.

Another steep climb but not as bad as Sigiriya which we did beforehand. You can actually climb the stairs or walk up a road. We found the road easier on the way down. There are five huge caves and all are filled with amazing buddha statues. Some with HUGE sleeping buddhas and others with lots of different smaller  buddha - truely incredible especially when you consider how old they  are. As with most attractions in sri lanka the entry fee includes an informative DVD .Shoes have to be left in lockers before entering the caves.Photos can be taken in all the caves.
Must go place-wait for sunset.Amazing view.Brilliant cave and nice Buddha statues, very peaceful and calm,good for short meditation.

The temple have quite a few caves. The caves have numerous statues of very olden era which depict different stories of Budhict culture and religion. To visit one has to climb up which sometimes difficult particularly for the elders. Feasibility of installing a cable car may be explored.

This is a unique construction done by the ancient kings during 16th or 17th century inside a rocky cave. Large number of similar statues have been built in a row which is a beautiful sight. The continuous droplets of water flowing on a bare rock which is being collected in to a large copper container is also amazing. It is a wonder of construction on a rock which has been done without the availability of modern tools or technology.
We traveled a little too late in the afternoon.  It became dark quickly and started to rain.  Traversing the steps at night were very difficult and not advised without as the rocks become slippery.

Please visit this commercial attraction if you have nothing else to do, it does have one special buddha cave worth seeing. However if you decide to wash your clothes instead or sleep in or do your nails, you will, in my opinion,have made the right decision. There are so many great places to visit in this country but this is not one of them.

Dambulla Cave Temple and the Golden Temple are the main attractions in Dambulla. This could be taken as a day trip either from Kandy or Sigiriya. The fees to enter this site is LKR 1300 and you need to pay an extra if you want to visit the museum. The hike up to the cave took around 20 minutes. Then you need to deposit your footwear outside the entrance of the temple and walk in to the ticket checking counter. There are five caves at this sites, all of them are hugely impressive. The lighting is pretty good inside these dark caves and flash photography is prohibited. It took around an hour for me to explore all the caves. Then on your way down you can spot the Sigiriya rock which is quiet a distance from here. The Golden Temple is not so impressive, but worth a look.

The caves are accessed by a steep walk up the hill, though the views of the surrounding countryside (including Sigiriya) are impressive as are the caves. As with other temples, footwear needs to be removed, but we were able to leave our socks on to walk around. Our guidebook suggested starting at the far end of the caves and working back towards the entrance, and we found this to be good advice. The frescoes and statues inside the caves were impressive and well worth the price of admission.

The climb up the steps to the Caves is slightly hard work, but well worth the effort.  The five caves themselves are hugely impressive - the Buddhas, the artwork on the ceilings, the carvings. A world-class attraction.

Although when you arrive you don't believe that it's going to be worth it but since you're there you decide you will do the climb, and then you reach the monastery which doesn't look very old.But then when you walk in the big cave you just don't believe it.I really liked it and for me it was one of the best 'archaeological sites i visited in Sri Lanca.

dont fall for fake guides who will pester you along the way to the cave. You need to hire one more guide inside the cave. Not well lit and you  may need a torch while coming back in the evening. No sign boards

The rating of this site might depend very much on people's interest in Buddhism and Buddhism's art. We loved the caves and found them great both esthetically and historically. The climb up to the caves was not as spectacular as in Sigiriya, but was beautiful and pleasant enough. Make sure you get tickets before starting to take the stairs. We found the tickets stall was closed so proceeded to go up, only to be told after half way that we had to go down again to buy tickets, and it seemed to be something usual there.
The people coming for the Buddha rituals are very friendly. They have not objection in you taking pictures with them. Just don't turn your back to the Buddha statue, it's disrespectful to them.
Rock tempels are great! We did not visited the museum but we went up to the tempels itself! Nice, real and not busy. For the ladies; Dress correct.

The "caves" are interesting, the painted ceiling is the best feature of this site, the white painted facade, the picture you see on all the ads is far better than the inside, a lot of steps to climb in the heat just to be disappointed!  Defiantly not worth the money, the golden Buddha at the temple is billed as the biggest in the world!  It's not even the biggest in Sri Lanka

Dambulla Cave Temple or the Golden Cave Temple is a beautiful site. The temple is ideal for people interested in history/ancient paintings and statues. Though the guides and vendors can be really pushy, so be prepared to be rude to them. The view from the temple is fantastic. Only thing to avoid is going during the afternoon. The rock gets very hot and we were literally toasted hiking up right in the sun. And carry frozen water bottles for your own good!

Long hike up (but not compared to Sigiriya!) but well worth the effort. Old and atmospheric caves with fascinating statues and paintings. you could feel the age of some of them and kids felt like they were in an Indiana Jones film :-). Golden Buddha at the entrance impressive, but the museum so-so.

There are five caves (shrine rooms) in Dambulla temple. All of these caves arc full of statues of Buddha and various personages of the Buddhist Order or History. There are 150 Buddha images in these caves. Cave No. 5 (the last in order) has no historical value as it was done in the second decade of this century. All of the other caves contain statues and paintings representing various epochs of Sinhalese sculpture and painting.The early paintings of Dambulla are believed by some to belong to the 8th century A. C. But this cannot be proved at all because of over painting. Nevertheless this place is a mine of decorative designs, the patterns of which resemble those of Sigiriya. To a student of the history of Buddhism a careful study of the paintings of Dambulla provides a good deal of source material. It is generally accepted that the classical school of Sinhalese painting ceased to exist after the fall of the Polonnaruve kingdom at the end of the twelfth century. There are no extant examples of this style after the 13th century. It is from the 17th and 18th centuries that we have, once again, examples of the work of a school of indigenous painters. This new school does not seem to have had its roots in the artistic traditions which created the masterpieces of Sigiriya and Polonnaruva. Its style is purely two dimensional; in compositions it does not exhibit the skill of the masters of earlier epochs. In its conventions, particularly in the decorative designs and in the representation of trees and creepers, it does not seem to have any connection with the earlier art of the Island. This School seems to have been influenced by the Schools of painting which flourished in the Deccan (Southern India) under the patronage of Muslim rulers. The frescoes which adorn the cave of Dambulla represent this new school of Sinhalese painting, Inside the cases of this temple the whole surface of the rock is completely covered with paintings, The earliest phase is believed to be on Cave No. 2, and these consist of decorative designs as surmised above, it is not possible to identify any one of these as actually belonging to a very much earlier period. Nevertheless, the designs themselves show close affinity to Sigiriya ceiling ornamentation. There may have been old painting at this place but perhaps these are lost or have been painted over later. It can be surmised that the designs of the decorative patterns, embody ancient ideas and may even be considered as continuing tradition of the designs at Sigiriya. But as the Dambullu Tudapata referred to above clearly reveals cave No. 1, 2 and 4 of Dambulla were painted by the Kandyan artists of the seventeenth century by the order of king Senarat (1604-1635 A.C). In the reign of Kirti Sri Rajasinha, the paintings of Dambulla were renovated and over painted again. Paintings in Cave No. 4 clearly represent the new school of Sinhalese painting which flourished in the Kandyan provinces after the 17th century.

This was possibly my favourite site in Sri Lanka, although less imposing than Sigiriya, and less significant than other cultural triangle sites. The way the temples are built into this dramatic rock face, high above the surrounding plain, makes it a stunning place to look at. The many cave rooms are packed with buddhas and the cave ceilings painted intricately. But it was the sense of peace and other-worldliness that made it really special. We went at the end of the day, around 4pm, as the clouds rolled in, and that made it much cooler to climb the steps up to the temple, and easier on bare feet as you walk around the temple complex. In fact, had we visited in the intense heat of the day, I don't think we would have lasted long - bare feet on the burning paving stones would have been too much for us. (this was a real problem at Polunnaruwa, for example). The climb up to the temple is no problem really - our 8 year old bounded up and the 4 year old did fine too - but beware: the ticket office is at the bottom, and isn't that easy to spot. The temple wasn't overrun by tourists either - possibly because it was late in the day, which made it easier to enjoy the peace and tranquility of the site. It's a short tuk-tuk ride from the centre of Dambulla where we were staying, and it took us about 1.5 - 2 hours in total.

The Dumbulla Cave Temples are by far one of the best preserved of the ancient Cave Temples in Sri Lanka. When you enter the temple complex at the base of the giant rock/ hill it all looks very commercialized and yes over the past 10 years or so, with all of the funding from various entities and china the temple authorities have started to diverge from the actual philosophy of Buddhism. However, what you are here to see is not at the bottom of the hill but at the top of the rock. You need to climb about 20-30 minutes up this huge Granite monolith and I would advise getting there early. The rock absorbs and radiates heat and by mid day climbing up what looks like a short distance can be very tiring. When you finally reach the ancient temple at the top you will be confronted by an atmosphere, that despite all the people feels tranquil. The stars of this temple are all of the fantastically preserved cave paintings and Buddha statues. What will confront you is difficult to describe and even the photographs I have added here do not do the location justice. My advice is not to miss this if you are in Sri Lanka and definitely if you are in the Sigiriya area. The management of this temple has changed dramatically over the past 10-20 years and not for the best in my opinion so go to see this, before the red tape and greed for money take over all of the true Buddhist influence left here. There is an entrance fee and you can buy tickets at the base of the hill where you enter the complex (well sign posted) and this includes entrance to a museum (which I skipped as I'm not a fan of what these money spinners have done to the place) - but you should have a look. Also as you walk up you will find many people selling drinks and snacks to help as the short climb is steep and strenuous (be warned).

The caves are situated next to a gargantuan hideous golden seated Buddha and accompanying 'museum' with life size mannequins of monks.  Looks bit like a cheap adventure playground.  We did not go in... Once you have bought tickets to the caves, you climb a reasonably steep path for about 10 minutes.  Shoes taken off outside the gates (another fee please!).  I suggest you start at the far end and work backwards as they get grander.  The buddha statues are nice but it is really the mural paintings which caught my attention.  Very beautiful and the repetitive nature added to their beauty.  A torch would be useful although the lighting is reasonable.  Not sure why flash photography is allowed - I suggest UNESCO investigate - I did not use flash. The caves are lovely but once again a bitter taste is left in your mouth for the extortionate fees which you have to pay (for a similar fee, in India you get entry to the Taj Mahal while for the far grander Ajanta caves, entry is a third of what you pay at Dambulla).

To me one of the 3 top attraction in Sri Lanka. Outstanding place has to be done no matter what.

The temples are a unique and important historical site because of the mix of age as well as style of the statues and paintings.
